result.text: ChronoR addresses temporal link prediction on temporal knowledge graphs, a challenging problem due to non-stationary, heterogeneous data and complex temporal dependencies. Its key insight is to model relation- and time-conditioned interactions as k-dimensional rotations so that applying a learned rotation to a head-entity embedding moves it close to the corresponding tail embedding, thereby naturally encoding temporal and multi-relational dynamics. The method jointly learns dense embeddings for entities, relations, and time and parameterizes a rotation operator in high-dimensional space for each (relation, time) pair; training minimizes distance between rotated heads and tails so the model captures rich temporal–relational interactions and outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on benchmark temporal KG link prediction tasks.

The paper tackles efficient, symmetry-preserving prediction of quantum Hamiltonian matrices for molecular systems, where maintaining SE(3) equivariance typically conflicts with computational and memory efficiency. The key insight is an architectural design that enforces SE(3)-equivariance while drastically reducing costly tensor-product operations and preventing exponential channel growth as atom types increase. The authors propose QHNet, an SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network that restructures equivariant message passing to cut tensor products by 92%, streamlines channels to limit dimensional blowup, and uses this lightweight equivariant circuitry to predict Hamiltonian entries. On four MD17 molecular datasets QHNet matches state-of-the-art accuracy with much faster runtimes and about 50% lower memory consumption.

The paper tackles the problem of choosing layerwise sparsity for magnitude-based neural network pruning, where prior work relies on heuristics or costly hyperparameter searches and performance depends critically on per-layer sparsity allocation. Their key insight is that pruning decisions should account for each layer’s contribution to the model-level ℓ2 distortion, so weight magnitudes can be rescaled into an importance score that reflects the global impact of removing parameters. They propose LAMP (layer-adaptive magnitude-based pruning), a simple, hyperparameter-free scoring scheme that rescales magnitudes by layer-level statistics to produce layerwise sparsities for global pruning, and show empirically on image classification tasks (including weight-rewinding setups) that LAMP consistently outperforms popular baselines. The method is lightweight to compute and requires no expensive tuning while yielding better sparsity–performance tradeoffs than existing layerwise allocation strategies.

The paper addresses the challenge of designing practical, high-performing active learning algorithms that work with deep neural networks by revisiting Fisher-information–based selection objectives. Its key insight is that bounds on maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) error expressed via the Fisher information can guide selection of informative batches, and that this classic criterion can be made tractable and efficient for neural models by exploiting linear-algebraic structure. The authors propose BAIT, an algorithm that selects batches by optimizing a Fisher-information–based bound on MLE error and implements this optimization with scalable matrix computations suited to modern hardware. Empirically, BAIT consistently outperforms prior active learning methods on both classification and regression tasks and is adaptable to different model architectures.

The paper tackles the problem of making neural architecture search (NAS) fast and broadly applicable to diverse, under-explored domains beyond computer vision, where AutoML could have the most impact. The key insight is that fixing a standard CNN topology but searching only over operation choices—specifically kernel sizes and dilations—gives rich multi-resolution feature extraction while dramatically reducing the search space, and that leveraging the Fourier diagonalization of convolution lets one efficiently compute mixtures of these operations. Building on this, the authors propose DASH, a differentiable NAS algorithm that uses Fourier-based diagonalization to perform weight-sharing over operation mixtures with improved asymptotic complexity, yielding up to 10× faster search in practice; they evaluate DASH on ten varied tasks (e.g., PDE solving, protein folding, heart disease detection) and show it outperforms state-of-the-art AutoML on most tasks while keeping search-plus-retraining overhead low (often under 2× the training time of a baseline CNN).

The paper addresses the slow and memory-intensive training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for large-scale scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis. Its key insight is that scene decomposition combined with a distributed consensus optimization—specifically using ADMM—lets multiple local 3DGS models cooperate to learn a single high-quality global model while reducing per-node load and improving convergence stability. Methodologically, DOGS splits a scene into K spatial blocks, runs K local 3DGS trainings on slave nodes that periodically enforce consensus on shared Gaussian parameters with a global model on the master via ADMM, discards the local models after training, and uses only the global model for inference; this yields over 6× faster training on large scenes while maintaining or improving rendering quality.

The paper tackles the tension in offline reinforcement learning between conservatism—necessary to avoid overestimation under distribution shift—and robustness to observation deviations (e.g., sensor noise or adversarial perturbations), which excessive conservatism can undermine. The key insight is that introducing a conservative smoothing regularizer that enforces consistency and lowered value estimates not only at dataset states but also for nearby perturbed states can simultaneously preserve safety under distribution shift and improve robustness to observation errors. Methodologically, RORL augments standard offline RL by applying regularization on both the policy and value function for states in a neighborhood around dataset states, coupled with conservative value estimation for those neighborhoods; the authors provide tighter suboptimality bounds in linear MDPs and empirically show improved benchmark performance and resilience to adversarial observation perturbations.

result.text: The paper tackles fast, high-quality photo-realistic free-viewpoint rendering from posed RGB images without 3D supervision, addressing blurriness and slow ray marching in prior neural implicit approaches. Its key insight is to combine learned local implicit fields with an explicit sparse voxel octree so that geometry and appearance are modeled per voxel, enabling pruning of empty space and more accurate ray-geometry intersections. The method progressively learns the sparse voxel structure and per-voxel neural fields via differentiable ray marching from images, yielding over an order-of-magnitude faster inference than NeRF while improving visual quality, and enabling practical scene editing, composition, multi-scene and dynamic/large-scale rendering.

result.text: The paper tackles offline reinforcement learning where standard off-policy methods fail due to extrapolation error from out-of-distribution (OOD) actions in a fixed dataset. Its key insight is that explicit policy constraints are unnecessary if one can quantify epistemic uncertainty and perform pessimistic value updates: penalizing Q-values where uncertainty is high prevents overestimation on OOD actions while still permitting generalization. The method, Pessimistic Bootstrapping for RL (PBRL), estimates uncertainty via disagreement among an ensemble of bootstrapped Q-functions, applies a pessimistic penalty proportional to that disagreement during value updates, and supplements this with a novel OOD sampling scheme; the authors prove that this combination yields a valid uncertainty quantifier in linear MDPs and empirically outperforms prior offline RL methods on D4RL benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed/federated optimization by unifying two previously separate approaches for gradient compression—variance-reduced unbiased compressors (DIANA) and error-feedback for biased contractive compressors (EF21)—into a single framework that can handle both. The key insight is that compressors can be characterized by two parameters (bias and variance), and by designing an algorithm that exploits both error feedback and variance-reduction ideas one can recover DIANA and EF21 as special cases while enabling a broader class of compressors. The proposed method introduces a new algorithm (EF-BV) that operates with this generalized compressor class, combines independent randomness across workers with an error-correction mechanism, and leverages variance reduction to improve convergence as the number of workers grows. The authors prove linear convergence under suitable conditions, showing that EF-BV inherits the practical benefits of biased compressors like top-k and the theoretical scaling advantages of randomized unbiased schemes.

result.text: The paper addresses the quadratic memory and compute bottleneck of standard Transformer attention that prevents scaling to long sequences. Its key insight is that a carefully designed sparse attention pattern—combining local sliding windows, random global connections, and a small set of global tokens—retains the representational power of full attention (universal approximation and Turing completeness) while reducing complexity from quadratic to linear. The method, BigBird, implements this sparse attention in a Transformer architecture, proves theoretical guarantees about expressivity, and empirically demonstrates the ability to process sequences up to eight times longer than prior models on the same hardware, yielding large gains on long-context NLP tasks (e.g., QA, summarization) and enabling applications like genomics.

result.text: The paper tackles catastrophic overfitting in single-step adversarial training, a sudden collapse where models become vulnerable to multi-step attacks (PGD) despite appearing robust to single-step attacks (FGSM). The key insight is that using only maximal-perturbation single-step examples concentrates training on boundary points and ignores the continuum of adversarial directions, which distorts the decision boundary and creates a highly curved loss surface that single-step updates cannot reliably defend. The authors analyze this mechanism and propose a simple remedy—augmenting or modifying single-step training to include non-maximal or diversified adversarial examples (thereby sampling the adversarial direction more broadly) to regularize curvature and preserve robustness—showing this prevents catastrophic overfitting and enables single-step procedures to resist multi-step attacks.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of completing temporal knowledge graphs by predicting missing future facts, noting that many relations exhibit repeated patterns over time that standard time-aware embedding methods do not explicitly exploit. The key insight is that temporal prediction can be improved by combining generation from the global entity vocabulary with a time-aware copying mechanism that directly references historically observed facts when repetition is likely. The authors introduce CyGNet, a sequential copy-generation network that models entity and time dynamics and learns a switching mechanism to either copy past fact objects (when repetition is detected) or generate new objects from the full vocabulary, and they evaluate it on five benchmarks showing improved performance on both repetitive and novel fact prediction.

result.text: The paper tackles the limited data efficiency and expressivity of graph neural networks for predicting molecular and tensorial properties, which arises in part from using rotation-invariant representations that discard directional information. Its key insight is that enforcing rotational equivariance in message passing—so node features transform appropriately under rotations—retains essential geometric information and boosts learning efficiency and accuracy while allowing compact models. The authors introduce PaiNN, a polarizable atom interaction neural network that uses equivariant atom-wise features and equivariant message and update functions to predict scalar and tensorial quantities, demonstrating improved benchmark performance, smaller/faster models, and leveraging the learned representations to predict tensor properties and molecular spectra. Applied to spectrum simulation, PaiNN achieves 4–5 orders of magnitude speedup over electronic structure calculations while maintaining accuracy.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of producing high-performing sparse neural networks in a single training run to enable deployment on resource-constrained devices without the extra cost of post-hoc retraining. Its key insight is that allowing the sparsity pattern to change dynamically during training and using a feedback mechanism to reactivate weights that were pruned prematurely prevents irreversible loss of useful parameters and yields better final models. The proposed method integrates dynamic allocation of which weights are kept or dropped with a feedback signal that can revive trimmed weights, producing a sparse trained model in one pass (with optional further retraining) and demonstrating on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet that these models match dense baselines and outperform prior pruning schemes lacking feedback.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between the likelihoods produced by diffusion ODEs (probability flow ODEs of diffusion models) and those of leading likelihood-based generative models, aiming to improve maximum likelihood estimation for deterministic diffusion-based flows. The key insight is that reparameterizing the vector field (velocity parameterization), reducing variance during training, applying a high-order flow matching fine-tuning objective with error bounds, and using a training-free truncated-normal dequantization at evaluation can jointly close the training–evaluation gap and produce smoother, more accurate ODE trajectories. Methodologically, the authors introduce velocity parameterization and variance-reduction strategies to accelerate and stabilize training, derive an error-bounded high-order flow matching loss for finetuning the learned ODE, and propose truncated-normal dequantization for evaluation without retraining; combined, these techniques yield state-of-the-art likelihoods on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 without variational dequantization or augmentation.

The paper tackles AutoML’s challenge of automatically finding appropriate neural operations for novel, diverse domains by enabling users to discover task-specific inductive biases from data. Its key insight is that a broad, expressive class of operations—XD-Operations—can mimic the beneficial inductive biases of standard multi-channel convolutions while subsuming many existing, domain-specific operators, so searching this space can adapt architectures to varied tasks. Methodologically, the authors define a transformation that converts a conventional backbone (e.g., ResNet) into a search space over XD-Operations and traverse it with a simple weight-sharing search scheme, demonstrating across PDE solving, protein folding distance prediction, and music modeling that architectures found in the XD-Operations space yield consistently lower errors than baseline networks and often outperform expert-designed domain-specific models.

result.text: The paper addresses why standard multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) struggle to learn high-frequency functions in low-dimensional regression tasks common in vision and graphics, limiting their ability to represent detailed 3D geometry and signals. The key insight is that MLPs exhibit a spectral bias—favoring low-frequency components—because their effective kernel (via the neural tangent kernel) lacks high-frequency sensitivity, but this can be remedied by preprocessing inputs with a random Fourier feature mapping that converts the NTK into a stationary kernel with controllable bandwidth. The method is to apply a simple Fourier feature transform to input coordinates before feeding them to an MLP, choose the feature scale to match task-specific frequency content, and thereby enable the network to learn and represent high-frequency detail; empirical results and NTK analysis demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of offline reinforcement learning with learned dynamics models, where existing model-based approaches require explicit uncertainty estimates—difficult to obtain with complex function approximators—to safely plan under model bias. The key insight is that pessimism can be achieved by directly regularizing the value function on out-of-support state-action pairs produced by model rollouts, yielding conservative value estimates without any explicit uncertainty quantification. COMBO implements this by learning a dynamics model from logged data, generating synthetic rollouts, and applying a conservative penalty that lowers value estimates for out-of-distribution tuples so the policy optimization maximizes a provable lower bound on true policy value; the authors prove this bound is tighter than prior bounds and empirically demonstrate strong performance on standard and image-based offline RL benchmarks.

The key insight is that maintaining the best online approximation of the past under a chosen importance measure can be cast as projecting the signal onto an evolving polynomial basis (HiPPO), which yields optimal continuous-time updates and subsumes prior architectures like the LMU and gating mechanisms. Methodologically, HiPPO derives closed-form recurrent update rules for coefficients of these polynomial projections (with a particularly effective variant HiPPO-LegS based on scaled Legendre polynomials) and integrates them as memory dynamics in RNNs, giving provable timescale robustness, bounded gradients, and empirical gains on tasks including permuted MNIST and out‑of‑distribution temporal generalization.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of reliably estimating confidence for large language model (LLM) predictions, noting that many LLMs are poorly calibrated and resist standard post-hoc calibration techniques. Its key insight is that calibration can be derived from the model’s own behavior by measuring consistency across multiple stochastic generations: agreement among sampled answers serves as a proxy for true confidence. The authors propose three consistency-based measures computed from random generations, evaluate them across eleven models (open and closed) and nine reasoning datasets, and show these measures reduce calibration error compared to prior approaches; they also find that factors like intermediate explanations, model scale, and larger sample sizes improve calibration while instruction-tuning hinders it, and that consistency-derived confidence can even boost downstream performance, with practical guidance on picking metrics based on model traits such as instruction-tuning and RLHF exposure.

The paper addresses the gap between score-matching objectives used to train score-based generative models and the true maximum likelihood objective for the associated score-based diffusion ODEs, showing that matching only first-order scores does not guarantee optimal ODE likelihood. The key insight is that the ODE negative log-likelihood can be controlled by bounding not just the first-order score error but also second- and third-order score errors, so high-order score matching is necessary to close the gap between score-matching and maximum likelihood. The authors derive bounds linking ODE likelihood to first–third order score-matching errors and propose a practical high-order denoising score matching algorithm that enforces these higher-order constraints (with guarantees that higher-order errors are controlled by training error and lower-order errors), and they demonstrate empirically improved likelihood on synthetic data and CIFAR-10 while preserving sample quality.

result.text: The paper addresses making second-order (Newton-type) optimization practical for federated learning by overcoming privacy, model-class, and communication-compression challenges that have limited prior Hessian-based approaches. The key insight is a novel communication-efficient Hessian-learning scheme that does not reveal training data to the server, works beyond generalized linear models, and is compatible with general contractive compressors (e.g., Top-K, Rank-R) without requiring error feedback, yielding Hessian estimates that converge to the true Hessian at the optimum with rates independent of condition number, dataset size, and compression variance. Methodologically, the authors introduce the FedNL family—core FedNL plus variants supporting partial participation (FedNL-PP), globalization via cubic regularization or line search (FedNL-CR, FedNL-LS), and bidirectional compression (FedNL-BC)—and prove local convergence guarantees while empirically demonstrating state-of-the-art communication efficiency versus baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses whether sparse transformer attention—designed to reduce the quadratic O(n^2) pairwise attention cost—can retain the universal approximation power of dense transformers and how sparsity pattern and level affect expressivity. The key insight is that surprisingly few connections suffice: under simple sufficient conditions on the sparsity graph, attention layers with only O(n) nonzero connections per layer can still approximate any sequence-to-sequence function that a dense transformer can. The authors formalize a unifying framework capturing many existing sparse attention schemes, prove universality results for families of sparsity patterns (identifying the connectivity properties required), and construct architectures and proofs showing O(n)-connected layers achieve the same function class as dense attention. They validate these theoretical findings with experiments comparing different sparsity patterns and levels on standard NLP tasks, illustrating practical tradeoffs between efficiency and performance.

The paper addresses the problem of reliably estimating confidence for large language model (LLM) predictions, noting that many LLMs are poorly calibrated and resist standard post-hoc calibration techniques. Its key insight is that calibration can be derived from the model’s own behavior by measuring consistency across multiple stochastic generations: agreement among sampled answers serves as a proxy for true confidence. The authors propose three consistency-based measures computed from random generations, evaluate them across eleven models (open and closed) and nine reasoning datasets, and show these measures reduce calibration error compared to prior approaches; they also find that factors like intermediate explanations, model scale, and larger sample sizes improve calibration while instruction-tuning hinders it, and that consistency-derived confidence can even boost downstream performance, with practical guidance on picking metrics based on model traits such as instruction-tuning and RLHF exposure.

The paper addresses the complexity and fragmented design choices in diffusion-based generative models that obscure which components truly drive sample quality and efficiency. Methodologically, the authors formalize this design space, identify and apply specific improvements to sampling algorithms, training objectives, and network preconditioning, and demonstrate their modular benefits by retrofitting prior pretrained score networks and retraining models to achieve state-of-the-art FIDs (e.g., CIFAR-10 unconditional and class-conditional) with far fewer network evaluations.

result.text: The paper tackles improving online knowledge distillation, which traditionally transfers only class probabilities between simultaneously trained networks and thus overlooks rich spatial and intensity cues in feature maps. The key insight is that adversarial learning can transfer feature-map-level knowledge more effectively than direct alignment losses (e.g., L1) by matching feature distribution rather than forcing pixelwise correspondence. The method trains multiple networks jointly with per-network discriminators that treat the network’s own feature maps as fake and others’ as real, so each network is trained to fool its discriminator and thereby learn the feature distribution of its peers, and introduces a cyclic learning scheme to scale this to more than two networks. Experiments on classification across architectures show substantial performance gains, particularly when pairing small and large networks.

The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed/federated optimization by unifying two previously separate approaches for gradient compression—variance-reduced unbiased compressors (DIANA) and error-feedback for biased contractive compressors (EF21)—into a single framework that can handle both. The key insight is that compressors can be characterized by two parameters (bias and variance), and by designing an algorithm that exploits both error feedback and variance-reduction ideas one can recover DIANA and EF21 as special cases while enabling a broader class of compressors. The proposed method introduces a new algorithm (EF-BV) that operates with this generalized compressor class, combines independent randomness across workers with an error-correction mechanism, and leverages variance reduction to improve convergence as the number of workers grows. The authors prove linear convergence under suitable conditions, showing that EF-BV inherits the practical benefits of biased compressors like top-k and the theoretical scaling advantages of randomized unbiased schemes.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of choosing and hand-designing structured linear transformations (e.g., low-rank, sparse, permutation, Fourier) in neural networks, which requires costly trade-offs between speed, memory, and accuracy. The key insight is that a single, richly expressive family of matrices—kaleidoscope matrices (K-matrices)—can provably approximate any commonly used structured linear map with near-optimal parameter and arithmetic complexity, enabling a learnable universal substitute for many hand-crafted transformations. Methodologically, the authors define the K-matrix family, prove its representational and complexity guarantees, implement a practical and efficient layer, and empirically validate end-to-end learning of K-matrices to replace channel shuffles, filter-bank preprocessing, and latent permutations, as well as to accelerate Transformers, showing substantial accuracy gains or speedups across ImageNet, TIMIT, permuted image classification, and machine translation.

result.text: The paper tackles the computational cost of adversarial training, challenging the belief that strong iterative adversaries like PGD are necessary to learn robust deep networks. result.text: The paper tackles gloss-to-pose (G2P) translation within Sign Language Production, converting gloss sequences into continuous sign pose sequences, a task challenged by the continuous, variable-length, and spatial-temporal nature of pose data. Its key insight is to recast continuous pose generation as a discrete sequence modeling problem by learning a compact, quantized latent codebook for poses and then modeling that discrete prior with a diffusion-based denoising process suited to variable-length sequences. Methodologically, they introduce Pose-VQVAE to encode continuous pose sequences into discrete latent codes, propose G2P-DDM—a discrete denoising diffusion model that generates length-varied discrete sequences—and augment generation quality with CodeUnet to capture spatial-temporal dependencies plus a heuristic sequential clustering scheme to predict sequence lengths; combined, these components yield state-of-the-art G2P performance on a public SLP benchmark.

The paper tackles improving sample quality and likelihood of diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) when generating with a limited subset of timesteps by addressing how to choose the model covariance given that the model mean is imperfect. The key insight is that the optimal diagonal or full covariance for a DPM can be expressed in closed form but must be corrected when the mean estimate is biased; both the optimal and corrected covariances decompose into conditional expectations over functions of the latent noise, which can be learned. They therefore propose to estimate these conditional expectations via neural networks (implementing the diagonal case for efficiency) with parameter sharing and a two-stage training procedure, yielding improved likelihoods and notably better sample quality in few-step generation across discrete and continuous timesteps.

args.text: We propose MaskDiff: a discrete diffusion prior for one-shot, layer-conditioned sparsity mask synthesis. Treat each layer’s binary pruning mask as a discrete sequence and train a denoising diffusion model with a VQ-style codebook of local mask patterns, conditioned on layer metadata and a target budget, so variable-length handling maps to predicting per-layer keep counts. We bootstrap supervision from high-performing masks produced by L2-distortion-aware LAMP and movement-based criteria, and incorporate a dynamic-sparse feedback phase that intermittently reactivates tokens; at inference, optional guidance from L2 distortion and movement scores steers sampling toward higher-utility masks. This unifies allocation and structure search into a lightweight generator that yields diverse, budget-compliant masks in a single pass, enabling rapid cross-architecture transfer and potentially matching iterative pruning without costly hyperparameter sweeps.

args.text: RegimeSwitchTKG is a regime-switching forecasting model that disentangles periodic, trend, and shock dynamics in temporal knowledge graphs. It parameterizes a mixture-of-operators over entity embeddings—periodic components use time-conditioned rotations, trend components use smooth time translations, and a sparse copy head reuses historically observed facts—while a contrastively trained gate decides when predictions should be history-driven versus exogenous. To handle non-historical regimes and ensure inductive generalization, the model augments the mixture with an interpretable temporal-rule scorer that injects time-consistent logical evidence and with learnable “shock” pseudo-entities attended during exogenous regimes. Joint training aligns regime decisions, operator outputs, and rule scores via multi-view contrastive losses and yields calibrated, explainable forecasts.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between the community standard of "adaptive attacks" for evaluating adversarial defenses and the reality that many such evaluations are incomplete, leaving purported defenses vulnerable. Its key insight is that failures to fully adapt attacks often stem from methodological oversights—such as not modeling the defense's transformations, gradient masking, randomized or non-differentiable components, or incorrect threat models—rather than from genuine robustness, so systematically constructing stronger adaptive strategies can break many published defenses. The authors analyze thirteen recent defenses and distill practical techniques (e.g., white-box modeling of all defense components, gradient estimation or proxy gradients for non-differentiable parts, expectation over transformation for randomness, careful loss/attack selection, and verification-style checks) to craft complete adaptive attacks, demonstrating how to modify attacks to account for each defense’s specifics. Their method is less a single algorithm than a prescriptive evaluation methodology for designing and documenting adaptive attacks so defenses are tested against the strongest feasible adversary.

result.text: FetchSGD addresses the dual challenges in federated learning of heavy communication costs and degraded convergence when client participation is sparse. The key insight is to use a linear, mergeable Count Sketch to compress client model updates so that momentum and error accumulation can be maintained centrally inside the sketch rather than on each client, which preserves state across intermittent clients and enables high compression without losing critical optimization history. Concretely, each client sketches its local gradient/update with a Count Sketch, the server merges these sketches to form an aggregate sketch, performs momentum and error correction in sketch space, and reconstructs sparse updates for model updates; the authors prove convergence guarantees for this procedure and validate it empirically on ResNets and a transformer showing strong communication savings and robust convergence.

The paper studies open-set recognition (OSR), i.e., deciding when a test sample does not belong to any training class, and shows that this capability is strongly correlated with a classifier’s closed-set accuracy across losses, architectures, benchmarks and large-scale ImageNet. The key insight is that improving closed-set classification quality alone substantially improves open-set “none-of-above” decisions, so sophisticated OSR-specific tricks add little beyond what a better classifier already provides. Methodologically, the authors take a simple maximum-logit scoring baseline and boost its closed-set accuracy (via standard training improvements) to achieve state-of-the-art OSR performance, apply the same idea to enhance a prior SOTA method (narrowing the gap), and introduce the Semantic Shift Benchmark that focuses evaluation on true semantic novelty to show the marginal difference between the strong baseline and prior art.

This paper addresses learning mappings (operators) between infinite-dimensional function spaces, specifically for predicting solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) from input functions, in a way that generalizes across different discretizations and resolutions. The key insight is that a single neural architecture parameterized once can represent such operators by composing nonlinear activations with integral operators whose kernels are implemented via graph-based message-passing, enabling discretization-invariant learning. The method, called a Neural Operator or graph kernel network, approximates the integral kernel by graph convolution/message-passing on a mesh or point cloud, stacks these integral layers with nonlinearities to form an operator network, and trains the shared kernel parameters so the same model generalizes across finite-difference, finite-element, and varying-resolution discretizations. Experiments on PDE tasks demonstrate that this approach achieves the desired resolution and method invariance while matching or improving on state-of-the-art solvers.

result.text: Multiviz addresses the challenge of interpreting black‑box multimodal models by proposing a practical, stagewise framework to visualize how different modalities contribute to and interact within a model’s reasoning. Its key insight is that interpretability can be decomposed into four complementary stages—unimodal importance, cross‑modal interactions, multimodal representations, and multimodal prediction—which together reveal how modalities individually influence outputs, how they relate to one another, how those relations are encoded as decision‑level features, and how those features are composed into final predictions. The method implements a suite of analysis tools that operate across diverse modalities, models, and tasks to quantify per‑modality contributions, expose cross‑modal dependencies, map concepts to internal features, and enable simulation and error analysis; experiments on eight models across six real‑world tasks demonstrate that MultiViz helps users simulate predictions, assign interpretable concepts, diagnose misclassifications, and guide model debugging.

The paper tackles the challenge of offline reinforcement learning where standard off-policy methods overestimate action values due to distributional shift between a static dataset and the learned policy, causing poor performance especially on complex, multi-modal data. The key insight is to learn a conservative Q-function that intentionally underestimates values for out-of-distribution actions so that the Q-estimate lower-bounds the true policy value, preventing spurious optimistic updates. Methodologically, Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) adds a simple Q-value regularizer to the Bellman error objective that penalizes Q-values of actions sampled from a broad set (e.g., policy and dataset actions) while preserving accuracy on dataset actions; this regularizer can be implemented on top of existing deep Q-learning or actor-critic algorithms and is shown theoretically to produce a value lower bound and empirically to yield substantially better returns across discrete and continuous benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed/federated optimization by unifying two previously separate approaches for gradient compression—variance-reduced unbiased compressors (DIANA) and error-feedback for biased contractive compressors (EF21)—into a single framework that can handle both. The key insight is that compressors can be characterized by two parameters (bias and variance), and by designing an algorithm that exploits both error feedback and variance-reduction ideas one can recover DIANA and EF21 as special cases while enabling a broader class of compressors. The proposed method introduces a new algorithm (EF-BV) that operates with this generalized compressor class, combines independent randomness across workers with an error-correction mechanism, and leverages variance reduction to improve convergence as the number of workers grows. The authors prove linear convergence under suitable conditions, showing that EF-BV inherits the practical benefits of biased compressors like top-k and the theoretical scaling advantages of randomized unbiased schemes.

result.text: The paper tackles data sparsity in multi-criteria (3D user-item-criterion) recommender systems by integrating side information and cross-domain knowledge into tensor decomposition. The key insight is that combining Tucker tensor decomposition with deep neural encoders for side information, constrained to be orthogonal and denoising, yields more stable, comparable latent factors while a shared core tensor (with cross-domain alignment) transfers knowledge across domains. The method, Deep Transfer Tensor Decomposition (DTTD), links per-mode latent factors from Tucker decomposition to orthogonal constrained stacked denoising autoencoders (OC-SDAEs) that learn robust user/item embeddings from side data, uses a common core tensor to bridge domains, and applies a cross-domain alignment algorithm to resolve rotation mismatches between source and target core tensors. Empirical results demonstrate that DTTD achieves better recommendation accuracy than state-of-the-art baselines.

ChronoR addresses temporal link prediction on temporal knowledge graphs, a challenging problem due to non-stationary, heterogeneous data and complex temporal dependencies. Its key insight is to model relation- and time-conditioned interactions as k-dimensional rotations so that applying a learned rotation to a head-entity embedding moves it close to the corresponding tail embedding, thereby naturally encoding temporal and multi-relational dynamics. The method jointly learns dense embeddings for entities, relations, and time and parameterizes a rotation operator in high-dimensional space for each (relation, time) pair; training minimizes distance between rotated heads and tails so the model captures rich temporal–relational interactions and outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on benchmark temporal KG link prediction tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses molecular conformation generation—predicting stable 3D atomic coordinates from 2D molecular graphs—where prior methods first predict interatomic distances and then reconstruct coordinates, a pipeline that compounds errors from noisy distance predictions. The key insight is to bypass explicit distance-to-coordinate reconstruction by directly learning the gradient field of the log density (the score) of atomic coordinates, which lets one sample stable conformations via Langevin dynamics; to handle the roto-translation equivariance of coordinate scores, the authors show this is equivalent to estimating score fields over interatomic distances. The method, ConfGF, adapts score-based generative modeling to estimate these distance-based gradient fields and then integrates them to produce coordinate samples using equivariant Langevin dynamics, yielding significantly improved performance over prior state-of-the-art models across multiple benchmarks.

args.text: Active high-order diffusion training: use a Fisher-information–guided curriculum over (data, time) pairs to directly reduce the high-order score errors that bound ODE negative log-likelihood. Building on theory linking ODE likelihood to 2nd/3rd-order score errors, we define an acquisition score that estimates each example–time pair’s contribution to these errors via a Fisher kernel of the score network under velocity parameterization and flow-matching. We implement scalable batch selection with BAIT-style linear algebra using Jacobian- and Hessian-vector products from autodiff to target pairs with the largest estimated high-order error. This yields a training schedule that concentrates updates where they most tighten the likelihood bound, improving ODE likelihood and stability with fewer steps and complementing post-hoc high-order flow-matching finetuning.

result.text: The paper addresses continuous super-resolution of screen content images (SCIs), which differ from natural images and must be upscaled to arbitrary scales after aggressive downsampling and compression for bandwidth savings. The key insight is to treat SR as an implicit coordinate-to-pixel prediction problem where query pixel values can be inferred from learned feature "keys" via an implicit transformer that aggregates information from similar neighboring pixels using an implicit position encoding. The proposed Implicit Transformer Super-Resolution Network (ITSRN) extracts image features at key coordinates and uses the implicit transformer plus position encoding to produce high-quality continuous SR at arbitrary ratios. They validate ITSRN on newly constructed SCI1K and SCI1K-compression benchmarks, showing substantial improvements over existing continuous and discrete SR methods on both compressed and uncompressed SCIs.

args.text: Frequency-aware distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting: decompose each Gaussian’s parameters (position, covariance shape, color/opacity) into polynomial/Fourier subbands and run ADMM consensus on coefficient blocks with band-specific penalties and communication schedules. Low-frequency geometry bands synchronize frequently and globally to stabilize large-scale structure, while high-frequency detail/appearance bands synchronize sparsely and locally, reducing bandwidth and preventing over-smoothing; penalties adapt online using per-band variance/uncertainty. Practically, project per-Gaussian attributes into a Fourier/PNF basis, perform block-wise ADMM on shared-region coefficients, and recompose for rendering; this yields faster, more stable training on large scenes with 2–3× lower communication and improved fine-detail fidelity compared to uniform consensus. The approach leverages spectral decomposition for interpretability and control while preserving 3DGS efficiency.

result.text: The paper addresses modelling partially-observed, irregularly-sampled multivariate time series where standard neural ODEs are limited because trajectories are fixed by initial conditions and cannot be adjusted by later observations. The key insight is to replace autonomous neural ODEs with neural controlled differential equations (neural CDEs), which treat the observed time series as a control signal that continuously influences the hidden state, allowing the model to incorporate new information as it arrives. Methodologically, they parameterize the CDE vector field with neural networks, use an interpolation of discrete observations to form a continuous control path, and train the system end-to-end using memory-efficient adjoint-based backpropagation across observation times. Empirically and theoretically, neural CDEs achieve state-of-the-art performance on irregular time-series tasks, enjoy universal approximation guarantees, and generalize or subsume prior ODE-based sequence models.

result.text: The paper addresses the limited scope of existing neural architecture search (NAS) benchmarks, which focus on a few well-studied tasks (e.g., image classification) and thus leave open how NAS methods perform across broadly different domains. Its key insight is that evaluating NAS across a diverse set of tasks reveals robustness issues and can invalidate common conclusions drawn from narrow benchmarks, motivating a standard, diverse evaluation suite. The authors introduce NAS-Bench-360, a curated collection of ten tasks spanning varied domains, dataset sizes, dimensionalities, and objectives that remain compatible with CNN-based search spaces, and for two tasks provide precomputed performance for 15,625 architectures to enable fast, reproducible NAS experiments. Using this suite, they show that modern NAS methods often perform inconsistently and sometimes catastrophically on out-of-distribution tasks, demonstrating the need for more comprehensive benchmarking.

The paper tackles the problem of making generative image steganography practical and generic by satisfying security, capacity, and robustness simultaneously for both lossless and lossy channels. Its key insight is that provable security can be achieved by modulating secret bits in a way that preserves the input distribution to the generator, while robust and accurate recovery can be obtained via a learned extractor and optional attack-aware training. The method, StegaStyleGAN, introduces a Distribution-Preserving Secret Data Modulator (DP‑SDM) to embed secrets into generator inputs without altering their distribution, a Secret Data Extractor (SDE) to recover embedded data, and an Image Attack Simulator (IAS) used during training to produce two variants—StegaStyleGAN‑Ls for lossless channels and StegaStyleGAN‑Ly for lossy channels—with the same network architecture; it also supports conditional steganography via GAN inversion and empirically outperforms prior art.

The paper addresses how to provide differential privacy for linear sketches—compact, fast summaries used for frequency estimation, top-K, and distributional queries in streaming/turnstile models—so sensitive data can be protected without destroying utility. The key insight is that adding a small, carefully calibrated amount of randomness at sketch initialization (rather than per-update) suffices to achieve differential privacy while preserving the linearity and algorithmic guarantees of the sketches. Methodologically, the authors prove privacy and utility bounds for this initialization-noise approach, adapt it to make a leading turnstile quantile sketch private, and empirically validate that the differentially private sketches closely match the accuracy and qualitative behavior of nonprivate sketches on synthetic and real datasets.

result.text: The paper studies open-set recognition (OSR), i.e., deciding when a test sample does not belong to any training class, and shows that this capability is strongly correlated with a classifier’s closed-set accuracy across losses, architectures, benchmarks and large-scale ImageNet. The key insight is that improving closed-set classification quality alone substantially improves open-set “none-of-above” decisions, so sophisticated OSR-specific tricks add little beyond what a better classifier already provides. Methodologically, the authors take a simple maximum-logit scoring baseline and boost its closed-set accuracy (via standard training improvements) to achieve state-of-the-art OSR performance, apply the same idea to enhance a prior SOTA method (narrowing the gap), and introduce the Semantic Shift Benchmark that focuses evaluation on true semantic novelty to show the marginal difference between the strong baseline and prior art.

result.text: The paper addresses why standard multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) struggle to learn high-frequency functions in low-dimensional regression tasks common in vision and graphics, limiting their ability to represent detailed 3D geometry and signals. The key insight is that MLPs exhibit a spectral bias—favoring low-frequency components—because their effective kernel (via the neural tangent kernel) lacks high-frequency sensitivity, but this can be remedied by preprocessing inputs with a random Fourier feature mapping that converts the NTK into a stationary kernel with controllable bandwidth. The method is to apply a simple Fourier feature transform to input coordinates before feeding them to an MLP, choose the feature scale to match task-specific frequency content, and thereby enable the network to learn and represent high-frequency detail; empirical results and NTK analysis demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness.

result.text: The paper addresses estimation in binary logistic regression for rare-events (highly imbalanced) data, where informative cases are much fewer than controls. The key insight is that information and asymptotic variance scale with the number of events, not the total sample size, so subsampling controls can retain statistical efficiency while greatly reducing cost. The authors derive the asymptotic distribution of the MLE showing variance shrinks at the rate 1/(#events), prove that under-sampling a small fraction of nonevents can yield the same asymptotic distribution as the full-data MLE, and show that common practice of over-sampling (replicating) events can be computationally wasteful and may decrease estimation efficiency.

The paper tackles the tension in offline reinforcement learning between conservatism—necessary to avoid overestimation under distribution shift—and robustness to observation deviations (e.g., sensor noise or adversarial perturbations), which excessive conservatism can undermine. The key insight is that introducing a conservative smoothing regularizer that enforces consistency and lowered value estimates not only at dataset states but also for nearby perturbed states can simultaneously preserve safety under distribution shift and improve robustness to observation errors. Methodologically, RORL augments standard offline RL by applying regularization on both the policy and value function for states in a neighborhood around dataset states, coupled with conservative value estimation for those neighborhoods; the authors provide tighter suboptimality bounds in linear MDPs and empirically show improved benchmark performance and resilience to adversarial observation perturbations.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of finding hidden input parameters that produce desired observations in generic inverse problems and argues that inverse methods should be evaluated by how solution quality improves over time rather than by a single best guess. The key insight is that many deep-learning–based inverse methods act as stochastic samplers of the solution space, so benchmarking should treat them as time-dependent search processes and that combining a learned forward model with gradient-based search can exploit this viewpoint. Methodologically, the authors introduce time-to-solution benchmarking across four tasks (two prior benchmarks, one toy visualization, and a new metamaterial design task), compare state-of-the-art inverse models under this metric, and propose the “neural-adjoint” approach which trains a neural network surrogate of the forward process and then uses backpropagation through that surrogate to iteratively optimize inputs, demonstrating superior performance in several settings.

The paper investigates how Transformers perform in-context learning (ICL) for linear regression, challenging the view that they emulate Gradient Descent (GD) and asking whether they can realize faster, second-order optimization behavior. The key insight is that Transformer layers empirically and theoretically approximate Iterative Newton’s Method rather than GD, yielding exponentially faster convergence: successive layers' predictions linearly match Newton iterations (with each middle layer roughly implementing three Newton steps), enabling effective learning even on ill-conditioned data where GD fails. Methodologically, the authors combine empirical experiments comparing layer-wise outputs to Newton and GD trajectories and show faster convergence and robustness on challenging datasets, and they provide a constructive proof that a Transformer can implement k Newton iterations using k + O(1) layers, formalizing the capacity for second-order in-context optimization.

The paper studies how dataset features shape neural network decision boundaries by linking feature discriminativeness to sample distance from the boundary, using adversarial-robustness tools to probe boundary geometry. The key insight is that CNNs are highly invariant to non-discriminative features and that decision boundaries are sustained only by specific discriminative features present during training, so perturbing those features can collapse or reorient the boundary. Methodologically, the authors systematically tweak training samples along controlled feature directions and measure resulting shifts in boundary distance on large-scale vision datasets, revealing extreme sensitivity to small, directed perturbations and showing that inducing invariance in some directions (as in adversarial training) explains robustness.

args.text: We propose a regime-adaptive semi-parametric TKG forecaster that unifies temporal rule-guided retrieval with parametric time-conditioned embeddings to handle both recurrent patterns and shock-like, non-historical events. A time-indexed memory of past facts is augmented with TLogic-derived temporal rule closures to propose copy candidates, while a ChronoR-style rotation scorer evaluates all candidates to allow truly novel generation; a CENET-inspired gating head outputs candidate-wise history-reliance weights that interpolate between retrieval and parametric scores rather than a single global mask. Training uses contrastive supervision to align retrieval and parametric signals on history-driven queries and decouple them on non-historical ones, with an auxiliary distillation loss transferring rule evidence into the parametric scorer for better cold-start generalization. Compared to CyGNet’s switch, this fine-grained, rule-aware copy/generate mechanism improves OOD and shock robustness while retaining interpretability via explicit rule/rationale attributions.

Its key insight is that provable security can be achieved by modulating secret bits in a way that preserves the input distribution to the generator, while robust and accurate recovery can be obtained via a learned extractor and optional attack-aware training. The method, StegaStyleGAN, introduces a Distribution-Preserving Secret Data Modulator (DP‑SDM) to embed secrets into generator inputs without altering their distribution, a Secret Data Extractor (SDE) to recover embedded data, and an Image Attack Simulator (IAS) used during training to produce two variants—StegaStyleGAN‑Ls for lossless channels and StegaStyleGAN‑Ly for lossy channels—with the same network architecture; it also supports conditional steganography via GAN inversion and empirically outperforms prior art.

args.text: We propose Consistency-Aware Movement Pruning (CAMP), which uses agreement across multiple stochastic generations during fine-tuning as a supervisory signal to guide which weights to keep or drop. Concretely, we define a disagreement loss over K sampled outputs (e.g., pairwise disagreement or entropy of the answer distribution) and accumulate first-order scores for each weight based on how its updates reduce disagreement, akin to movement pruning but targeted at preserving the model’s self-consistency. To allocate sparsity across layers without costly tuning, we rescale these per-weight scores with LAMP-style layerwise normalization to derive a globally balanced pruning mask. We hypothesize CAMP yields better calibration and accuracy at high sparsity for LLMs than magnitude- or movement-only baselines, with modest overhead by reusing the same stochastic generations needed for confidence estimation.

result.text: Active high-order diffusion training: use a Fisher-information–guided curriculum over (data, time) pairs to directly reduce the high-order score errors that bound ODE negative log-likelihood. Building on theory linking ODE likelihood to 2nd/3rd-order score errors, we define an acquisition score that estimates each example–time pair’s contribution to these errors via a Fisher kernel of the score network under velocity parameterization and flow-matching. We implement scalable batch selection with BAIT-style linear algebra using Jacobian- and Hessian-vector products from autodiff to target pairs with the largest estimated high-order error. This yields a training schedule that concentrates updates where they most tighten the likelihood bound, improving ODE likelihood and stability with fewer steps and complementing post-hoc high-order flow-matching finetuning.

args.text: I propose Learned Spectral Operator Search (LSOS): replace the fixed FFT basis in Fourier Neural Operators with a learnable, universal structured transform (e.g., K-matrices) and perform a small, differentiable search over mixtures of spectral multipliers and basis choices, akin to DASH’s efficient operation-mixture search. By weight-sharing these spectral mixtures across layers and regularizing the transforms for stability, LSOS can discover task-specific band-limited operators and anisotropic bases that better match nonstationary PDE spectra while preserving discretization invariance. This keeps operator learning fast (search cost comparable to training) and more expressive than fixed Fourier multipliers, enabling adaptation across diverse PDE families without hand-crafted priors. Empirically, LSOS would be validated on Burgers’, Darcy, and Navier–Stokes with varying boundary conditions and heterogeneities, testing resolution generalization and wall-clock savings versus FNO and graph-based operators.

We propose Stagewise Consensus 3DGS, a distributed training scheme that reduces communication and improves surface fidelity by transitioning from volumetric to surface-focused consensus during optimization. Inspired by stagewise rendering in occupancy models, we begin with DOGS-style ADMM consensus over coarse, volumetric Gaussian statistics to quickly align global structure, then progressively restrict synchronization to a narrow band around an estimated surface extracted from the evolving splat field (e.g., via differentiable signed-distance proxies). In the surface phase, only boundary and near-surface Gaussians are synchronized with stronger penalties and normal/tangent-plane alignment losses on anisotropic covariances, while interior/empty-space Gaussians use event-triggered, sparse updates; a coarse-to-fine Gaussian hierarchy supports asynchrony and further cuts bandwidth. This schedule is expected to sharpen cross-partition surfaces, suppress ghosting, and yield faster convergence with significantly fewer communicated parameters on large scenes.

Adaptive Bias–Variance Compression (ABVC) for federated optimization tunes, per client and round, the bias–variance operating point of a generalized compressor to minimize bits-to-accuracy under heterogeneity and partial participation. ABVC combines EF-BV’s error feedback with variance reduction via gradient-difference tracking in the MARINA style, and augments updates with a lightweight Hessian-learning module to form diagonal/low-rank preconditioners that set client-specific compression budgets; once the preconditioner stabilizes, we enable Nesterov-style acceleration as in ACGD. We hypothesize linear convergence under PL/strongly convex objectives with rates that smoothly interpolate between unbiased-VR and biased-contractive regimes, and improved scaling with the number of workers due to independent randomness and preconditioned error dynamics. Empirically, on vision/NLP FL benchmarks with top-k and low-rank compressors, ABVC should reduce communication at fixed accuracy and time-to-ε versus EF-BV, MARINA, and FedNL variants.

args.text: Feature-Diverse Single-Step Adversarial Training (FD-SSAT): replace the single FGSM direction with a small set of orthogonalized, feature-targeted directions obtained by differentiating through lightweight linear probes trained online to decode multiple discriminative factors from intermediate representations. Per minibatch, allocate the perturbation budget across the standard loss gradient, the dominant probe, and several subdominant probes selected by low decodability or low margin, and add a GradAlign-style regularizer to stabilize these directions within the epsilon ball. This broad, feature-grounded sampling of adversarial rays flattens local curvature that triggers catastrophic overfitting while counteracting SGD’s tendency to over-rely on the simplest feature. A simple curriculum shifts budget from easy to hard probes as margins equalize, aiming to preserve multi-step robustness with single-step training and to retain complementary features for better generalization.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of lip reading from silent video, where visual lip movements are inherently ambiguous and homophenes (different sounds with similar lip shapes) make one-to-many viseme-to-phoneme mapping difficult. Its key insight is to learn and store audio representations jointly with visual features in a memory structure so that, at inference time, visual-only inputs can retrieve plausible audio candidates and thus complement missing acoustic information and disambiguate homophenes. The method, Multi-head Visual-audio Memory (MVM), trains on audio-visual pairs to populate a value memory of audio knowledge and multi-head key memories of visual features, uses multi-head attention-like retrieval to extract multiple candidate audio features per visual input (implementing explicit one-to-many mapping), and applies retrieval at multiple temporal scales to leverage context for better discrimination.

The paper addresses the challenge of designing principled adaptive optimization methods for federated learning to improve convergence and accuracy while respecting client privacy and system heterogeneity. The key insight is that federated optimizers can be understood via decompositions of the ordinary differential equations (ODEs) corresponding to centralized adaptive optimizers, which reveals how momentum and adaptive terms should be allocated between global and local updates. Building on this analysis, the authors propose FedDA, a momentum-decoupled adaptive method that applies global momentum throughout local iterations to accelerate convergence and then uses full-batch gradient steps near the end of training to mimic centralized behavior and correct inconsistencies introduced by adaptive adaptation.

args.text: We propose Occupancy-Gated Multiband Consensus for distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting, which augments ADMM-based global–local training with a sparse-voxel occupancy curriculum that transitions from volumetric to surface-focused sampling and gates both Gaussian birth/death and consensus penalties to overlaps along likely surfaces. Each Gaussian’s appearance is predicted by a lightweight polynomial neural field head driven by Fourier features, decomposing radiance into low/high-frequency bands; the system communicates only low-band statistics globally each round and restricts high-band consensus to neighboring blocks, cutting bandwidth while stabilizing high-frequency learning. Training begins with coarse voxels and low-band consensus to bootstrap geometry, then sharpens voxels and enables high-band consensus as surfaces emerge, reducing spurious cross-block coupling. This yields fewer Gaussians, faster convergence, and crisper renderings on large scenes by combining distributed consensus with sparse-voxel guidance and frequency-aware parameterization.

result.text: MOPO addresses offline reinforcement learning where policies must be learned from a fixed dataset despite harmful distributional shift away from the data support. The key insight is that model-based methods can outperform model-free ones in offline settings but need an explicit mechanism to penalize model uncertainty so learned policies do not exploit erroneous model predictions; framing offline model-based RL as a penalized MDP yields a lower bound on true return. The method thus learns a dynamics model with Lipschitz regularization, estimates model uncertainty (variance), and subtracts an uncertainty-dependent penalty from imagined rewards during planning/optimization, producing a practical algorithm that empirically outperforms standard model-based and state-of-the-art model-free offline RL on benchmarks and tasks requiring generalization.

result.text: The paper addresses whether linear-transformer architectures can perform sophisticated in-context learning beyond simple tasks, specifically investigating their ability to solve implicit linear regression when training data is corrupted by varying noise levels. The key insight is that each layer of a linear transformer encodes and updates an implicit weight vector for the regression problem and that the layerwise computations implement a form of preconditioned (and learned) gradient descent that can incorporate momentum and noise-adaptive rescaling. Methodologically, the authors prove this interpretation formally for linear attention, then empirically train linear transformers on noisy regression tasks and analyze the learned layerwise updates to show the emergence of a novel optimization algorithm that matches or outperforms baselines by adaptively adjusting step directions and scales according to estimated noise.

result.text: The paper addresses the lack of principled, tractable guidance methods for controllable generation with generative models defined over discrete state-spaces, a capability well-developed for continuous diffusion and flow models but missing for applications like molecules and biological sequences. Its key insight is that framing discrete generative dynamics as continuous-time Markov processes allows one to derive tractable guided sampling schemes analogous to continuous-space guidance, enabling steering of the model toward a target posterior or property-conditioned distribution. The proposed method, Discrete Guidance, constructs and uses continuous-time Markov transition dynamics on the discrete state-space together with score-like or value-based guidance terms to modify sampling trajectories, and demonstrates efficacy by guiding generation of small molecules, DNA, and protein sequences to satisfy desired properties.

args.text: We propose LC-Score, a fast conformer generator that estimates distance-based score fields using locally complete 1-hop geometric descriptors and lightweight equivariant message passing. Concretely, we condition edge-local score experts on ComENet-style complete neighborhood measurements and couple them with a sparse set of torsion/ring "couplers," implemented via PaiNN-like equivariant updates, to preserve SE(3) symmetry while modeling long-range correlations without quadratic message mixing. Training follows ConfGF’s denoising score matching but uses a local-to-global noise schedule with constraint-aware regularizers for chirality, rings, and stereochemistry; inference performs block-wise equivariant Langevin updates with cached local Jacobians for sub-quadratic runtime. This yields faster sampling, improved torsion diversity, and higher validity on large molecules relative to prior score-based conformer methods.

result.text: The paper addresses reducing uplink communication in federated learning under realistic challenges—partial client participation and heterogeneous data—while handling the distortion introduced by communication compression. Its key insight is that the classical stochastic controlled averaging (SCA) can be reformulated into an equivalent but simpler and more communication-efficient implementation that halves uplink cost and serves as a foundation for compression-aware algorithms. Building on that reformulation, the authors develop two algorithms—SCALLION for unbiased compressors and SCAFCOM for biased compressors—that integrate compressed updates without extra assumptions on compression error or limits on heterogeneity, and they prove improved communication and computation complexity relative to prior work. Empirically, both methods match full-precision FL performance with much less uplink transmission and beat recent compressed-FL baselines under the same communication budget.

result.text: Active high-order diffusion training: use a Fisher-information–guided curriculum over (data, time) pairs to directly reduce the high-order score errors that bound ODE negative log-likelihood. Building on theory linking ODE likelihood to 2nd/3rd-order score errors, we define an acquisition score that estimates each example–time pair’s contribution to these errors via a Fisher kernel of the score network under velocity parameterization and flow-matching. We implement scalable batch selection with BAIT-style linear algebra using Jacobian- and Hessian-vector products from autodiff to target pairs with the largest estimated high-order error. This yields a training schedule that concentrates updates where they most tighten the likelihood bound, improving ODE likelihood and stability with fewer steps and complementing post-hoc high-order flow-matching finetuning.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of standard graph convolutional networks on meshes, which use isotropic kernels and thus ignore local orientation and geometric structure, reducing expressivity for tasks that depend on directional information. The key insight is to extend convolutions to be gauge equivariant and anisotropic so that filters respond to orientation and transform consistently under changes of local frames, and to carry orientation-aware features across the mesh via parallel transport. The method implements Gauge Equivariant Mesh CNNs by equipping each mesh vertex with a local frame (gauge), designing anisotropic convolutional kernels that are equivariant to gauge changes, and using geometric message passing that parallel-transports orientation-carrying features along edges before aggregation, yielding substantially more expressive models than conventional GCNs.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of poor and noisy geometry reconstruction in neural volume rendering, where prior methods model geometry indirectly via a generic density field and extract surfaces from arbitrary density level sets. The key insight is to reverse this relationship by modeling volume density as an explicit function of a signed distance function (SDF), specifically using the Laplace cumulative distribution function applied to the SDF, which provides a strong geometric inductive bias, enables a bound on opacity approximation error for accurate ray sampling, and facilitates disentanglement of shape and appearance. The method implements this SDF-to-density mapping within a neural volume rendering pipeline, uses the error bound to drive efficient and precise ray sampling for tight coupling of geometry and radiance, and trains the model in an unsupervised multiview setting to produce higher-fidelity geometry and allow swapping of shape and appearance across scenes.

result.text: MOReL addresses offline reinforcement learning: how to learn a high-performing policy using only a fixed dataset of past environment interactions without further online data. The key insight is to build a pessimistic model-based surrogate (a P-MDP) that deliberately underestimates value in parts of the state-action space with high model uncertainty, so that policy performance in the real environment is lower-bounded by its performance in the P-MDP and model exploitation is avoided. The method learns a transition/reward model and an uncertainty-aware penalty to construct the P-MDP from the offline data, then performs planning or policy optimization inside this P-MDP to obtain a near-optimal policy; MOReL is shown to be minimax optimal (up to log factors) and empirically matches or exceeds prior offline RL baselines.

args.text: We propose AdaMix-EFVR, an accelerated, adaptive bias–variance mixed compression scheme that unifies EF-BV-style error feedback with DIANA/MARINA-type variance reduction and adds Nesterov acceleration on the server. Each client maintains a control variate and EF memory and, at each round, chooses a mixture between an unbiased randomized compressor and a biased contractive compressor via a lightweight proxy (residual norm and gradient-disagreement), defaulting to gradient-difference compression when heterogeneity is high, while preserving independent randomness across workers. For smooth strongly convex problems, the target complexity is O((1+E[ω_t])√(L/μ) log(1/ε)) with improved scaling in the number of workers, and under PL conditions we expect linear convergence to a neighborhood without fixing the mixture a priori. This closes the gap between accelerated compressed methods and error-feedback–based biased compressors and adapts in real time to bandwidth fluctuations and partial participation.

We propose a Block-State Newton Transformer that fuses an SSM sublayer with block-wise attention to perform in-context second-order optimization over long sequences. The SSM maintains HiPPO-style streaming sketches of feature and cross-moment statistics across the full context and converts them into lightweight diagonal-plus-low-rank inverse-curvature preconditioners that are broadcast to each attention block. Conditioned on these preconditioners, the block attention sublayer implements iterative Newton-like updates for in-context learning, yielding robustness on ill-conditioned tasks; a neural CDE formulation can continuously refine the curvature state under irregular sampling. We hypothesize improved sample efficiency and long-context generalization versus pure attention and prior SSM–Transformer hybrids, validated on streaming linear regression, program induction with sparse signals, and long-context language modeling adaptation.

We propose a controllable sampler for temporal KG forecasting that casts future event generation as a continuous-time Markov jump process over (subject, relation, object, time), and guides sampling with a combination of learned scores and temporal constraints. Concretely, we use a ChronoR-style scorer to define base jump intensities, augment them with a CyGNet-inspired copy kernel for periodic/repetitive facts, modulate reliance on history via a CENET-style contrastive switch, and add a TLogic-derived temporal-rule potential as a guidance term; these components are fused using discrete-time-to-continuous-time guidance techniques for CTMCs to steer samples toward constraint-satisfying high-probability futures. The result is a calibrated, diversity-preserving posterior over future links that supports controllable conditioning (e.g., enforcing/relaxing rules, injecting exogenous temporal priors) and yields improved uncertainty estimates and what-if counterfactual forecasting. We expect gains on event-style datasets where repetition and rules coexist with regime shifts, and provide both ranked predictions and sampled trajectories for evaluation.

We propose Joint Equivariant Hamiltonian–Score Modeling (JEHS), a single SE(3)-equivariant GNN that co-trains to predict local Hamiltonian matrix elements and a conformation score field, coupling them through a physics-informed consistency that aligns the score with the negative gradient of an energy derived from the predicted Hamiltonian (e.g., tight-binding or learned surrogate). Architecturally, we use a lightweight equivariant message-passing core for efficient Hamiltonian prediction and equivariant features, and estimate distance-based scores for roto-translation handling; the two heads share representations and are tied by a force-consistency loss via differentiable eigen-decomposition. At inference, we perform equivariant Langevin sampling guided jointly by the score and Hamiltonian-derived forces to generate energetically plausible, property-conditioned conformers while also predicting spectra from the same pass. This unifies electronic-structure awareness with conformation generation, improving data efficiency and computational cost over training separate models and yielding better downstream property prediction and conformer quality.

result.text: The paper addresses slow convergence in federated learning arising from non-i.i.d. client data, which the authors attribute in part to catastrophic forgetting during local client updates that degrades performance on data learned by other clients. Their key insight is to alleviate this forgetting by regularizing local training with a loss evaluated on pseudo data that encode the global model's knowledge of previous clients, thereby preserving cross-client information while clients train locally. They propose FedReg, which generates pseudo samples from the global model and adds a regularization term using these pseudo data during each client's local optimization, accelerating convergence and improving robustness and privacy against gradient inversion attacks. Experiments show FedReg notably speeds up training—especially for deep networks and highly non-i.i.d. data—while enhancing classification privacy and attack resilience.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of making neural architecture search (NAS) fast and broadly applicable to diverse, under-explored domains beyond computer vision, where AutoML could have the most impact. The key insight is that fixing a standard CNN topology but searching only over operation choices—specifically kernel sizes and dilations—gives rich multi-resolution feature extraction while dramatically reducing the search space, and that leveraging the Fourier diagonalization of convolution lets one efficiently compute mixtures of these operations. Building on this, the authors propose DASH, a differentiable NAS algorithm that uses Fourier-based diagonalization to perform weight-sharing over operation mixtures with improved asymptotic complexity, yielding up to 10× faster search in practice; they evaluate DASH on ten varied tasks (e.g., PDE solving, protein folding, heart disease detection) and show it outperforms state-of-the-art AutoML on most tasks while keeping search-plus-retraining overhead low (often under 2× the training time of a baseline CNN).
