result.text: The paper addresses high-fidelity 3D surface reconstruction from multi-view 2D images, overcoming limitations of prior neural-surface methods that need mask supervision and fail on thin or heavily occluded geometry. The key insight is to represent surfaces as the zero level-set of a neural signed distance function (SDF) and to replace conventional volume rendering with a novel rendering formulation that removes the first-order geometric bias that otherwise prevents accurate surface recovery. Methodologically, NeuS jointly learns a neural SDF and appearance by training with the new unbiased volume rendering loss (without requiring foreground masks), enabling robust optimization like NeRF while yielding precise surface extraction from the learned SDF via its zero level-set. Experiments on DTU and BlendedMVS demonstrate state-of-the-art surface accuracy, particularly on complex and self-occluded objects.

args.text: Unify second-order federated optimization with communication-efficient variance reduction by combining FedNL’s Hessian learning with MARINA-style compressed difference updates, wrapped in EF-BV’s bias–variance unified error-correction. Each client maintains dual memories—a gradient residual for error-feedback and a Hessian control variate—and transmits compressed differences of its local gradient and a few Hessian–vector products along server-specified probes, using independent randomness and error-feedback when compressors are biased. The server updates global control variates and applies them for curvature-aware preconditioning, yielding local superlinear convergence under standard smoothness/strong-convexity near the optimum and communication that scales with the variance of differences rather than raw signals; partial participation and bidirectional compression emerge as special cases. We hypothesize robustness to data heterogeneity via cross-worker variance reduction and provide PL/EM-based guarantees for nonconvex regimes.

result.text: The paper tackles hallucinations in large language models—incorrect factual generations—by leveraging the observation that factual knowledge is often localized in specific transformer layers. Its key insight is that contrasting logits from later versus earlier layers can amplify signals corresponding to factual content while attenuating spurious generations, without requiring retrieval or fine-tuning. The method, called Decoding by Contrasting Layers (DoLa), computes next-token probabilities by projecting hidden states from different layers to the vocabulary, subtracting (or otherwise contrasting) earlier-layer logits from later-layer logits, and decoding from the resulting distribution; this simple post-hoc decoding rule consistently improves truthfulness across multiple-choice and open-ended benchmarks, e.g., boosting LLaMA family models on TruthfulQA by ~12–17 percentage points.

args.text: We propose Layer-Anchored Diversified FGSM (LAD-FGSM), a fast single-step adversarial training scheme that generates multiple non-maximal perturbations by targeting small, orthogonal changes in intermediate-layer feature directions that are discriminative yet under-utilized. We identify candidate feature axes by periodic linear probes to rank features by decodability at initialization and during training, then project their unit changes back to input via local Jacobians, mixing these input-space perturbations with standard FGSM to sample a broader adversarial direction set and reduce boundary curvature. A simple curriculum gradually shifts weight from easy to harder feature directions and increases inner-loop attack quality using FOSC-based triggers and gradient-alignment monitoring, preventing catastrophic overfitting while retaining FGSM-level cost. This unifies diversified single-step training, gradient alignment, and feature-level inductive bias control, promising robustness that approaches multi-step methods without their compute.

We propose Guided-TKG, a discrete-guidance sampler for temporal knowledge graph event forecasting. Future-link generation is cast as a continuous-time Markov process over candidate (relation, tail, time) states whose base transition intensities are derived from a ChronoR-style rotational score, then energy-shaped by: (i) rule-based potentials from TLogic’s temporal rules to bias toward time-consistent reasoning chains, (ii) a CENET-inspired history-dependency gate that adaptively balances rule/copy signals versus non-historical exploration, and (iii) a CyGNet-like copy prior that boosts intensities for historically repeating facts. Guided sampling operates at inference time without retraining the base scorer, producing calibrated probabilities and rule-grounded explanations while improving accuracy for sparse-history entities. We will evaluate on standard TKG benchmarks with ablations for each guidance source and report both ranking metrics and explanation fidelity.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of lip reading from silent video, where visual lip movements are inherently ambiguous and homophenes (different sounds with similar lip shapes) make one-to-many viseme-to-phoneme mapping difficult. Its key insight is to learn and store audio representations jointly with visual features in a memory structure so that, at inference time, visual-only inputs can retrieve plausible audio candidates and thus complement missing acoustic information and disambiguate homophenes. The method, Multi-head Visual-audio Memory (MVM), trains on audio-visual pairs to populate a value memory of audio knowledge and multi-head key memories of visual features, uses multi-head attention-like retrieval to extract multiple candidate audio features per visual input (implementing explicit one-to-many mapping), and applies retrieval at multiple temporal scales to leverage context for better discrimination.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of extreme pruning at initialization, where existing skeletonization methods degrade sharply beyond ~95% sparsity and can even underperform random pruning. The key insight is to choose a subnetwork with maximum foresight connection sensitivity (FORCE): select connections whose perturbation would have the largest impact on loss, and update importance progressively so previously unimportant weights can become important later. Methodologically, the authors propose an efficient approximate FORCE maximization algorithm that progressively prunes a network at initialization rather than one-shot removing, enabling iterative re-evaluation of connection importance and preserving trainability. Empirically, this progressive skeletonization lets networks retain accuracy at very high sparsities (up to 99.9%) and outperforms recent initialization-pruning baselines across many tasks.

args.text: I propose Operator-aware Differentiable NAS (OpD-NAS) tailored to PDE neural operators: a search space that composes discretization-invariant operator layers (spectral Fourier layers and hierarchical inducing-point graph operator layers) interleaved with learnable universal structured linear maps to shuttle between grid, graph, and Fourier representations. OpD-NAS uses Fourier-diagonalized weight-sharing to rapidly mix and prune spectral mode subsets and inducing-point schedules, while K-matrix layers flexibly approximate the inter-representation transforms with near-optimal complexity. The search objective explicitly enforces resolution generalization by evaluating candidate architectures under random mesh coarsening/refinement and grid–graph resamplings as a cheap proxy for multi-discretization performance. We hypothesize this yields compact operator networks that generalize across meshes and PDE families with search overhead comparable to DASH and superior accuracy vs. hand-tuned FNO variants.

Surface-Consistent Distributed Gaussian Splatting augments DOGS-style distributed 3DGS with a shared implicit SDF that serves as a geometry prior and consensus anchor. Each worker jointly optimizes local Gaussians and a local SDF via SDF-to-density rendering losses, while ADMM enforces consensus on the SDF and on Gaussians in overlaps; per round, Gaussians are projected toward the SDF zero level set and their anisotropy aligned to SDF normals. A curriculum shrinks Gaussian covariances from volumetric to near-surface as the SDF stabilizes—akin to a volumetric-to-surface transition—suppressing ghost density and fixing block seams to enable more aggressive spatial partitioning with higher fidelity. The SDF is discarded after training, preserving pure 3DGS inference, but yields faster, stabler large-scene training and sharper geometry than DOGS alone.

result.text: The paper addresses limitations of standard score-based diffusion models that use Gaussian (Brownian) noise—namely slow sampling convergence (high NFE), limited diversity and mode collapse on imbalanced data—by asking whether a non-Gaussian stochastic process can improve sampling speed and diversity. The key insight is that isotropic α-stable Lévy processes, which are heavy-tailed and can make large jumps, yield a different forward-noise geometry that permits faster exploration of the data manifold and alleviates mode-collapse while still supporting a principled reverse-time dynamics. Concretely, the authors derive an exact reverse-time stochastic differential equation for Lévy-driven forward dynamics, propose a fractional denoising score-matching objective to estimate the score under α-stable noise, and implement the Lévy-Itô Model (LIM), demonstrating empirically on CIFAR-10, CelebA and imbalanced CIFAR10LT that LIM achieves substantially better FID, recall and faster wall-clock sampling (e.g., 1.58 FID and 0.7006 recall on CelebA with 2× speedup) compared to Gaussian DDPM baselines.

The paper addresses convergence and complexity of distributed stochastic gradient methods under communication constraints and delays, covering quantized, error‑compensated, and delayed SGD variants. Its key insight is a unified analytical framework — a single theorem — that captures arbitrary compression operators, error feedback, delay, variance reduction, and sampling, which yields tighter (often best-known) complexity bounds for existing schemes and enables new algorithmic combinations. Methodologically, the authors instantiate this framework to derive convergence rates for a family of 16 new methods, including EC-SGD-DIANA (error feedback plus biased compression of gradient differences) and EC-LSVRG-DIANA (adding variance reduction for finite-sum problems), and prove these methods converge to the exact optimum in expectation with a constant stepsize for convex and strongly convex objectives when workers compute full or variance-reduced gradients.

result.text: The paper investigates why transformer models exhibit emergent in-context few-shot learning despite not being explicitly trained for it, attributing the phenomenon to properties of the training data rather than solely to architecture or objective. The key insight is that naturalistic distributional features—burstiness (clustered occurrences), many rare classes, dynamic item meanings, and skewed (Zipfian) frequency distributions—make models more likely to learn to use context at inference time, and that these properties differ markedly from i.i.d. supervised training. Methodologically, the authors run controlled experiments comparing transformers and recurrent models trained on synthetic datasets with varying distributional properties, showing that transformers develop in-context learning under bursty, rare-class, and dynamic-meaning regimes (and can support both in-context and weight-based learning when trained on Zipfian data), whereas recurrent architectures do not exhibit the same behavior.

args.text: I propose feature-subspace diversified single-step adversarial training to prevent catastrophic overfitting while mitigating simplicity bias. Instead of a single maximal pixel-space FGSM step, each iteration estimates a low-rank basis of discriminative input-gradient directions (e.g., running PCA of per-batch gradients or Fisher directions) and samples a non-maximal perturbation by randomly mixing several basis vectors with an annealed magnitude schedule that cycles across subspaces and spectral bands. This broad, structured sampling regularizes loss-surface curvature akin to diversified FGSM and gradient-alignment, while explicitly discouraging reliance on a single simplest feature that sustains the decision boundary. The method adds modest overhead (rank-8–16 basis) and is compatible with random-initialized FGSM; we track gradient-alignment and PGD robustness over training to verify stability and reduced overfitting.

result.text: The paper addresses how to recover true labels and improve classifier generalization when training data contain noisy labels, noting existing approaches require modifying or retraining classifiers and may not suit pre-trained models. The key insight is that instead of changing the classifier, one can model a “noisy prediction” transition from true labels to the classifier’s observed predictions and then invert that mapping to calibrate predictions back to true labels using a generative-model-based transition matrix. The method, called Noisy Prediction Calibration (NPC), estimates this transition matrix via a generative model as a post-processing step that corrects outputs from any pre-trained classifier (given access to training instances and their predictions), and the authors prove its theoretical alignment with standard transition-matrix approaches while demonstrating improved empirical performance on synthetic and real datasets.

args.text: We propose EquiFlow-H, a conditional SE(3)-equivariant flow on Hermitian operator space that generates molecular Hamiltonians H(R) given atomic geometry. The model conditions on globally complete yet 1-hop computable geometric descriptors (à la ComENet) and uses a QHNet-style lightweight equivariant message-passing backbone to parameterize a flow that transports a simple Gaussian Hermitian prior to H(R) while enforcing Hermiticity, orbital block structure, and distance-based sparsity. Training uses flow matching in operator space together with a geometry-consistency regularizer that aligns directional derivatives ∂H/∂d_ij along a pretrained distance-score field (from ConfGF), improving smoothness and out-of-distribution stability; PaiNN-style equivariant feature channels provide compact vector/tensor carriers. EquiFlow-H yields calibrated uncertainty via sampling, supports multiple Hamiltonians consistent with uncertain geometries, and scales to larger, multi-species systems without costly tensor products.

result.text: The paper addresses reducing uplink communication in federated learning under realistic challenges—partial client participation and heterogeneous data—while handling the distortion introduced by communication compression. Its key insight is that the classical stochastic controlled averaging (SCA) can be reformulated into an equivalent but simpler and more communication-efficient implementation that halves uplink cost and serves as a foundation for compression-aware algorithms. Building on that reformulation, the authors develop two algorithms—SCALLION for unbiased compressors and SCAFCOM for biased compressors—that integrate compressed updates without extra assumptions on compression error or limits on heterogeneity, and they prove improved communication and computation complexity relative to prior work. Empirically, both methods match full-precision FL performance with much less uplink transmission and beat recent compressed-FL baselines under the same communication budget.

result.text: The paper tackles the slow sampling speed of diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs), which typically require hundreds or thousands of neural-network evaluations to generate samples. The key insight is an exact formulation of the diffusion ODE solution that analytically isolates the linear part and, after a change of variables, rewrites the remaining contribution as an exponentially weighted integral of the neural network, enabling high-order numerical integration rather than leaving everything to black-box ODE solvers. Based on this, the authors derive DPM-Solver, a dedicated high-order ODE solver with convergence-order guarantees that works for both discrete- and continuous-time DPMs without additional training and drastically reduces required function evaluations. Empirically, DPM-Solver produces high-quality samples in about 10–20 evaluations (e.g., 4.70 FID at 10 steps and 2.87 FID at 20 on CIFAR-10) and yields roughly 4–16× speedups over prior training-free samplers.

args.text: We propose Operator-Aware NAS that searches directly over neural operator parameterizations for PDE families by instantiating a fixed operator-topology whose layers can be Fourier neural operator blocks, hierarchical graph operator blocks, or gauge-equivariant anisotropic kernels, and learning a relaxed mixture over these choices. Building on DASH’s Fourier-diagonalized weight sharing, we extend diagonalization to jointly mix spectral truncations, dilation/radial profiles, and anisotropic orientations, while using multiresolution inducing-point factorizations to efficiently relax graph-kernel choices, yielding a single differentiable super-operator with near-constant overhead per candidate. The search objective meta-trains across discretizations and boundary-condition regimes to prefer discretization-invariant, data-efficient inductive biases, then fixes the discovered operator recipe for final training. We hypothesize this will deliver FNO-like zero-shot resolution generalization with order-of-magnitude faster search than hand-tuned operator design, and outperform single-family operators on mixed-geometry PDE benchmarks.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of how to train implicit neural representations (INRs) for surface reconstruction without having to choose between occupancy or signed distance formulations and without incurring unknown biases from existing losses. The key insight is to draw an analogy to phase transitions in fluids and design a loss whose learned density converges to an occupancy function while its log-transform converges to a distance function, thereby unifying both representations in the limit. Methodologically, the authors propose and analyze this phase-transition-inspired loss, prove that its minimizer satisfies reconstruction constraints and minimizes surface perimeter (imposing a useful minimal-surface inductive bias), and demonstrate that training INRs with this loss yields state-of-the-art reconstructions on standard benchmarks.

args.text: Levy-robust offline RL: replace Gaussian/local smoothing in robust offline RL with alpha-stable Lévy perturbations applied in a learned latent space to model rare, large observation shifts that Gaussian noise misses. We then regularize policy and value on Lévy-perturbed dataset states and on Lévy-augmented model rollouts, while applying conservative value penalties (as in CQL/COMBO) so Q-values lower-bound return over a heavy-tailed contamination neighborhood. Finally, adapt the tail index α by minimizing CVaR of TD errors on held-out data, yielding suboptimality guarantees under ε-contamination and improved robustness to bursty sensor faults/adversarial patches without undue conservatism on in-distribution states.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of reducing communication in distributed stochastic gradient methods while retaining fast convergence when using general (possibly biased) gradient compressors, where naive compression creates persistent errors that slow or break convergence and it was unknown whether error compensation can be combined with Nesterov-style acceleration. The key insight is that error compensation can be incorporated into an accelerated variance-reduced framework in a way that controls the compression error and preserves accelerated linear rates under standard smoothness and strong-convexity assumptions. Concretely, the authors design an error-compensated loopless Katyusha algorithm that maintains and corrects compression residuals while applying the loopless accelerated variance-reduction updates, and they prove an accelerated linear convergence bound for any compressor satisfying a contraction property. Empirically, the method achieves the same optimization accuracy with substantially fewer communication rounds than prior error-compensated algorithms, demonstrating that acceleration and error feedback are compatible in practice.

result.text: The paper addresses understanding and improving linearized self-attention by connecting it to Fast Weight Programmers (FWPs), i.e., systems where a slow network programs a fast memory via additive outer-product updates, and identifies capacity and adaptability limitations in recent linear attention variants. Its key insight is that linearized attention is formally equivalent to classic outer-product FWPs, which suggests replacing purely additive programming instructions with delta-rule-like updates and learned, dynamic learning rates so the fast memory can correct and adapt mappings from keys to values. Methodologically, the authors derive this equivalence, analyze memory capacity, introduce a delta-rule-inspired update and a new kernel for linearizing attention, and validate the approach on synthetic retrieval tasks, machine translation, and language modeling, showing improved adaptability and performance.

args.text: I propose Feature-Coverage Adversarial Training (FC-AT), which counteracts simplicity bias and the single-direction focus that triggers catastrophic overfitting by forcing reliance on multiple discriminative features. In each batch, we train lightweight linear probes on frozen intermediate activations to identify the currently easiest, most decodable feature; we then craft adversarial examples by (i) adding a small targeted perturbation that suppresses this easy feature’s decodability, and (ii) maximizing loss with a non-maximal step constrained to be approximately orthogonal to the FGSM direction to explore alternative adversarial directions. We maintain gradient alignment with a GradAlign-style penalty and adaptively ramp the strength and convergence of the orthogonal inner maximization using a FOSC-based schedule, avoiding early instability while increasing coverage later. By diversifying adversarial directions and distributing boundary support across features, FC-AT should prevent catastrophic overfitting and improve both robust and natural accuracy.

result.text: The paper tackles lip-to-speech synthesis, specifically the challenge of recovering accurate audio from visual lip movements where local viseme-to-phoneme mappings are ambiguous due to homophenes and variable speaker/global context. The key insight is that combining local visual features with a learned global visual context via attention can disambiguate mapping and improve synchronization between lip motion and generated speech. The authors propose VCA-GAN, a GAN-based generator that injects global context encoded from local features through a visual context attention module and integrates audio-visual attention, and they train it with an added synchronization contrastive loss to enforce temporal alignment. Experiments show this approach yields state-of-the-art multi-speaker lip-to-speech synthesis with improved clarity and timing.

args.text: We propose DP-FetchSketch: endow FetchSGD’s Count Sketch aggregation with (ε,δ)-differential privacy by injecting a small, calibrated, one-time initialization noise into the sketch as in private linear sketches, so the merged server-side sketch is private with respect to any single client update while preserving linearity, momentum, and error-feedback in sketch space. This avoids per-update noise and leaves client encoders unchanged, requiring only modified heavy-hitter recovery that de-biases estimates and adapts thresholds to the known initialization noise. We derive utility bounds showing the added variance scales with sketch dimensions (not the number of participating clients) and combine participation sampling for amplification to reach user-level privacy across rounds, maintaining convergence and accuracy close to FetchSGD under the same high uplink compression.

result.text: I propose Learned Spectral Operator Search (LSOS): replace the fixed FFT basis in Fourier Neural Operators with a learnable, universal structured transform (e.g., K-matrices) and perform a small, differentiable search over mixtures of spectral multipliers and basis choices, akin to DASH’s efficient operation-mixture search. By weight-sharing these spectral mixtures across layers and regularizing the transforms for stability, LSOS can discover task-specific band-limited operators and anisotropic bases that better match nonstationary PDE spectra while preserving discretization invariance. This keeps operator learning fast (search cost comparable to training) and more expressive than fixed Fourier multipliers, enabling adaptation across diverse PDE families without hand-crafted priors. Empirically, LSOS would be validated on Burgers’, Darcy, and Navier–Stokes with varying boundary conditions and heterogeneities, testing resolution generalization and wall-clock savings versus FNO and graph-based operators.

result.text: The paper tackles the model selection dilemma for heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, where lack of counterfactuals makes it hard to know which estimator will perform best in practice. Its key insight is that there is no universal winner: the effectiveness of a selection criterion depends on a complex interplay between the selection strategy, the set of candidate estimators, and the data-generating scenario, so understanding success and failure modes is more informative than declaring a single best method. To investigate this, the authors perform a systematic empirical study comparing a range of selection criteria across diverse estimators and datasets, characterizing when particular criteria succeed or fail and deriving desiderata for more revealing future evaluations rather than proposing a one-size-fits-all solution.

args.text: Certified-Conservative Offline RL (CC-ORL): combine pessimistic value estimation for OOD actions with randomized smoothing of the critic to learn a smoothed Q that certifies a per-state lower bound over an L2 perturbation ball around each logged observation. We further adapt the robustness radius per state via split-conformal calibration on held-out offline data, maintaining target coverage of real observation noise while avoiding excessive uniform conservatism. The policy then maximizes this certified lower-bound Q under the data-supported action distribution, yielding robustness to bounded adversarial/sensor perturbations and distribution shift without sacrificing value.

result.text: The paper tackles the gap between Bayesian uncertainty estimates from Gaussian Process (GP) regression and the need for rigorous frequentist confidence bounds in safety-critical applications, where existing provable bounds are too conservative to be practical. Its key insight is to derive new concentration inequalities and error decompositions that yield explicit, computable frequentist uncertainty bounds for GP regression which are significantly tighter than prior theoretical guarantees while still remaining provably valid. The method combines refined analysis of the GP posterior, sharper control of information gain and effective dimension, and handling of model misspecification to produce bounds that degrade gracefully under mismatch; these bounds are efficiently evaluable and demonstrated empirically to enable safer, more practical learning-based control.

args.text: Curvature-Sketch State Transformer (CSST): a hybrid block-attention + SSM layer that performs second-order in-context learning at long range. The SSM sublayer maintains an online, low-rank/sketched summary of curvature and cross-covariance (e.g., X^T X and X^T y) via HiPPO-style polynomial memories and delta-rule fast-weight updates, yielding a running quasi-Newton state that is cheap to carry across blocks. The block Transformer sublayer mixes local features and reads this state to execute Woodbury-style Newton steps (or preconditioned updates) per block, realizing the empirically/theoretically observed Newton-like ICL in a subquadratic, parallelizable architecture. This unifies and generalizes preconditioned linear-attention updates, recovers them as a special case when the sketch rank is small, and should improve robustness on ill-conditioned, very long sequences.

We propose a Mixture-of-Temporal-Reasoners for TKG forecasting that adaptively routes each query among three complementary engines: a repetition-aware copy module for cyclic/recurrent facts, a temporal rule reasoner for interpretable multi-hop chains, and a non-historical prior that captures exogenous, first-time events. A ChronoR-style relation–time rotational embedding conditions both the router and the modules, enabling continuous-space grounding of rules and robust generalization across timestamps. The router is trained with contrastive supervision that compares historical versus counterfactual non-historical signals, learning when to copy, infer via rules, or generate from priors, and a calibrated ensembling loss balances precision and recall. This hybrid, gated design targets strong performance on mixed datasets that contain periodic, compositional, and novel events, surpassing single-paradigm models.

We propose DiffStega-NS, a distribution-preserving steganography scheme for diffusion generators that encodes secrets along directions locally orthogonal to the score field throughout denoising, ensuring the induced sampling trajectory leaves the image marginal unchanged to first order. Concretely, at each step we project a secret-conditioned perturbation onto the nullspace of the score Jacobian (approximated via low-rank probes) and adapt its amplitude with a likelihood-ratio acceptance test, while a Secret Trajectory Extractor decodes bits from the full denoising trace for robustness. An Attack-Aware Diffusion Augmentor simulates common lossy channels (compression, rescaling, mild crops/noise) during training and we interleave lightweight ECC across steps, yielding two variants for lossless vs. lossy channels analogous to prior GAN-based designs but on diffusion backbones with classifier-free guidance and inversion support. This design brings provable-style distribution preservation and high capacity to diffusion models and empirically targets state-of-the-art recovery under both clean and perturbed conditions.

result.text: The paper studies how the number of clients sampled per round (cohort size) affects model quality and training dynamics in federated learning, addressing scalability, analogies to centralized batch-size effects, and how to exploit large cohorts. The key insight is that increasing cohort size yields both familiar large-batch phenomena (diminishing returns, generalization gaps) and federated-specific issues (training instabilities, fairness degradation and client heterogeneity interactions) so larger cohorts are not uniformly beneficial. The authors empirically analyze many realistic federated settings, quantifying performance, convergence, and fairness as cohort size grows, and compare algorithmic choices and hyperparameter scaling strategies to identify which adjustments (e.g., learning-rate schedules, aggregation rules) mitigate problems and when larger cohorts help versus hurt.

args.text: We propose Certified Smoothed Conservative Offline RL (CSCORL), which unifies conservative value learning with certifiable robustness to observation perturbations. Instead of enforcing smoothness only empirically, CSCORL trains a Lipschitz-regularized encoder and critic to maximize a certified lower bound of Q over an Lp ball around each dataset observation (via bound propagation or randomized smoothing), while applying a CQL-style penalty to out-of-support actions within that neighborhood. The perturbation radius is adapted per-state using epistemic uncertainty (e.g., ensemble disagreement), tightening certificates where data support is strong and expanding conservatism where it is weak. This yields provable robustness certificates on policy value under observation noise/attacks and mitigates overestimation under distribution shift, improving safety without excessive conservatism.

result.text: The paper addresses the vulnerability of out-of-distribution (OOD) detection methods to adversarial examples and shows that many recent defenses fail when evaluated with strong, end-to-end PGD attacks and larger perturbations (e.g., ε=8/255 on CIFAR-10), often performing worse than random under attack. The key insight is that robust OOD detection requires exposing the detector during training to adversarial perturbations of both in-distribution and out-of-distribution samples, which suggests leveraging generative OOD approaches and adversarial training rather than defenses that only consider weak attacks or in-distribution robustness. The proposed method, Adversarially Trained Discriminator (ATD), combines a pre-trained robust classifier to extract stable features with a generator that synthesizes OOD examples, and trains the discriminator adversarially on both real and generated OOD plus perturbed in-distribution data; this yields substantially higher robust AUROC on CIFAR-10/100 while preserving standard AUROC and classification accuracy.

args.text: We propose Curvature-Augmented Block-State Transformers (CABST), extending BST with a continuous-time state that tracks multi-scale gradient and curvature statistics of the in-context task. A neural CDE driven by HiPPO-projected token features maintains streaming estimates of Fisher/Hessian-like preconditioners; each block then performs a few quasi-Newton in-context updates, using the SSM/CDE state to precondition local block attention computations. We add auxiliary layer-wise losses that align intermediate predictions with successive Newton iterates, yielding faster convergence on ill-conditioned sequences and stronger out-of-distribution generalization. CABST preserves BST’s subquadratic efficiency while improving long-range language modeling and algorithmic ICL benchmarks.

We propose feature-targeted fast adversarial training: within each batch, generate multiple non-maximal single-step perturbations that are constrained to align with distinct discriminative feature directions identified by lightweight linear probes at intermediate layers, and schedule their step sizes via a dynamic convergence proxy. By explicitly sampling adversarial directions tied to boundary-sustaining features and gradually increasing per-feature difficulty, the method reduces loss-surface curvature in the adversarial subspace, prevents catastrophic overfitting, and counters SGD’s simplicity bias by forcing the model to learn beyond the simplest feature. Practically, we alternate standard loss, GradAlign-style gradient alignment, and a probe-weighted adversarial loss that rotates through feature-aligned directions with a curriculum informed by FOSC-like criteria, achieving multi-step robustness at near-FGSM cost. This combines diversified, non-maximal single-step examples with feature-aware curricula to stabilize single-step training and broaden robustness.

Neuro-symbolic temporal QA that composes learned temporal logical rules with question-calibrated multi-hop embeddings. We first extract weighted, time-consistent rules from the TKG (in the style of TLogic) and, given a question, a small controller (in the spirit of CENET) predicts whether the query is history-driven and gates a rule-grounding module that expands answer candidates and produces differentiable, time-aligned proof paths. These rule-evidence features are fused with TempoQR/QC-MHM's question- and KG-aware embeddings via cross-attention to score answers, enabling interpretable rationales and improved generalization to unseen query types. The model trains end-to-end by distilling from rule-augmented supervision and contrastive signals over history vs. non-history queries, and can be evaluated on CronQuestions and event-forecasting benchmarks.

We propose StegaLLM, a distribution-preserving steganography scheme for large language model outputs that embeds bits by modulating token choices within the model’s native next-token distribution under a tight KL-divergence budget. Inspired by DP-SDM for images, we implement a restricted-token search guided by API logprobs to select among near-equiprobable candidates so that per-token statistics remain indistinguishable, yielding a covert channel without detectable distributional shifts; when logprobs are unavailable, transfer/prefill strategies approximate the target distribution. A learned text extractor, trained with an attack simulator that mimics real channels (e.g., truncation, paraphrasing, light editing), enables robust recovery under lossy conditions while preserving semantic fidelity. We outline finite-sample detectors and prove that, under the KL constraint, detection advantage is bounded, enabling practical capacities (e.g., fractional bits/token) with security and robustness across popular LLM APIs.

We propose PrivSketch-FedOpt, a federated optimizer that merges Count Sketch–compressed client updates into a single differentially private, stateful sketch on the server. The sketch is initialized with calibrated noise to satisfy client-level central DP and clients apply norm clipping before sketching; optimizer state (momentum and error feedback) is maintained and updated directly in sketch space, while an ODE-guided decoupling applies global momentum throughout local steps with a late-stage correction without reconstructing dense states. The server reconstructs only sparse top-K coordinates for broadcast, yielding strong communication savings and robustness to partial participation; we provide convergence under biased compressors and non-i.i.d. data and track privacy via participation subsampling and a moments accountant across rounds. Empirically, PrivSketch-FedOpt matches or surpasses nonprivate, sketched FL under similar compression and outperforms compression-aware baselines at the same budget, while sustaining accuracy at stricter privacy than per-round Gaussian mechanisms.

result.text: The paper tackles the slow sampling bottleneck of diffusion models (DMs), which typically need hundreds to thousands of discretization steps to produce high-quality samples. The key insight is that discretization error—particularly how the learned diffusion process is numerically integrated—dominates sample quality, and that the learned stochastic dynamics exhibit a semilinear structure that can be exploited. Building on this, the authors introduce the Diffusion Exponential Integrator Sampler (DEIS), which applies exponential integrator techniques from ODE solvers to the DM sampling ODE/PDE, reducing discretization error by treating linear and nonlinear components separately and thereby enabling accurate sampling with very few score evaluations. DEIS is model-agnostic, works with pre-trained DMs, and empirically achieves state-of-the-art low-NFE performance (e.g., high-quality CIFAR-10 samples in ~10–15 steps).

result.text: I propose Operator-aware Differentiable NAS (OpD-NAS) tailored to PDE neural operators: a search space that composes discretization-invariant operator layers (spectral Fourier layers and hierarchical inducing-point graph operator layers) interleaved with learnable universal structured linear maps to shuttle between grid, graph, and Fourier representations. OpD-NAS uses Fourier-diagonalized weight-sharing to rapidly mix and prune spectral mode subsets and inducing-point schedules, while K-matrix layers flexibly approximate the inter-representation transforms with near-optimal complexity. The search objective explicitly enforces resolution generalization by evaluating candidate architectures under random mesh coarsening/refinement and grid–graph resamplings as a cheap proxy for multi-discretization performance. We hypothesize this yields compact operator networks that generalize across meshes and PDE families with search overhead comparable to DASH and superior accuracy vs. hand-tuned FNO variants.

args.text: Consensus SDF-Tiles is a distributed, large-scene neural surface reconstruction method that partitions the scene into overlapping spatial tiles and trains per-tile hybrid radiance–SDF models. Each worker begins with volumetric rendering and progressively anneals to a narrow-band SDF rendering schedule driven by a local uncertainty metric (e.g., depth-hit variance), while an ADMM consensus layer enforces cross-tile agreement on SDF value, normals, and radiance along overlap rays. To stabilize early training we introduce slack variables on density with penalties that are relaxed early and tightened as surfaces sharpen; at convergence only a single global SDF/radiance field remains and yields watertight, seam-free meshes. This combines DOGS-style distributed consensus with NeuS/VolSDF geometry priors and occupancy-to-surface curricula to enable city-scale reconstruction with faster training and higher-fidelity geometry.

We propose Accelerated Bidirectional EF-BV (ABEFBV), a federated optimizer that layers Nesterov/Catalyst-style acceleration over the EF-BV unified bias–variance compression, applies contractive compressors on both uplink and downlink, and preserves error-feedback memories across rounds even under partial participation via a server-side residual reservoir. The key insight is that EF-BV’s two-parameter compressor model enables a clean coupling between acceleration and error compensation: by using a loopless accelerated variance-reduced core with independent randomness and periodic full-precision syncs, we can obtain accelerated linear rates whose constants depend on the bias/variance parameters similarly to ACGD for unbiased compression and to accelerated EC-Katyusha for contractive compressors. For partial participation and heterogeneous data, we incorporate MARINA-style control variates and probabilistic refresh to bound drift of stale residuals, while bidirectional compression follows FedNL-BC’s design to keep server broadcasts communication-efficient without breaking the analysis. The theory predicts improved communication complexity over EF-BV and non-accelerated error-feedback baselines, closes the gap to accelerated uncompressed methods when compressor variance is small, and recovers known special cases when downlink is uncompressed or participation is full.

We propose a Block-State Quasi-Newton Transformer that marries state-space memory with second-order in-context optimization. An SSM/HiPPO-style sublayer maintains per-token running sufficient statistics (e.g., feature means and covariances) via linear-time updates, exposing a low-rank preconditioner that the subsequent block-attention sublayer uses to perform one quasi-Newton step on the implicit task defined by the prompt; stacked layers thus trace an L-BFGS/iterative-Newton trajectory with O(n) memory and subquadratic compute. Trained on synthetic and natural tasks with ill-conditioned spectra and bursty, Zipfian distributions, the model learns to switch between first- and second-order updates and generalizes to very long contexts, outperforming pure attention on ICL convergence and pure SSMs on short-range adaptation. This design formalizes and extends observed Newton-like ICL and preconditioned updates while leveraging BST-style SSM–attention hybrids for scalability.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of aligning language models to user intentions when training data provides explicit scalar rewards rather than only pairwise preferences, observing that existing methods like DPO are specialized for implicit reward signals. Its key insight is that Noise Contrastive Estimation (NCE) can unify and extend preference-based alignment by directly learning a policy from explicit reward annotations, and that DPO emerges as a special case of an InfoNCA objective under pairwise preference data. The authors propose two algorithms—NCA, which maximizes absolute likelihoods of favored responses, and InfoNCA, which adjusts relative likelihoods across responses—showing that NCA avoids the decreasing-likelihood issue seen in DPO/InfoNCA and better preserves chosen-response probabilities. Empirically, with Mistral-8*7B and 7B models, both methods outperform preference baselines when reward data are available, and NCA yields notably stronger results than DPO on challenging reasoning tasks such as math and coding.

args.text: We propose CRoME, a counterfactual rule-guided mixture-of-experts for temporal KG forecasting that adaptively routes each query to repetition-driven or extrapolative reasoning. First, we extract time-consistent temporal rules and paths and compute counterfactual ablations along those paths to estimate a causal history-dependence signal, which trains a gate in the spirit of contrastive dependence modeling. When the gate predicts repetition, a CyGNet-style copy expert retrieves and copies historically consistent objects; otherwise, a ChronoR-style rotation expert extrapolates future links, and both experts are calibrated by rule-based evidence. Training uses self-supervised interventions that mask/shift histories to supervise the gate and a selective distillation loss that aligns the mixture toward the expert that most improves counterfactual likelihood.

args.text: We propose DP-FetchDA: a communication-efficient federated optimizer that unifies FetchSGD’s sketch-based aggregation with differentially private linear sketches and momentum placement guided by adaptive-FL ODE insights. The server maintains a persistent Count Sketch that is made differentially private via one-time, calibrated initialization noise; clients send Count-Sketch-compressed local updates each round, which the server merges and updates entirely in sketch-space with global momentum and error-feedback before reconstructing a top-K sparse model delta to broadcast. This preserves optimization history under intermittent participation, achieves central DP for the full training trace without per-update noise, and scales sketch width/depth with cohort size to balance variance and privacy amplification by subsampling. We hypothesize tighter utility–privacy tradeoffs than per-round/client noise baselines and convergence comparable to nonprivate compressed FL on heterogeneous data.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation that standard score-based generative models (SGMs) use overly simplistic diffusion processes, which make the denoising task harder and thus limit synthesis quality. Its key insight is to replace the usual overdamped diffusion with a critically-damped Langevin diffusion (CLD) that augments data with velocity-like auxiliary variables, coupling them as in Hamiltonian dynamics so the model need only learn the conditional velocity score—a simpler objective than the full data score. Methodologically, the authors derive a new score-matching objective for CLD, propose an efficient sampler tailored to the second-order dynamics, and demonstrate empirically that CLD-based SGMs and the new solver yield better synthesis quality than prior SGMs (and outperform standard solvers like Euler–Maruyama) for comparable architectures and compute.

result.text: We propose Operator-Aware NAS that searches directly over neural operator parameterizations for PDE families by instantiating a fixed operator-topology whose layers can be Fourier neural operator blocks, hierarchical graph operator blocks, or gauge-equivariant anisotropic kernels, and learning a relaxed mixture over these choices. Building on DASH’s Fourier-diagonalized weight sharing, we extend diagonalization to jointly mix spectral truncations, dilation/radial profiles, and anisotropic orientations, while using multiresolution inducing-point factorizations to efficiently relax graph-kernel choices, yielding a single differentiable super-operator with near-constant overhead per candidate. The search objective meta-trains across discretizations and boundary-condition regimes to prefer discretization-invariant, data-efficient inductive biases, then fixes the discovered operator recipe for final training. We hypothesize this will deliver FNO-like zero-shot resolution generalization with order-of-magnitude faster search than hand-tuned operator design, and outperform single-family operators on mixed-geometry PDE benchmarks.

args.text: I propose an ADMM-based distributed training scheme for neural SDF volume renderers that scales to large scenes by partitioning space into overlapping blocks and enforcing cross-block consensus on geometry and appearance. Each worker optimizes a local SDF and radiance with NeuS/VolSDF rendering, while a master maintains a global SDF whose values and normals on overlap samples are matched via ADMM penalties and dual updates; a second consensus term aligns per-ray opacity/color for rays traversing multiple blocks. We leverage the VolSDF SDF-to-density mapping to define a shared narrow band that stabilizes sampling across workers and synchronize signed-distance offsets to keep zero-level sets consistent, periodically merging local encodings into the global model for fast inference. This aims to deliver DOGS-like distributed speed-ups with improved surface fidelity and memory locality for SDF-based methods, enabling large-scale reconstruction without mask supervision.

result.text: The paper addresses the limited expressive power and interpretability of existing graph kernels and message-passing GNNs, which struggle with hand-crafted features and are bounded by the Weisfeiler–Lehman test. Its key insight is to integrate graph kernels directly into the GNN message-passing mechanism by using trainable small "hidden" graphs as kernel-based filters—analogous to convolutional filters in CNNs—so that node updates reflect learned subgraph similarity rather than only aggregated neighbor features. The proposed KerGNN framework computes kernel similarities between network-learned filter graphs and local subgraphs to update node embeddings, subsuming standard MPNNs as special cases, and is trained end-to-end for graph tasks. Empirical results show competitive or improved classification performance and enhanced interpretability because the learned filters reveal meaningful local graph structures.

The paper tackles the problem of aligning language models to user intentions when training data provides explicit scalar rewards rather than only pairwise preferences, observing that existing methods like DPO are specialized for implicit reward signals. Its key insight is that Noise Contrastive Estimation (NCE) can unify and extend preference-based alignment by directly learning a policy from explicit reward annotations, and that DPO emerges as a special case of an InfoNCA objective under pairwise preference data. The authors propose two algorithms—NCA, which maximizes absolute likelihoods of favored responses, and InfoNCA, which adjusts relative likelihoods across responses—showing that NCA avoids the decreasing-likelihood issue seen in DPO/InfoNCA and better preserves chosen-response probabilities. Empirically, with Mistral-8*7B and 7B models, both methods outperform preference baselines when reward data are available, and NCA yields notably stronger results than DPO on challenging reasoning tasks such as math and coding.

result.text: The paper addresses decentralized stochastic variational inequalities (VIs)—a unifying framework for games, saddle-point, and equilibrium problems—over fixed and time-varying networks, where both communication and local computation costs are critical but poorly understood. Its key insight is that tight lower bounds can be established separately for communication rounds and local stochastic iterations, and that algorithms can be designed to simultaneously attain these bounds, proving optimality across decentralized stochastic, decentralized deterministic, and centralized stochastic regimes. Methodologically, the authors derive information-theoretic lower complexity bounds and then construct accelerated variance-reduced primal-dual algorithms that carefully balance gossip/consensus steps with variance-reduction and step-size schedules to match the bounds. Empirical experiments on representative VI problems validate that the proposed methods achieve the predicted optimal rates in practice.

The paper investigates how the choice between sparse ratings and pairwise rankings as feedback protocols affects alignment and evaluation of large language models (LLMs), addressing the problem that different sparse-feedback formats may yield inconsistent preferences and thus unreliable alignment. The key insight is that ratings and rankings often disagree—about 60% for both human and AI annotators—because of systematic annotator biases (e.g., humans give denser responses higher ratings but favor accuracy in pairwise comparisons), and that these protocol-induced differences change which model appears better under different evaluation methods. Methodologically, the authors analyze preference consistency across human and AI annotators, quantify disagreement between inferred preferences from ratings versus rankings, identify bias patterns explaining the inconsistency, and empirically show that models aligned with ranking data are preferred under rank-based evaluation but not under rating-based evaluation, demonstrating protocol-dependent evaluation outcomes.

args.text: We propose DP-Init Sketch FedDA, a federated optimizer that maintains a persistent, mergeable Count Sketch at the server initialized with calibrated differential privacy noise, preserving linearity for extreme compression while providing client-level DP. Clients send clipped, optionally biased-compressed updates as sketches; the server merges them and performs global momentum and error-feedback–corrected adaptive preconditioning directly in sketch space per an ODE-based decomposition, then reconstructs sparse updates to update the model. The single-noise initialization, combined with clipping and participation-aware sensitivity bounds, yields tight multi-round privacy accounting under partial participation, while an SCA-compatible schedule supports both unbiased and biased compressors with convergence guarantees. We hypothesize this design matches full-precision FL accuracy at 50–200× uplink reduction and delivers practical client-level DP with modest utility loss on non-i.i.d. benchmarks.

Solver-matched likelihood training for diffusion ODEs: directly optimize a discretized log-likelihood surrogate that upper-bounds the probability-flow ODE NLL under a chosen high-order sampler (e.g., DPM-Solver/DEIS) and a fixed NFE budget. We derive a quadrature-aware loss by expanding the continuous-time likelihood bound into local score/velocity errors transported through the solver’s coefficients (Butcher tableau/exponential-integrator weights), and backpropagate through one-step unrolled solver kernels using adjoint or implicit differentiation with control variates to keep variance and memory low. Coupled with velocity parameterization and high-order flow-matching finetuning, we jointly learn the score and a step schedule that minimize this surrogate at fixed NFE, yielding discretized trajectories with provably tighter NLL than continuous-time–trained baselines at equal sampling cost.

result.text: The paper tackles unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) where spurious correlations between domain-invariant features (like class identity) and domain-specific features (like environment) learned from the labeled source domain fail to generalize to the unlabeled target domain. Its key insight is to give the unlabeled target domain equal status to the source by enforcing that a single invariant classifier be simultaneously consistent with source labels and with the intrinsic cluster structure of the target data, thereby removing spurious correlations that are inconsistent in the target. The method, called Invariant CONsistency learning (ICON), trains a classifier to minimize supervised loss on source samples while enforcing consistency between its predictions and unsupervised target clusters (e.g., via pseudo-labeling or clustering-based constraints), effectively aligning class predictions across domains without treating target data merely as auxiliary. Experiments on Office-Home, VisDA-2017, and WILDS 2.0 show ICON achieves state-of-the-art or improved performance compared to conventional UDA methods.

The paper addresses why polynomial neural networks (PNNs), particularly the Π-Net parametrization, excel at tasks requiring high-frequency detail despite the well-known neural network spectral bias that favors low frequencies. The key insight is that multiplicative polynomial interactions alter the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) eigen-spectrum, producing larger eigenvalues for higher-frequency components and thus accelerating their learning compared with standard networks. Methodologically, the authors derive a spectral analysis of the NTK for PNNs, characterize how the Π‑Net parametrization shifts spectral bias toward higher frequencies, and validate the theory with extensive experiments on synthetic and vision tasks showing faster convergence of high-frequency modes.

result.text: The paper addresses improving human alignment of large language models by avoiding the complexity and instability of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and the information loss of reducing multi-sample comparisons to pairwise contrasts. Its key insight is that alignment can be framed as matching the model’s probability ranking over multiple candidate responses to human preference rankings, and that extending pairwise contrasts to full preference rankings yields richer supervisory signal. The proposed method, Preference Ranking Optimization (PRO), is a supervised fine-tuning algorithm that iteratively contrasts candidates within n-length preference lists so the model both prioritizes the best reply and progressively orders the remaining responses, thereby aligning output probabilities with human judgments. result.text: The paper addresses how to leverage machine learning to improve practical combinatorial optimization by replacing heuristic components of exact solvers and tailoring solvers to instance distributions rather than treating instances in isolation. The paper tackles offline reinforcement learning where standard off-policy methods fail due to extrapolation error from out-of-distribution (OOD) actions in a fixed dataset. Its key insight is that explicit policy constraints are unnecessary if one can quantify epistemic uncertainty and perform pessimistic value updates: penalizing Q-values where uncertainty is high prevents overestimation on OOD actions while still permitting generalization. The method, Pessimistic Bootstrapping for RL (PBRL), estimates uncertainty via disagreement among an ensemble of bootstrapped Q-functions, applies a pessimistic penalty proportional to that disagreement during value updates, and supplements this with a novel OOD sampling scheme; the authors prove that this combination yields a valid uncertainty quantifier in linear MDPs and empirically outperforms prior offline RL methods on D4RL benchmarks.

This yields an effective compression parameter that shrinks with anisotropy reduction from preconditioning and iteration complexity governed by the preconditioned condition number, unifying acceleration, hybrid compression, and second-order curvature learning in one provably analyzable template. We hypothesize linear rates for strongly convex objectives with constants depending on the learned preconditioner’s accuracy and the hybrid compressor’s bias–variance mix, and robustness to partial participation via the difference-based steps.

result.text: The paper addresses graph classification by leveraging counts of graph homomorphisms from a chosen family F into an input graph G as features that are invariant under isomorphism and under permutations within F. The key insight is that vectors of homomorphism numbers form universal embeddings for all F-invariant functions: by selecting a sufficiently rich family F, any classifier that depends only on F-indistinguishability can be approximated arbitrarily well. Methodologically, the authors formalize this universality, define the notion of F-indistinguishability, and show that when F is restricted to graphs of bounded treewidth the homomorphism counts can be computed efficiently, yielding a practical and theoretically grounded approach to graph representation and classification.

args.text: We propose SketchAdam-FL, a federated optimizer that merges client updates in sketch space while supporting adaptive preconditioning and differential privacy. Each client transmits two mergeable sketches—a Count Sketch of its gradient and a sketch of elementwise squared gradients—so the server maintains global momentum and second-moment accumulators directly in sketch space; ODE insights from federated adaptive methods guide which terms remain global vs. local, preserving adaptive benefits under partial participation. The server performs momentum/RMS updates on the merged sketches, reconstructs a sparse preconditioned update to broadcast, and injects a one-time initialization noise into the sketches to achieve privacy without per-round noise. This yields communication-efficient, privacy-preserving adaptive FL that preserves optimization history across intermittent clients and admits convergence analysis.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of decomposing images of an object into shape, spatially-varying BRDF, and per-image illumination—an important but underconstrained task that existing neural renderers (e.g., NeRF/NeRD) handle poorly, especially for detailed illumination recovery. Its key insight is to replace the expensive analytic illumination integral in rendering with a learned neural query—Neural-PIL—that effectively pre-integrates lighting effects, and to regularize decomposition with learned low-dimensional smooth manifold priors for BRDF and illumination. The method trains a reflectance decomposition network that predicts geometry, BRDF parameters, and per-image lighting while using Neural-PIL to produce rendered radiance efficiently; separate auto-encoders enforce compact, smooth latent spaces for BRDF and illumination to stabilize and improve recovery. This combination yields more accurate BRDF and lighting estimates and enables higher-fidelity novel view synthesis and relighting than prior approaches.

result.text: The paper addresses temporal knowledge graph event forecasting, specifically the difficulty of predicting future interactions for entities lacking useful historical recurrence or periodicity. Its key insight is that future events arise from both historical dependencies and unobserved non-historical factors, so modeling and contrasting these two sources can reveal whether a query depends on past events and which candidate entities are most plausible. The proposed Contrastive Event Network (CENET) learns historical and non-historical dependency signals, uses contrastive learning on query representations to decide whether the current moment is history-driven, trains a binary classifier to produce a boolean mask over candidate entities, and applies this mask during inference to improve ranking. Evaluated on five benchmarks, CENET substantially outperforms prior methods, notably improving Hits@1 by at least 8.3% on event-based datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses improving human alignment of large language models by avoiding the complexity and instability of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and the information loss of reducing multi-sample comparisons to pairwise contrasts. result.text: The paper addresses whether federated averaging (FedAvg) can still achieve linear speedup in convergence under realistic federated learning conditions—non-i.i.d. data and partial worker participation—rather than the usual i.i.d. and full-participation assumptions. The key insight is that with appropriately chosen two-sided learning rates and accounting for local updates, FedAvg attains provable linear-speedup convergence rates that scale with the number of participating workers: O(1/√(mKT)+1/T) for full participation and O(1/√(nKT)+1/T) for partial participation, where K is local steps, T is communication rounds, m total workers and n workers per round. Methodologically, the authors analyze FedAvg in non-convex settings to derive these bounds, show that increasing local steps can aid convergence up to a limit of T/m, and validate the theory with experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10.

args.text: We propose Heteroscedastic Listwise NCE (HL-NCE), which unifies explicit scalar-reward alignment with listwise preference supervision by extending NCA to jointly model per-response uncertainty and normalize over n-candidate lists. HL-NCE adds a variance head that estimates heteroscedastic reward noise and reweights each response by inverse uncertainty, while a listwise contrastive normalizer across on- and off-policy candidates preserves chosen-response likelihood and mitigates reward-scale shifts. A self-normalizing correction term guarantees non-decreasing likelihood for top-ranked answers, and a boundary-focused sampler draws hard negatives near the policy’s indifference region to improve sample efficiency. By combining NCA’s stability with PRO’s richer listwise signal and RRHF’s simple ranking pipeline, HL-NCE improves calibration and robustness on long-form reasoning without PPO-style instabilities.

result.text: The paper tackles link forecasting on temporal knowledge graphs, where existing embedding-based approaches often lack explainability and struggle with predicting future events while preserving temporal consistency. The proposed method, TLogic, extracts weighted temporal rules from random walk patterns, uses them to rank candidate future links by aggregating rule evidence with time-consistent grounding, and demonstrates improved predictive performance and human-readable explanations on three benchmarks compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

args.text: I propose Group-Orbit Consistent Adaptation (GO-CA), which unifies cluster-consistency UDA with group-theoretic disentanglement by explicitly modeling target-domain variability as latent group actions (orbits) and enforcing classifier invariance along these orbits. Concretely, we alternate between (i) discovering target partitions/orbits via IP-IRM–style invariance induction and contrastive partitioning, and (ii) training a single classifier to be accurate on labeled source while remaining constant along each discovered target orbit, with group-averaging regularization and pseudo-augmentations that apply learned generators to source to break spurious correlations. This turns target clusters into structured, group-aligned constraints that remove target-inconsistent features while preserving class structure, yielding robustness under large shifts. We expect GO-CA to outperform pure consistency UDA on Office-Home, VisDA, and WILDS by improving alignment across domain-specific transformations.

args.text: I propose a phase-adaptive federated optimizer that unifies accelerated compressed first-order training with curvature-adaptive second-order steps under the EF-BV compressor model. In the early phase, run an accelerated compressed method while concurrently learning a Hessian surrogate via communication-efficient sketches; both gradients and curvature messages use hybrid biased/unbiased compressors selected per-coordinate based on estimated curvature to minimize EF-BV error terms. When the surrogate passes a verifiable quality test, switch to preconditioned Newton-like updates with error-feedback and variance reduction across clients, yielding accelerated global convergence and superlinear local rates under strict communication budgets. The analysis targets preserving the (1+ω) acceleration dependence, the compressor-robust linear rates of EF-BV, and the compression-invariant local convergence of Hessian-learning by explicitly bounding the switching time via the surrogate’s information gain.

result.text: The paper tackles the limited expressive power of standard permutation-equivariant message-passing graph neural networks, which struggle to capture basic topological properties of graphs. Its key insight is to augment messages with unique node identifiers (one-hot encodings) that let each node build a local context matrix encoding rich joint feature–topology information while preserving permutation equivariance. The method propagates these one-hot identifiers through message-passing layers to assemble per-node local context matrices, applies learnable transformations and pooling to produce node representations, and demonstrates empirically that this structural message-passing framework more accurately predicts diverse graph topological properties while remaining computationally efficient.

args.text: We propose Listwise Calibrated NCA (LC-NCA), a single-model alignment objective that unifies scalar-reward NCA with listwise preference ranking. For each prompt, LC-NCA learns a per-prompt temperature to calibrate heterogeneous human reward scales into a target distribution over all candidates, then optimizes a hybrid loss that (i) maximizes absolute likelihood of the top-rated response with a non-decrease constraint relative to the SFT anchor and (ii) applies an InfoNCA-style listwise contrast to correctly order the remaining candidates. When only orderings are available, LC-NCA collapses to a PRO/RRHF-style ranking loss; with calibrated rewards it behaves like NCA while avoiding decreasing-likelihood pathologies and improving sample efficiency by reusing all candidates as informative negatives. We hypothesize LC-NCA offers PPO-free stability while preserving high chosen-response probability and yielding stronger math/coding performance under mixed reward/ordering supervision.

result.text: TempoQR addresses the problem of answering complex natural-language questions that require temporal reasoning over Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGs), going beyond prior work that targets only single-fact temporal queries. The key insight is that grounding a question in both entity and time-aware embedding spaces—by augmenting textual question representations with context-sensitive entity embeddings and question-specific time embeddings—enables richer temporal scope resolution and multi-hop reasoning. Methodologically, TempoQR uses three specialized modules to produce a textual question encoding, to fuse that encoding with embeddings of entities mentioned in the question, and to generate time embeddings tailored to the question’s temporal scope, then employs a transformer-based encoder to fuse these signals and predict answers from the TKG. Experiments show this embedding-based fusion approach substantially improves accuracy (by 25–45 percentage points) on complex temporal questions and generalizes better to unseen question types.

args.text: We propose Protocol-Robust Preference Alignment, a unified latent-utility framework that models annotator protocol as a causal observation layer so policies trained on mixed ratings and rankings align consistently across evaluation schemes. Concretely, a shared latent utility u(x,y) feeds protocol-/annotator-conditioned heads: per-annotator monotone-spline Gaussian models for ratings and a Plackett–Luce head for full or partial rankings; joint maximum likelihood calibrates a single reward surface while disentangling systematic biases identified between protocols. We then fine-tune the policy to minimize worst-case regret over a plausible set of protocol mixtures (distributionally robust optimization), yielding outputs whose preference ordering is invariant to whether evaluation uses ratings or rankings. An active data component targets high-disagreement prompts to elicit dual-protocol labels, tightening the bridge between heads and improving cross-protocol generalization.

result.text: The paper addresses why and how training a compact student model to mimic a larger teacher’s class probabilities (knowledge distillation) can outperform direct training on labels and how to make distillation more reliable. The key insight is to view distillation as a semiparametric inference problem where the student is the finite-dimensional target, the true Bayes class probabilities are an infinite-dimensional nuisance, and the teacher provides a plug-in nuisance estimate, which lets one analyze the impact of teacher error on student risk using modern semiparametric tools. Methodologically, the authors derive prediction-error guarantees for standard distillation under this framework and propose two practical improvements—cross-fitting to reduce overfitting bias from the teacher, and loss correction to adjust for teacher underfitting—then empirically validate that these enhancements consistently improve student performance on tabular and image benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of modeling and scoring atomic-resolution protein conformations—typically solved with hand-designed physics-inspired energy functions—by proposing a learned alternative trained only on crystallographic structures. The key insight is that an energy-based model (EBM) can implicitly learn the physicochemical constraints and interaction patterns governing stable side-chain and backbone arrangements from data alone, without incorporating explicit handcrafted physical terms. Methodologically, the authors train an EBM on atomic coordinates from crystallized proteins and evaluate it on the rotamer recovery task, showing performance comparable to the Rosetta energy function and demonstrating via analysis of outputs and hidden representations that the model captures meaningful physicochemical properties relevant to protein energetics.

args.text: I propose Catalyst-accelerated gradient-difference compression (Cat-MARINA): wrap MARINA’s biased, variance-controlled compressed-difference estimator in an outer proximal (Catalyst) loop to induce Nesterov-style acceleration on the anchor sequence. Each outer iteration defines a proximal subproblem solved by an inner MARINA-like method that uses contractive compressors with EF-BV–style variance control and periodic exact gradients, ensuring the compressed bias remains bounded so the outer acceleration is valid without error feedback. Under PL/strong convexity, this should yield accelerated linear rates with only a multiplicative (1+ω) penalty akin to accelerated compressed GD and improved dependence on the number of workers, while retaining MARINA’s practicality for heterogeneous data; for nonconvex settings, we expect faster convergence to ε-stationarity in PL regions. Compared to EF21/EF-BV and accelerated error-compensated VR baselines, Cat-MARINA avoids error feedback, leverages gradient-difference compression, and remains compatible with partial participation.

We propose Curvature-Programmed In-Context Learning (CP-ICL): a transformer that explicitly constructs and refines low-rank curvature preconditioners across layers by using linearized attention fast weights with delta-rule updates to accumulate token–feature covariances, followed by Newton-style updates in later layers. To avoid the attention low-rank bottleneck and enable richer curvature sketches, we decouple head dimension from head count, and at inference time we contrast earlier- vs later-layer logits to gate when second-order steps are trusted. Training aligns intermediate layer predictions with successive Newton iterates on synthetic and real tasks (e.g., heteroscedastic linear regression, sparse logistic regression), while supervising fast-weight states to approximate Fisher/K-FAC diagonals, yielding exponentially faster ICL and robustness on ill-conditioned prompts versus GD-like baselines. This unifies preconditioned ICL in linear transformers, fast-weight programming, and DoLa-style layer contrast into a practical architecture and decoding rule for second-order in-context learning.

We propose Uncertainty-weighted Unified Contrastive Alignment (UUCA), which models a latent utility u(x,y) with heteroscedastic noise and learns a policy with a single objective that fuses absolute and relative feedback. Concretely, we combine an NCE/NCA term on scalar rewards with a listwise Plackett–Luce ranking likelihood over candidate sets (reducing to pairwise when needed), and weight each example by its inferred reward uncertainty so noisier labels contribute less. To prevent the decreasing-likelihood pathology, we impose an explicit likelihood-preservation constraint that lower-bounds the log-probability of top-ranked responses from the data while still reshaping probabilities among suboptimal candidates. This yields an SFT-style, one-stage procedure that unifies scalar, pairwise, and listwise supervision and should be robust when mixing human and model-derived feedback of varying reliability.
