result.text: The paper addresses offline policy learning in contextual bandits with neural network function approximation, focusing on challenges from distributional shift, optimization, and generalization when only pre-collected data is available. Its key insight is that a pessimistic, SGD-based learning procedure can provably generalize to unseen contexts under a milder distributional-shift condition than prior work, without assuming any parametric reward structure, by combining algorithmic pessimism with neural-network-specific analysis of effective dimension. Methodologically, the authors propose an offline contextual bandit algorithm that performs online-style stochastic gradient descent with a pessimism regularizer to avoid overestimating unseen actions, provide theoretical guarantees showing sample-efficient generalization and improved computational and effective-dimension dependence compared to online counterparts, and validate the approach empirically on synthetic and real datasets.

args.text: SketchAdam-FL brings adaptive optimization into sketch-based federated aggregation: each client transmits two Count Sketches per round—one of its model update and one of its elementwise-squared update—so the server can maintain mergeable first- and second-moment accumulators and apply momentum/EMA in sketch space. The server reconstructs only a small set of coordinates to perform Adam/RMSProp-style updates with error feedback, querying v_i from the second-moment sketch only for those coordinates, while allocating momentum globally across local steps per the ODE decomposition. To control collision bias under partial participation and varying cohort sizes, the method uses cohort-aware sketch width and stable hashed seed reuse across rounds. We hypothesize linear-speedup-like convergence with communication comparable to FetchSGD and improved robustness on non-i.i.d. data where coordinate-wise adaptivity matters.

result.text: The paper tackles improving sample quality and likelihood of diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) when generating with a limited subset of timesteps by addressing how to choose the model covariance given that the model mean is imperfect. The key insight is that the optimal diagonal or full covariance for a DPM can be expressed in closed form but must be corrected when the mean estimate is biased; both the optimal and corrected covariances decompose into conditional expectations over functions of the latent noise, which can be learned. They therefore propose to estimate these conditional expectations via neural networks (implementing the diagonal case for efficiency) with parameter sharing and a two-stage training procedure, yielding improved likelihoods and notably better sample quality in few-step generation across discrete and continuous timesteps.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of improving reinforcement-learning-based heuristics for NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems by enabling effective and diverse search at inference time without costly per-instance fine-tuning. Its key insight is to anticipate the need for diverse, specialized policies during pre-training by learning a continuous latent space that parameterizes a distribution over policies, so that different latent codes produce complementary heuristics suited to different instance modes. The method, COMPASS, trains a policy network conditioned on a continuous latent vector and jointly learns the latent space so that searching in latent space at inference yields varied, high-quality solutions; this latent-space search outperforms prior single-policy sampling and expensive fine-tuning baselines across TSP, CVRP, and Job-Shop Scheduling benchmarks and generalizes better to procedurally transformed instance distributions.

args.text: We propose SDF-anchored polynomial neural radiance fields that decompose appearance into interpretable frequency subbands while using an SDF-to-density mapping to impose a strong geometric prior. A Fourier PNF head is attached on the learned surface via SDF normals and local coordinates, and each subband is rendered with a lightweight Neural-PIL that pre-integrates lighting per band to capture efficient, band-wise view-dependent effects. Training combines unbiased SDF volume rendering with a phase-transition–inspired surface regularizer, plus a frequency-targeted curriculum and cross-band consistency losses that encourage low bands to explain diffuse/low-frequency illumination and high bands to model specular/high-frequency detail. This yields sharper specularities, improved thin-structure geometry, and editable subband controls for relighting and texture transfer compared to standard SDF-NeRF baselines.

Uncertainty-Calibrated Decision Transformers (UCDT) for offline RL: train a return-conditioned sequence model with an uncertainty-weighted behavior cloning regularizer and conservative neighborhood smoothing. Concretely, augment the Decision Transformer loss with a KL penalty toward the behavior policy whose coefficient is proportional to epistemic uncertainty estimated via bootstrapped Q-ensemble disagreement, and apply RORL-style perturbed-state smoothing that penalizes confident action shifts in local neighborhoods to curb OOD exploitation and improve robustness. This preserves the simplicity of sequence modeling while instantiating pessimism adaptively where uncertainty is high, subsuming static BC-regularization and avoiding bootstrapping-induced overestimation common in Q-learning. We hypothesize improved reliability on D4RL under sensor noise and distribution shift with competitive returns versus conservative and uncertainty-based offline RL baselines.

We propose CurvMARINA, a communication-efficient second-order federated optimizer that learns a global Hessian model while transmitting only compressed Hessian–vector product differences with error-feedback and variance reduction. Building on difference compression ideas from MARINA and unified biased/unbiased compressor control, clients maintain local curvature predictors and periodically send contractively compressed updates of Hessian–vector deltas; the server aggregates them with error-feedback, forming a progressively accurate Hessian surrogate used in a Newton-like step with cubic regularization for globalization. We hypothesize (and outline a proof sketch) that CurvMARINA attains locally superlinear convergence with communication per round comparable to first-order methods, improving FedNL/NEWTON-LEARN by exploiting temporal curvature smoothness and variance-reduced curvature residuals. Empirically, we expect strong gains under Top-K or low-rank compressors and partial participation, especially on ill-conditioned, heterogeneous federated tasks where curvature changes slowly across rounds.

result.text: The paper studies the representational limits of temporal graph networks (TGNs), asking which dynamic graph properties different TGN designs can and cannot capture. The key insight is that the two main TGN families—walk-aggregating TGNs (WA-TGNs) and message-passing with memory TGNs (MP-TGNs)—are fundamentally incomparable in expressiveness, but MP-TGNs become as powerful as a newly proposed temporal Weisfeiler-Leman (WL) test when their update functions are injective, while both families still cannot compute certain global properties like girth and deep MP-TGNs render memory redundant. Methodologically, the authors develop novel separations and extensions of 1-WL to temporal graphs, derive theoretical prescriptions (injective updates and relative positional features), and instantiate these into PINT, an architecture combining injective temporal message passing with relative positional encodings that is provably more expressive than prior TGNs and empirically superior on benchmarks.

args.text: We propose Calibrated Listwise NCA (CL-NCA), which unifies explicit scalar rewards with multiway preference ranking by learning a monotonic calibration g(r) for reward scales and optimizing a mixed objective: an absolute-likelihood NCA term to guarantee non-decreasing likelihood of the top-rated response and a listwise InfoNCA/Plackett–Luce term over k candidates using utilities u_i = log pθ(y_i|x)/τ + g(r_i). To improve robustness under noisy or heterogeneous annotator signals, CL-NCA learns per-prompt temperatures, trims low-quality negatives, and enforces a small-KL trust region to the base model. This bridges settings covered by PRO (full rankings) and RRHF (best-of-n pools) while preserving the non-decreasing property emphasized by NCA, mitigating the decreasing-likelihood pathology seen in DPO/InfoNCA. We predict gains on math/coding and instruction-following when mixing explicit reward annotations with partial rankings or best-of-n data.

Guided Temporal KG Simulation recasts future-link prediction as guided sampling from a continuous-time Markov process over discrete events, enabling controllable, constraint-aware forecasting rather than only scoring candidates. A base intensity over candidate objects is induced by a temporal embedding model (e.g., relation–time rotations), and is modulated at sampling time by additive log-potentials derived from temporal logical rules, a copy/recurrence prior for periodic relations, and a history-versus-nonhistory gate that downweights history-driven guidance when exogenous factors dominate. Using discrete guidance for CTMCs, we can efficiently draw trajectories and marginalize to top-k predictions while attributing per-guidance contributions for explanations and supporting test-time constraints (e.g., enforce rule consistency or avoid banned entities). This neurosymbolic guided sampler is expected to improve Hits@k and calibration on event-based TKG benchmarks, particularly for cold-start or OOD settings where standard rankers fail.

args.text: Combine sketch-based communication in federated learning with differentially private initialization of the sketch to achieve client-level privacy at low utility cost. Concretely, extend FetchSGD so each client builds its Count Sketch with a calibrated, shared random initializer that makes the merged aggregate sketch (post-secure aggregation) differentially private to the inclusion/exclusion of any one client, while preserving linearity for server-side momentum and error feedback in sketch space. args.text: I propose Hessian Error-Feedback Newton Learning (HEFNL), a federated second-order method that ports EF-BV’s bias–variance compressor model to curvature communication. We propose Guided Temporal Event Sampling (GTES) for temporal KG forecasting: instead of point-scoring candidates, GTES generates calibrated distributions over future facts by simulating a continuous-time Markov process on (subject, relation, object, time) and applying discrete guidance during sampling. Private-FetchSketch: combine sketch-space aggregation in federated learning with differential privacy by applying initialization-time noise to the Count Sketch that the server maintains across rounds. We propose CADMo-FL: a cohort-adaptive double-compression optimizer with momentum decoupling for federated learning. Guided by an ODE view, it applies persistent global momentum through local steps and inserts brief uncompressed correction steps when n_t is small to counteract heterogeneity-induced drift. result.text: The paper tackles instabilities and suboptimal generation in training energy-based models (EBMs) with contrastive divergence by identifying missing components and practical enhancements. Its key insight is that a commonly neglected gradient term in contrastive divergence is tractable to estimate and crucial for stable training, and that combining this correction with data augmentation, multi-scale processing, and reservoir sampling further boosts robustness and sample quality. The method augments standard contrastive divergence by explicitly estimating the omitted gradient term during learning, integrates augmentation and multi-scale inputs to diversify and stabilize negative samples, and uses a reservoir of past samples to improve MCMC mixing and training dynamics, yielding more stable architectures and improved results on image generation, OOD detection, and compositional tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of current world models for sample-efficient RL: discrete latent representations often discard fine-grained visual detail that can be important for downstream control. Its key insight is that high-fidelity image generation via diffusion models can preserve visual detail in imagined trajectories, and that with the right architectural and training choices diffusion becomes practical and beneficial as a world model for RL. The authors introduce DIAMOND, a diffusion-based world model trained to predict environment frames and used to train agents entirely in imagination; they analyze design choices (conditioning, timestep handling, rollout strategy, and compute trade-offs), show that retaining visual fidelity improves policy learning, and demonstrate state-of-the-art results on Atari-100k (mean human-normalized score 1.46) as well as a standalone interactive neural game engine trained on CS:GO gameplay.

args.text: Temporal-KerGNN: a kernelized temporal message-passing GNN that learns a bank of small, time-aware motif filters and updates node states via similarities between local time-stamped neighborhoods and these motifs. Each layer maintains a sliding window and computes approximate homomorphism counts into bounded-treewidth temporal templates (estimated with streaming sketches/color-coding), using the resulting kernel scores as messages. By pairing injective update functions with relative temporal positional encodings, the model targets temporal-WL-level expressivity while retaining linear memory and offering interpretability through discovered temporal motifs. We hypothesize strong gains on dynamic motif and interaction forecasting tasks and provide a principled bridge between kernelized filters and universal homomorphism features in temporal graphs.

TempRank-NCA is a hybrid alignment method that learns a per-prompt temperature and reward shift to calibrate base-model log-probabilities into utilities, then optimizes a KL-constrained NCA objective on scalar-reward prompts and a listwise ranking loss on multi-candidate prompts. The temperature hypernetwork is trained to reconcile scalar rewards and observed rankings, weighting each example by estimated reward noise so that absolute likelihoods of top choices are preserved while relative ordering among close candidates improves. Interleaving these steps avoids the decreasing-likelihood pathology of purely relative objectives while exploiting richer listwise signal to shape the distribution without PPO. This unifies NCE-based absolute learning with PRO/RRHF-style ranking under a single calibrated-utility view and should yield stronger reasoning with better probability calibration.

result.text: The paper tackles temporal knowledge-graph question answering, where standard PLM-based question encoders miss temporally constrained entity dynamics and existing models fail to capture multi-hop relational structure needed for complex queries. The key insight is that calibrating question representations with time-aware KG concepts and explicitly modeling multi-hop propagation in the graph yields richer temporal-entity semantics and better multi-step reasoning. The proposed QC-MHM fuses question text with time-constrained KG concept embeddings to produce a calibrated query vector, applies a GNN layer to perform multi-hop message passing over the KG, and combines the calibrated question representation with GNN outputs to predict answers. Empirical evaluation on CronQuestions shows substantial gains (e.g., +5.1% Hits@1 on complex questions) and produces more interpretable, trustworthy predictions.

args.text: We propose Protocol-Shift-Robust Preference Alignment (PSR-PA), an offline alignment method that jointly models ratings and rankings via a shared latent utility with protocol- and annotator-specific observation models, and trains a policy with a pessimistic objective to guard against distributional shift across prompts and feedback protocols. Concretely, we fit a multi-annotator probabilistic layer that maps utilities to ratings (ordinal regression with density-sensitive bias terms) and to rankings (Plackett–Luce/Thurstone variants capturing accuracy–fluency tradeoffs), then perform supervised preference optimization on inferred utilities while applying pessimism-weighted losses in sparsely supported regions of the log. This unifies evidence that protocol choice induces systematic bias and that ranking-based optimization is strong, while importing pessimistic offline guarantees from contextual bandits to preference alignment. We hypothesize protocol-invariant evaluation stability and improved OOD generalization, and outline identifiability and generalization bounds under realistic coverage assumptions.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of designing principled adaptive optimization methods for federated learning to improve convergence and accuracy while respecting client privacy and system heterogeneity. The key insight is that federated optimizers can be understood via decompositions of the ordinary differential equations (ODEs) corresponding to centralized adaptive optimizers, which reveals how momentum and adaptive terms should be allocated between global and local updates. Building on this analysis, the authors propose FedDA, a momentum-decoupled adaptive method that applies global momentum throughout local iterations to accelerate convergence and then uses full-batch gradient steps near the end of training to mimic centralized behavior and correct inconsistencies introduced by adaptive adaptation.

result.text: The paper tackles the gap between deep reinforcement learning (DRL) and state-of-the-art heuristics for NP-hard routing problems by proposing a hierarchical two-policy framework called Learning Collaborative Policies (LCP). The key insight is that splitting exploration and exploitation into two specialized, interacting policies—a high-entropy seeder that generates a diverse set of candidate tours and a focused reviser that refines those candidates by partitioning routes into sub-tours—yields better solutions than a single DRL policy. Methodologically, the seeder is trained with an entropy-regularized reward to encourage wide coverage of the combinatorial action space, while the reviser operates on the reduced search space of each seed, concurrently optimizing sub-tours to minimize travel distance; iterating these two policies produces near-optimal solutions across TSP, PCTSP, and CVRP.

result.text: The paper tackles slow and view-entangled 3D-aware image synthesis caused by per-sample MLP-based radiance fields, which force costly ray sampling or low-res rendering with upsampling and can change object geometry/appearance with viewpoint. Its key insight is that sparse voxel grids combined with 3D convolutions, progressive growing, free-space pruning and regularization can replace monolithic MLPs to achieve fast, single-pass, and more 3D-consistent generation, while disentangling foreground (3D voxel grid) from background (2D) yields a compact scalable representation. The method builds a generator that produces a sparse volumetric feature grid for the foreground and a separate 2D background, renders images via a single forward pass through 3D convolutions and differentiable volume rendering, and applies pruning and progressive resolution increases during training to maintain efficiency and fidelity. As a result, VoxGRAF enables efficient, high-quality, and viewpoint-consistent novel-view synthesis without per-ray MLP queries.

Building on this, the authors derive FD reformulations of score matching and its variants and present a generic strategy to replace costly Hessian or higher-order derivative calculations with FD approximations, which reduce compute and memory overhead and improve numerical stability. They provide two concrete instantiations of SM objectives in FD form and empirically show that these FD-based methods match the performance of gradient-based methods while being substantially more computationally efficient.

result.text: The paper addresses the tradeoff between expressivity and scalability in permutation-equivariant graph learning: standard message-passing GNNs are insufficiently expressive to represent all permutation-equivariant functions, while higher-order architectures that are universal require tensorial or subgraph enumerations that scale exponentially and ignore graph sparsity. The key insight is that by using sparsity-aware heuristics inspired by graph isomorphism techniques, one can design permutation-equivariant networks whose computational cost adapts to the number of edges and local structure, yielding a continuum of models that interpolate between efficient message-passing and fully expressive higher-order schemes. Concretely, the authors introduce SpeqNets, a class of architectures that build higher-order representations only over selected node tuples determined by sparsity-sensitive selection rules and then apply permutation-equivariant aggregation and transformation, achieving universality while drastically reducing memory and time compared to full k-order methods. Empirically, SpeqNets retain much of the predictive power of expressive higher-order networks and outperform standard GNNs and graph kernels on node- and graph-level supervised tasks while scaling to larger, sparse graphs.

args.text: Real-world alignment datasets mix explicit scalar rewards and pairwise/listwise preferences and are collected off-policy from heterogeneous proposal distributions, which NCA/InfoNCA and ranking-based methods don’t correct for. We propose DR-MixNCE, a unified objective that embeds both scalar and preference signals into a contrastive likelihood while applying per-sample self-normalized importance weights from behavior-policy estimates and a doubly robust control-variate term to reduce variance. DR-MixNCE preserves NCA’s absolute-likelihood advantages but remains unbiased under off-policy sampling, and it integrates PRO/RRHF-style rankings via calibrated margins within the same estimator; a small trust-region KL to the reference policy stabilizes training and prevents chosen-probability collapse. Empirically, we hypothesize improved sample efficiency and stronger math/coding alignment when mixing sources (human, model, curated) and label types, especially under heavy distribution shift.

I propose a Rule-Guided Copy-or-Innovate forecaster for temporal knowledge graphs that decides, per (subject, relation, time) query, whether to (a) copy from recurrent historical patterns or (b) innovate via structured reasoning. It learns a contrastive history gate that predicts recurrence vs. novelty and, when recurrent, uses a CyGNet-style time-aware copy module; when novel, it aggregates interpretable temporal rules mined via TLogic with a ChronoR-style rotation scorer to infer plausible new tails. The gate is trained with contrastive supervision to separate history-driven from non-history-driven moments, improving both calibration and ranking under distribution shift. The model outputs rule traces for explanations in the innovate mode and retrieved event traces in the copy mode, unifying accuracy with interpretability.

We propose Protocol-Invariant Preference Modeling (PIPM), which learns a single latent utility for each (prompt, response) while using protocol- and annotator-specific link functions to map that utility—and observable response features like verbosity, safety, and style—into either ratings or pairwise rankings. A shared encoder predicts latent utility, while hierarchical calibration with anchor prompts and counterfactual feature perturbations identifies scales and disentangles protocol biases; training jointly maximizes likelihood across both protocols to estimate utility and link parameters. The learned utility serves as a protocol-robust reward for alignment and yields a calibrated evaluation metric consistent across protocols, mitigating effects like verbosity inflation and protocol-dependent model ordering. An active querying policy adaptively chooses ratings vs. rankings per prompt to most reduce uncertainty over utility and link parameters, stabilizing alignment under mixed-feedback settings.

result.text: The paper tackles the communication bottleneck in federated learning by asking whether the space spanned by model gradients over training is low-rank and can therefore be exploited to avoid sending full parameter updates. Observing in centralized training that gradients across epochs lie in a low-dimensional subspace with a few principal components explaining 95–99% of variance, the authors introduce Look-back Gradient Multiplier (LBGM), which recycles past gradient directions and transmits only scalar multipliers for those basis directions instead of full vectors. They analyze LBGM’s convergence to characterize the trade-off between reduced communication and potential accuracy loss, and empirically show that LBGM substantially cuts transmission costs across datasets and models while remaining compatible with and improvable by existing sparsification methods.

result.text: The paper tackles the gap between neural combinatorial optimization methods that produce good single-shot solutions and classical hand-crafted heuristics that effectively exploit available compute via search, aiming to give neural methods a search procedure that leverages solving time. args.text: We propose an error-bounded surface curriculum for neural SDF renderers that leverages the analytic opacity approximation bounds induced by SDF-to-density mappings to decide when and how to transition from volumetric to tight surface rendering. Concretely, we maintain per-ray bounds on residual transmittance and adaptively shrink sampling support around the zero level set while annealing the SDF-to-density scale, sending rays whose bounded error is below a threshold into an unbiased near-surface rendering regime and keeping the rest volumetric. We further stabilize learning with a phase-transition loss that unifies occupancy and signed distance, injecting a minimal-surface prior that preserves thin structures and suppresses spurious geometry during the transition. This controller-driven curriculum reduces samples, accelerates convergence, and improves surface fidelity over fixed schedules across scenes with large free space and fine detail.

result.text: The paper addresses limitations of standard score-based diffusion models that use Gaussian (Brownian) noise—namely slow sampling convergence (high NFE), limited diversity and mode collapse on imbalanced data—by asking whether a non-Gaussian stochastic process can improve sampling speed and diversity. The key insight is that isotropic α-stable Lévy processes, which are heavy-tailed and can make large jumps, yield a different forward-noise geometry that permits faster exploration of the data manifold and alleviates mode-collapse while still supporting a principled reverse-time dynamics. Concretely, the authors derive an exact reverse-time stochastic differential equation for Lévy-driven forward dynamics, propose a fractional denoising score-matching objective to estimate the score under α-stable noise, and implement the Lévy-Itô Model (LIM), demonstrating empirically on CIFAR-10, CelebA and imbalanced CIFAR10LT that LIM achieves substantially better FID, recall and faster wall-clock sampling (e.g., 1.58 FID and 0.7006 recall on CelebA with 2× speedup) compared to Gaussian DDPM baselines.

args.text: We propose Curvature-aware MARINA: a quasi-Newton variant that piggybacks compressed secant information onto MARINA’s gradient-difference messages to learn a streaming low-rank inverse-Hessian preconditioner at the server with no extra communication rounds. Clients maintain error-compensated memories of recent step and gradient-difference pairs, periodically sending a few contractively-compressed L-BFGS pairs or randomized curvature sketches that the server aggregates to update a Nyström/L-BFGS preconditioner used to precondition subsequent MARINA steps; a DCAC-style analysis yields convergence under biased compressors and predicts local superlinear behavior once curvature tracks the optimum. The method supports partial participation and bidirectional compression as in FedNL, targets nonconvex but PL objectives, and aims to reduce rounds by 1.5–3× versus first-order MARINA at the same bit budget under data heterogeneity.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of characterizing and bounding the separation power of arbitrary graph neural network (GNN) architectures—i.e., their ability to distinguish non-isomorphic graphs—without requiring bespoke analyses tied to specific models. Its key insight is to represent GNN computations as expressions in a procedural tensor language whose syntax (number of indices and nesting depth of summations) directly controls expressive power relative to Weisfeiler-Leman (WL) tests, making WL-based separation bounds immediate. Using this tensor-language view the authors define higher-order message-passing neural networks (k-MPNNs) as a natural extension of MPNNs, derive separation-power bounds and universality results by simple index/summation counting, and show how architectural choices map to WL strength. The resulting toolbox lets designers analyze and boost GNN separation power systematically—e.g., by increasing tensor order or summation depth—without deep familiarity with WL intricacies.

args.text: I propose Propensity-Corrected Listwise NCA (PC-ListNCA), a single-stage alignment objective that combines NCA’s absolute-likelihood anchoring with listwise ordering over n-candidate sets while correcting for mixed-source sampling bias. The loss maximizes log p(y*|x) with a barrier/floor on the chosen response and applies a soft-margin contrast against all other candidates using cross-batch negatives, weighting each contrast by inverse propensity of its sampling source to make updates invariant to candidate-set composition and size. This preserves chosen-response probabilities (addressing the decreasing-likelihood issue) while recovering the richer supervisory signal of listwise ranking from multi-candidate preferences. We hypothesize improved stability and generalization on math/coding and better off-policy robustness when combining explicit scalar rewards and preference data within the same batches.

Temporal KG forecasters often degrade under distribution shift, e.g., when recurrence patterns break or exogenous events alter dynamics. We propose Invariant Temporal Mechanisms for TKGs (ITM-TKG), which augments a strong temporal embedding backbone with a copy/generate switch and a history-vs-nonhistory gate, but trains them to isolate causal, time-invariant relational mechanisms by enforcing risk-invariance across pseudo-environments built from time windows and entity cohorts and by anchoring with interpretable rule-based features. Concretely, we regularize the model so that predictions supported by learned temporal rules remain stable across environments, while nuisance, time-specific signals are absorbed into separate components via gradient-penalized invariance objectives and counterfactual perturbations of rules and histories. This yields more reliable OOD forecasting and explanations under regime changes, improving robustness when recurrence weakens or novel entities emerge.

We propose Protocol-Invariant Preference Learning (PIPL), a unified alignment framework that learns a shared latent utility over model responses while modeling ratings and rankings as protocol-specific observation processes with annotator- and content-dependent biases (e.g., verbosity, style). Concretely, we fit a hierarchical Thurstone/Plackett–Luce–style model that jointly explains pairwise/listwise choices and cardinal scores, with nuisance terms for length and density and annotator-scale/anchoring, then train the LLM to match listwise probabilities induced by the inferred latent utility so that preferences are consistent across protocols. A cross-protocol calibration design with anchor prompts and randomized style perturbations identifies bias parameters and yields a reward that is robust to protocol switches, reducing the 60% disagreement and producing models that win under both rating- and ranking-based evaluations. This bridges pairwise/listwise alignment and cardinal feedback without RL instability, combining PRO-style listwise supervision with a principled debiasing and aggregation layer.

result.text: The paper tackles the communication bottleneck in federated learning by asking whether the space spanned by model gradients over training is low-rank and can therefore be exploited to avoid sending full parameter updates. Observing in centralized training that gradients across epochs lie in a low-dimensional subspace with a few principal components explaining 95–99% of variance, the authors introduce Look-back Gradient Multiplier (LBGM), which recycles past gradient directions and transmits only scalar multipliers for those basis directions instead of full vectors. They analyze LBGM’s convergence to characterize the trade-off between reduced communication and potential accuracy loss, and empirically show that LBGM substantially cuts transmission costs across datasets and models while remaining compatible with and improvable by existing sparsification methods.

result.text: The paper addresses the mismatch between standard diffusion generative models and the multi-scale, locally smoothing structure of images by proposing a generative process that explicitly reverses a PDE which erases fine-scale detail. The key insight is that running the heat equation with additive noise forward acts like a structured variational encoder that progressively removes high-frequency content, so stochastically inverting this heat dissipation yields a diffusion-like model with an implicit coarse-to-fine inductive bias and emergent disentanglement of global color and shape. Methodologically, the authors formalize the forward heat-plus-noise process as a variational approximation within the diffusion latent-variable framework, derive and train a corresponding reverse stochastic process that undoes heat diffusion on the image plane, and analyze its spectral behavior to connect and contrast it with standard diffusion models.

args.text: Introduce a curvature-aware SDF-to-density mapping for neural volume rendering that modulates the Laplace-CDF scale β(x) by local surface geometry, using Hessian-based curvature estimates from the SDF to temporarily thicken density near high-curvature or thin structures and anneal β(x) as uncertainty decreases. We extend the opacity error bound used for ray sampling to the spatially varying β(x), yielding provably accurate sampling while retaining the unbiased NeuS-style rendering loss. A phase-transition regularizer ties the induced occupancy to the log-distance field, encouraging minimal surfaces where evidence is weak while preventing over-smoothing on detailed regions. This plug-in mapping and loss stabilize early training and improve recovery of thin/occluded geometry, producing crisper surfaces and faster convergence across SDF-based reconstruction and 3D-aware synthesis.

result.text: The paper tackles the slow sampling speed of diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs), which typically require hundreds or thousands of neural-network evaluations to generate samples. The key insight is an exact formulation of the diffusion ODE solution that analytically isolates the linear part and, after a change of variables, rewrites the remaining contribution as an exponentially weighted integral of the neural network, enabling high-order numerical integration rather than leaving everything to black-box ODE solvers. Based on this, the authors derive DPM-Solver, a dedicated high-order ODE solver with convergence-order guarantees that works for both discrete- and continuous-time DPMs without additional training and drastically reduces required function evaluations. Empirically, DPM-Solver produces high-quality samples in about 10–20 evaluations (e.g., 4.70 FID at 10 steps and 2.87 FID at 20 on CIFAR-10) and yields roughly 4–16× speedups over prior training-free samplers.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of generating high-quality synthetic tabular data that must handle heterogeneous field types and missing values while providing strong privacy-utility tradeoffs. The key insight is that a masked-transformer architecture with tailored masking strategies can natively represent mixed-type columns, model dependencies between fields, and impute or generate missing entries, yielding better sample fidelity and privacy behavior than existing autoregressive or ad-hoc tabular generators. The method, TabMT, adapts masked-transformer blocks and introduces improved masking schemes and training protocols specifically for tabular structures, enabling conditional and unconditional sampling, native missing-value handling, and scalable training across very small to very large tables; empirical evaluation shows state-of-the-art generation quality and superior privacy-utility tradeoffs.

args.text: Introduce Temporal Homomorphism-augmented TGNs (THoG): augment injective, relative-position MP-TGNs with auxiliary channels that maintain incremental counts/similarities between small time-labeled pattern graphs and each node’s recent temporal neighborhood. By combining temporal WL–style injective updates with temporal homomorphism features (instantiated via KerGNN-like learned filter graphs rather than hand-picked motifs), the model can approximate any function that depends only on indistinguishability under a rich temporal pattern family, yielding provable expressivity gains. To remain scalable, we compute these features only over sparsity-selected node/edge tuples à la SpeqNets and update them in a streaming fashion as events arrive. We hypothesize strong improvements on dynamic link prediction, motif detection, and anomaly benchmarks, with PEG-style O(p)-equivariant treatment of positional channels to stabilize training and generalization.

Rank-to-Reward Calibrated NCA (RRC-NCA): given multi-candidate preference data, first infer per-prompt scalar utilities by fitting a Bradley–Terry/Plackett–Luce model to the human ranking (or best-of-n sets), with a temperature chosen to match the model’s current logit scale. Train the policy using an NCA objective to maximize absolute likelihood on high-utility responses while applying an InfoNCA-style relative adjustment among the remaining candidates to shape the full ordering. Mix these implicit utilities seamlessly with any explicit scalar rewards when available, and adaptively downweight the relative term where the utility posterior is uncertain to avoid overfitting to noisy or tied preferences. This hybrid preserves NCA’s non-decreasing chosen likelihood while retaining ranking-based supervision to order negatives, improving stability and sample efficiency over purely relative objectives.

We propose Rule-Contrastive Copy-or-Rotate (RCCR) for temporal KG forecasting: a hybrid that decides whether a query is history-driven by contrasting temporal logical rule evidence with a learned non-historical prior, then conditionally routes prediction. When history dominates, RCCR copies from a rule-grounded candidate pool augmented with recent recurrences to capture both multi-hop temporal logic and repetition; otherwise it generates via a time-conditioned rotation scorer to handle novel, non-recurrent events. A learned switch is trained with contrastive supervision to separate history vs. non-history regimes, and we add a lightweight conformal temporal calibration layer to output reliable prediction sets under non-stationarity. RCCR targets state-of-the-art accuracy while providing interpretable rationales (via the activated rules and copy sources) and calibrated uncertainty.

We propose Protocol-Invariant Preference Optimization (PIPO), which learns a shared latent utility for candidate LLM responses while explicitly modeling protocol- and annotator-specific observation models that map utilities to ratings or rankings (e.g., ordered logit with per-annotator thresholds and density sensitivity for ratings; Plackett–Luce/Thurstone with accuracy-vs-fluency weights for rankings). We fit the latent model on mixed-format data via variational EM, anchored by a small overlap set annotated in both formats, and then train the policy to maximize expected latent utility rather than protocol-specific labels. This unifies and extends ranking-based and pairwise-preference alignment, producing policies whose measured quality is stable across evaluation formats and reducing protocol-induced reversals. We also introduce protocol-robust evaluation by counterfactually mapping outputs into both formats using the learned observation models to report format-invariant scores.

result.text: The paper addresses slow convergence in federated learning arising from non-i.i.d. client data, which the authors attribute in part to catastrophic forgetting during local client updates that degrades performance on data learned by other clients. Their key insight is to alleviate this forgetting by regularizing local training with a loss evaluated on pseudo data that encode the global model's knowledge of previous clients, thereby preserving cross-client information while clients train locally. They propose FedReg, which generates pseudo samples from the global model and adds a regularization term using these pseudo data during each client's local optimization, accelerating convergence and improving robustness and privacy against gradient inversion attacks. Experiments show FedReg notably speeds up training—especially for deep networks and highly non-i.i.d. data—while enhancing classification privacy and attack resilience.

result.text: The paper addresses why differentially private (DP) learning sometimes avoids the expected degradation in utility as model dimension grows, a phenomenon at odds with classical bounds that worsen with model size. The key insight is that performance depends not on raw parameter dimensionality but on the magnitudes of gradients when projected onto low-dimensional subspaces—if gradients concentrate in a few principal directions then privacy noise has much less harm. Methodologically, the authors formalize this via a "restricted Lipschitz continuity" condition for convex objectives, prove improved excess empirical and population risk bounds that can be independent of ambient dimension under additional assumptions, and empirically validate that gradients during private fine-tuning of large language models are dominated by a few principal components, explaining why large pretrained models can be privately fine-tuned effectively.

The paper tackles the challenge of improving test-time search for learned sequential solvers of combinatorial optimization, where prior active search methods adapt all model weights per instance but are prohibitively costly and ineffective compared to specialized solvers. Its key insight is that adapting only a small subset of model parameters during instance-specific active search can retain most of the benefit of full fine-tuning while drastically cutting time and memory costs. Concretely, the authors propose and evaluate three efficient active-search variants that update only selected parameters (e.g., output layers or low-rank adapters) with reinforcement-learning style objectives at test time, and demonstrate these methods substantially boost solution quality over the base model, outperform other ML-based approaches and even beat the LKH3 heuristic on capacitated vehicle routing, while also enabling generalization to much larger instances than seen in training.

args.text: I propose an alpha-scheduled Lévy diffusion model that anneals the stability index from heavy-tailed (alpha < 2) early to Gaussian late, paired with a high-order jump-aware sampler that extends DPM-Solver’s exponential-integrator idea to reverse-time jump SDEs. Concretely, we split the reverse dynamics into a linear part with an analytic update and a nonlinear score integral, approximate small jumps by a diffusion surrogate while simulating large jumps via Poisson thinning to retain heavy-tailed exploration, enabling high-fidelity sampling in 10–20 steps. Training uses a hybrid objective that emphasizes fractional denoising score matching at early times and standard Gaussian DSM near the end of the schedule, computing the needed fractional operators via finite-difference directional-derivative reformulations for efficiency and stability. This design should improve recall and wall-clock speed on imbalanced datasets while allowing per-sample alpha(t) control (e.g., conditioned on score norms) to balance exploration and fidelity.

result.text: The paper addresses convergence and complexity of distributed stochastic gradient methods under communication constraints and delays, covering quantized, error‑compensated, and delayed SGD variants. Its key insight is a unified analytical framework — a single theorem — that captures arbitrary compression operators, error feedback, delay, variance reduction, and sampling, which yields tighter (often best-known) complexity bounds for existing schemes and enables new algorithmic combinations. Methodologically, the authors instantiate this framework to derive convergence rates for a family of 16 new methods, including EC-SGD-DIANA (error feedback plus biased compression of gradient differences) and EC-LSVRG-DIANA (adding variance reduction for finite-sum problems), and prove these methods converge to the exact optimum in expectation with a constant stepsize for convex and strongly convex objectives when workers compute full or variance-reduced gradients.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of enabling deep graph convolutional networks (GCNs) by tackling the common over-smoothing problem that causes node representations to become indistinguishable as layers increase. The key insight is that preserving initial node features via residual connections and using identity mapping can prevent feature collapse and stabilize propagation, allowing meaningful depth. They introduce GCNII, a simple extension of vanilla GCN that incorporates initial residual connections and identity mapping into each layer, with theoretical analysis and empirical results showing these techniques mitigate over-smoothing and let much deeper GCNs outperform prior methods on semi- and full-supervised graph tasks.

args.text: Propose Heteroskedastic Calibrated Contrastive Alignment (HCCA), which unifies NCE/InfoNCA’s absolute-likelihood training with listwise ranking while learning a per-prompt temperature τ(x) to match the heteroskedastic dispersion of reward signals. The objective combines (a) an NCE term on absolute rewards parameterized by τ(x), (b) a listwise Plackett–Luce ranking loss over candidates to refine ordering as in preference-ranking methods, and (c) a monotonicity penalty that enforces non-decreasing log-probability for the top-rated response relative to the base policy to avoid the decreasing-likelihood issue. We estimate τ(x) from features such as reward variance or pairwise margins (when only preferences are available) and base-policy entropy using a small calibrator network, enabling training on mixed datasets that contain scalar, listwise, or pairwise supervision by marginalizing missing components. This yields better calibration and preservation of chosen-response probability than InfoNCA alone while leveraging richer listwise supervision for fine-grained ordering.

We propose Protocol-Aware Preference Modeling (PAPM), which unifies ratings and rankings via a shared latent utility over prompt–response pairs and protocol-specific observation models that capture systematic biases (e.g., verbosity inflates ratings, accuracy dominates pairwise), augmented with annotator embeddings and context features for debiasing. Trained jointly on mixed-format feedback, PAPM yields a calibrated reward model and supports two downstream alignments: protocol-invariant alignment via distributionally robust optimization over protocol posteriors, and protocol-targeted alignment that explicitly matches a specified evaluation protocol. We add an active elicitation module that selects between rating or n-way ranking per prompt based on expected information gain per unit cost, plus a protocol-standardized leaderboard that reports utility under the inferred latent model to prevent protocol-induced reversals. By leveraging evidence of protocol disagreement and the strengths of ranking-based optimization, PAPM aims to reduce cross-protocol inconsistency and deliver models that generalize across format shifts while retaining the benefits of each feedback type.

We propose an adaptive Cohort- and Compression-Aware Federated Aggregation (CoCoA-FL) that jointly tunes per-round cohort size and per-client compression levels to maintain a target signal-to-noise ratio in stochastic controlled averaging under partial participation and heterogeneity. The server estimates cross-client gradient variance and compressor-induced distortion online (via residual/error-feedback statistics), then selects the cohort and allocates bit budgets to clients with highest marginal information gain per transmitted bit under a fixed uplink budget, optionally adjusting local steps to balance drift and variance. This yields convergence with linear-speedup characteristics at substantially lower average uplink than fixed-cohort or fixed-precision baselines, and mitigates the large-cohort instabilities by matching aggregation noise to a prescribed schedule. The framework unifies and extends compression-aware SCA and double-compression by making cohort size a controllable degree of freedom tied to measured compression noise rather than a static hyperparameter.

result.text: The paper tackles the slow sampling speed of diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs), which typically require hundreds or thousands of neural-network evaluations to generate samples. The key insight is an exact formulation of the diffusion ODE solution that analytically isolates the linear part and, after a change of variables, rewrites the remaining contribution as an exponentially weighted integral of the neural network, enabling high-order numerical integration rather than leaving everything to black-box ODE solvers. Based on this, the authors derive DPM-Solver, a dedicated high-order ODE solver with convergence-order guarantees that works for both discrete- and continuous-time DPMs without additional training and drastically reduces required function evaluations. Empirically, DPM-Solver produces high-quality samples in about 10–20 evaluations (e.g., 4.70 FID at 10 steps and 2.87 FID at 20 on CIFAR-10) and yields roughly 4–16× speedups over prior training-free samplers.

result.text: The paper addresses the poor generalization of supervised learning models for the traveling salesman problem (TSP), aiming to apply a model trained on small instances to arbitrarily large graphs. The key insight is to reuse a small pre-trained model as a localized feature extractor: by sampling and converting subgraphs from a large instance, producing heat maps that indicate promising edges or nodes, and then merging these heat maps to obtain a global guidance signal. The method combines graph sampling, conversion and heat-map merging to scale the small model to large instances, and feeds the resulting heat maps into a Monte Carlo Tree Search-based reinforcement learning solver to guide search; experiments on instances up to 10,000 vertices show substantially improved solution quality and generalization over prior ML-based TSP approaches.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of how to train implicit neural representations (INRs) for surface reconstruction without having to choose between occupancy or signed distance formulations and without incurring unknown biases from existing losses. result.text: This paper studies how transformer "induction heads" (IHs)—attention heads that implement a match-and-copy operation crucial for in-context learning—emerge during training and why multiple IHs and abrupt phase changes appear. The key insight is that IHs are diverse and additive products of three interacting subcircuits whose coordinated development produces the observed phase transition in loss, and that manipulating activations causally during training can reveal and control these dependencies. Methodologically, the authors train models on synthetic data, introduce an optogenetics-inspired causal framework that clamps or perturbs activations throughout training, and use these interventions to identify and characterize the distinct subcircuits, their interactions, and how they determine IH formation timing and multiplicity.

The paper addresses understanding and unifying convergence behavior of decentralized stochastic gradient methods that use local updates and operate over changing network topologies, a setting that encompasses many methods (gossip, synchronous, local/Federated SGD) previously analyzed separately. Its key insight is that a single, broadly applicable analytic framework—based on weak assumptions about smoothness, network mixing, and data heterogeneity—can interpolate between iid and highly heterogeneous data regimes and thereby recover or improve known rates (including linear rates in over-parameterized cases) for many special cases. Methodologically, the authors propose a general algorithmic template that allows local SGD steps combined with synchronous or pairwise gossip over adaptive graphs, and they derive universal convergence bounds for smooth convex and nonconvex objectives by carefully bounding consensus and optimization errors to yield unified complexity guarantees that match or tighten prior results.

args.text: I propose a differentiable, homomorphism-guided sparse higher-order GNN that adaptively allocates its higher-order computations only where they are most informative. Concretely, the model uses learned small filter graphs (à la KerGNN) to produce differentiable estimates of local homomorphism signals, computes gradient-based utility scores over candidate node tuples, and then applies a budgeted Gumbel-top-k selection to instantiate k-order message passing only on the selected tuples as in sparsity-aware higher-order schemes. Because the guidance draws from a universal family of pattern counts and the restricted higher-order module matches k-WL strength via tensor-order arguments, the architecture approaches k-WL–level expressivity while keeping cost near-linear in edges plus the selection budget. This yields accuracy gains on sparse graphs with rare or localized motifs and improves interpretability by exposing which motifs and tuples triggered higher-order expansion, outperforming heuristic tuple selection baselines.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem that standard training and evaluation metrics for summarization (predicting reference summaries and optimizing ROUGE) are poor proxies for true summary quality, limiting model progress. Its key insight is that models can be substantially improved by learning from human preferences: a learned reward model that predicts which of two summaries humans prefer provides a better training signal than reference likelihood or ROUGE. Methodologically, the authors collect a large dataset of human pairwise comparisons of summaries, train a reward model to predict those preferences, and then fine-tune a summarization policy with reinforcement learning to maximize that learned reward; this approach yields summaries that outperform supervised baselines and reference summaries on Reddit TL;DR and transfer well to CNN/DM without domain-specific tuning.

args.text: We propose Protocol-Consistent Reward Modeling (PCRM), a unified preference model that learns a shared latent utility for responses while fitting protocol- and annotator-specific link functions—Plackett–Luce for rankings, and ordinal logistic for ratings augmented with annotator leniency and density/verbosity biases. Trained jointly on pooled data plus a small “bridging” set receiving both protocols to fix identifiability, PCRM yields protocol-invariant scores for evaluation and alignment by optimizing a DPO/PRO-style objective against the shared utility. An active calibration module selects prompts/responses for dual-annotation where cross-protocol mappings are most uncertain, improving data efficiency. PCRM aims to eliminate protocol-dependent reversals, transfer better across rating- and rank-based evals, and provide clearer diagnostics of annotator and protocol effects.

result.text: We propose an adaptive Cohort- and Compression-Aware Federated Aggregation (CoCoA-FL) that jointly tunes per-round cohort size and per-client compression levels to maintain a target signal-to-noise ratio in stochastic controlled averaging under partial participation and heterogeneity. The server estimates cross-client gradient variance and compressor-induced distortion online (via residual/error-feedback statistics), then selects the cohort and allocates bit budgets to clients with highest marginal information gain per transmitted bit under a fixed uplink budget, optionally adjusting local steps to balance drift and variance. This yields convergence with linear-speedup characteristics at substantially lower average uplink than fixed-cohort or fixed-precision baselines, and mitigates the large-cohort instabilities by matching aggregation noise to a prescribed schedule. The framework unifies and extends compression-aware SCA and double-compression by making cohort size a controllable degree of freedom tied to measured compression noise rather than a static hyperparameter.

result.text: The paper addresses the complexity and fragmented design choices in diffusion-based generative models that obscure which components truly drive sample quality and efficiency. Its key insight is that sampling, training, and score-network preconditioning choices can be cleanly separated into a unified design space, and that several targeted modifications across these axes—rather than wholesale architectural changes—unlock large gains in speed and fidelity. Methodologically, the authors formalize this design space, identify and apply specific improvements to sampling algorithms, training objectives, and network preconditioning, and demonstrate their modular benefits by retrofitting prior pretrained score networks and retraining models to achieve state-of-the-art FIDs (e.g., CIFAR-10 unconditional and class-conditional) with far fewer network evaluations.

args.text: I propose Latent-Adapter Beam Search (LABS): shift test-time exploration from solution space to a compact latent policy–adapter space. Concretely, pretrain a z-conditioned routing policy and attach tiny low-rank adapters; at inference, run simulation-guided beam search over candidate (z, adapter) pairs, where rollouts score each candidate, adapters are updated by a few efficient active-search steps, and POMO-style multi-starts ensure symmetry coverage. This unifies latent diversity, parameter-efficient per-instance adaptation, and simulation-guided selection to yield diverse, high-quality heuristics at low cost. We expect LABS to outperform latent sampling, active search, and SGBS on TSP/CVRP and to extend to matrix-structured problems like FFSP when paired with a MatNet-style front end, especially under distribution shifts.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of poor and noisy geometry reconstruction in neural volume rendering, where prior methods model geometry indirectly via a generic density field and extract surfaces from arbitrary density level sets. The key insight is to reverse this relationship by modeling volume density as an explicit function of a signed distance function (SDF), specifically using the Laplace cumulative distribution function applied to the SDF, which provides a strong geometric inductive bias, enables a bound on opacity approximation error for accurate ray sampling, and facilitates disentanglement of shape and appearance. The method implements this SDF-to-density mapping within a neural volume rendering pipeline, uses the error bound to drive efficient and precise ray sampling for tight coupling of geometry and radiance, and trains the model in an unsupervised multiview setting to produce higher-fidelity geometry and allow swapping of shape and appearance across scenes.

result.text: This paper studies how transformer "induction heads" (IHs)—attention heads that implement a match-and-copy operation crucial for in-context learning—emerge during training and why multiple IHs and abrupt phase changes appear. The key insight is that IHs are diverse and additive products of three interacting subcircuits whose coordinated development produces the observed phase transition in loss, and that manipulating activations causally during training can reveal and control these dependencies. Methodologically, the authors train models on synthetic data, introduce an optogenetics-inspired causal framework that clamps or perturbs activations throughout training, and use these interventions to identify and characterize the distinct subcircuits, their interactions, and how they determine IH formation timing and multiplicity.

The paper tackles the gap between Bayesian uncertainty estimates from Gaussian Process (GP) regression and the need for rigorous frequentist confidence bounds in safety-critical applications, where existing provable bounds are too conservative to be practical. Its key insight is to derive new concentration inequalities and error decompositions that yield explicit, computable frequentist uncertainty bounds for GP regression which are significantly tighter than prior theoretical guarantees while still remaining provably valid. The method combines refined analysis of the GP posterior, sharper control of information gain and effective dimension, and handling of model misspecification to produce bounds that degrade gracefully under mismatch; these bounds are efficiently evaluable and demonstrated empirically to enable safer, more practical learning-based control.

args.text: We propose FastWeight-SpeqGNN, a permutation-equivariant GNN that couples sparsity-aware higher-order tuple selection with a fast-weight programmable message-passing mechanism. At each layer, a SpeqNet-style selector builds a small set of informative k-tuples; the model then writes delta-rule updates with learned, input-conditioned learning rates into a graph-local associative memory keyed by tuple structural signatures and features, enabling subsequent messages to retrieve example-specific interactions and rapidly correct tuple relations without retraining. This yields higher-order, instance-adaptive expressivity at sparsity-scaled cost, improving robustness to distribution shift and few-shot generalization compared to static higher-order schemes. We will test static variants on subgraph and graph-level tasks and extend to temporal graphs using injective updates and relative positional encodings to align with temporal-WL prescriptions.

I propose Off-Policy Calibrated NCE (OPC-NCE), an alignment objective that extends NCA/InfoNCA to heterogeneous candidate pools by adding principled off-policy correction and rank-to-reward calibration. For each training set of responses drawn from different sources (current policy, past checkpoints, other LLMs, humans), OPC-NCE estimates density ratios between the sampling distribution and the current policy via a lightweight discriminator, and applies self-normalized importance weights with control variates to stabilize the NCE objective while preserving chosen-response likelihoods. When only rankings are available, it maps ranks to calibrated pseudo-rewards via isotonic regression, unifying scalar and ranking supervision in a single contrastive loss; negatives are adaptively sampled from a reward-conditioned buffer to target the decision boundary rather than far-easy negatives. This yields the simplicity and likelihood preservation of NCA while robustly handling the best-of-n, mixed-source setting of RRHF and the full-list supervision of PRO.

result.text: The paper tackles temporal knowledge base completion—predicting time-sensitive facts like (US, has president, ?, 2012)—by extending static link-prediction models to handle facts that hold only during particular time intervals. Its key insight is that temporal KBs can be modeled as fourth-order tensors (subject, predicate, object, time) and that adapting canonical tensor decompositions and complex-valued factorization (ComplEx) with time-aware factors and tailored regularizers better captures temporal dependencies. The authors propose a temporal extension of ComplEx (and related tensor-decomposition formulations) with new regularization schemes that enforce structured temporal smoothness and parameter sharing, demonstrate improved link-prediction performance, and introduce a much larger Wikidata-derived temporal benchmark to evaluate temporal and non-temporal methods.

args.text: We propose Pessimistic Preference Alignment (PePA), an offline alignment algorithm that merges multi-protocol preference supervision with bandit-style pessimism to handle prompt distribution shift. PePA learns from full preference rankings (and maps ratings into rankings via a bias-corrected annotator model) while training the policy with a pessimism regularizer that down-weights or penalizes candidate responses in low-support regions, using uncertainty derived from a reward model’s epistemic variance and an effective-dimension proxy. Concretely, we extend ranking-based preference optimization with a lower-confidence bound objective on response utilities so the model preserves alignment where data are plentiful and avoids overconfident shifts where data are scarce, and we pair this with offline counterfactual evaluation to validate policy improvements under domain shift. Experiments under synthetic and real prompt shifts show PePA retains preference quality out-of-distribution better than standard ranking- or rating-based alignment, and reduces protocol-induced evaluation reversals by jointly modeling annotator biases.

result.text: The paper addresses reducing uplink communication in federated learning under realistic challenges—partial client participation and heterogeneous data—while handling the distortion introduced by communication compression. Its key insight is that the classical stochastic controlled averaging (SCA) can be reformulated into an equivalent but simpler and more communication-efficient implementation that halves uplink cost and serves as a foundation for compression-aware algorithms. Building on that reformulation, the authors develop two algorithms—SCALLION for unbiased compressors and SCAFCOM for biased compressors—that integrate compressed updates without extra assumptions on compression error or limits on heterogeneity, and they prove improved communication and computation complexity relative to prior work. Empirically, both methods match full-precision FL performance with much less uplink transmission and beat recent compressed-FL baselines under the same communication budget.

result.text: The paper tackles the inefficiency of training larger transformer models from scratch when smaller pretrained instances exist, asking how to reuse their parameters to speed up scaling. Its key insight is that a learned linear mapping from smaller to larger model parameters can effectively transfer knowledge, and that this mapping can be made tractable and inductive by factoring it into separate width- and depth-growth operators and imposing Kronecker structure to encode architectural priors. The method, called LiGO, trains these factored linear growth operators to map parameters of a pretrained small transformer into initial weights for a larger transformer, and empirical results on language and vision transformers show LiGO reduces training compute by up to 50% and outperforms other reuse-based initialization baselines.

args.text: I propose a subband-aware neural rendering curriculum that fuses polynomial neural fields (PNFs) with SDF-based volume rendering to improve reflectance decomposition and geometry fidelity. Radiance is decomposed into Fourier PNF subbands and trained with a band-specific regime: low-frequency bands use volumetric rendering to provide dense gradients, while high-frequency bands rapidly transition to surface-focused rendering via an SDF/occupancy schedule driven by per-band convergence criteria. The SDF-to-density mapping enforces tight shape–appearance coupling, and a Neural-PIL module pre-integrates lighting in the low-frequency channels to stabilize per-image illumination estimation. This design aims to yield sharper speculars and textures with consistent surfaces, faster convergence, and better BRDF/illumination disentanglement than monolithic radiance fields.

result.text: The paper addresses how and in what order neural networks learn statistical structure from data, testing the distributional simplicity bias (DSB) that networks acquire low-order statistics before higher-order correlations. The key insight is that networks early in training implicitly match maximum-entropy distributions whose low-order moments equal the training set, and this preference can be observed in both continuous and discrete domains by linking token n-gram frequencies to moments of embedding vectors. Methodologically, the authors provide theoretical equivalence for discrete tokens, measure performance on maximum-entropy surrogates across training to show early-stage alignment and later divergence, and use optimal transport to edit low-order class statistics—demonstrating that early-training networks treat edited samples as belonging to the target class—supported by experiments on LLMs and code release.

The paper addresses the problem of obtaining reliable uniform error bounds for Gaussian process (GP) models in safety-critical applications when kernel hyperparameters are unknown, a setting where existing guarantees typically fail. The key insight is that one can construct a data-driven confidence region over hyperparameters and then derive a probabilistic upper bound on the GP model error that holds uniformly for any hyperparameter inside that region, avoiding the need for prior bounds on hyperparameters. Methodologically, the authors develop algorithms to estimate this hyperparameter confidence set from observed data, use it to compute robust GP error bounds, and apply these bounds to provide performance guarantees for learning-based control; experiments demonstrate better empirical tightness than standard and fully Bayesian GP approaches.

result.text: The paper studies how recurrent neural circuits can reliably encode time-varying stimuli despite intrinsic neuronal noise, heterogeneous synaptic weights, chaotic dynamics, and synaptic delays, and asks which circuit features enable error scaling better than the classical 1/√N law. Its key insight is that tight balance between strong feedforward drive and equally strong recurrent feedback implements predictive coding that cancels errors and can produce superclassical 1/N scaling, and that this benefit can be maintained or degraded depending on the degree of balance, weight disorder, noise and delays. To make these dependencies tractable the authors introduce an analytically solvable model that separates the degree of balance from weight disorder and develop a mean-field theory that quantifies coding accuracy as a function of noise, chaos, delays and balance, thereby unifying and extending previous balanced network and predictive coding models.

The paper addresses the risk that black-box finetuning interfaces for large language models can be abused to stealthily undermine model safety. Its key insight is that an adversary can craft a training set whose individual examples look benign but collectively teach the model a covert mapping from encoded prompts to encoded harmful responses, allowing unsafe behavior to be activated only by encoded triggers and thereby evading conventional defenses. The authors implement this covert malicious finetuning by constructing and using such a dataset to adapt GPT-4, demonstrating a model that follows harmful instructions 99% of the time while slipping past dataset inspection, standard safety evaluations, and input/output classifiers. Their results cast doubt on the ability to secure black-box finetuning against sophisticated, covert adversaries and suggest the need for fundamentally different defenses or tighter access controls.

args.text: TriMix-TKG is an adaptive mixture-of-experts framework that unifies temporal rule reasoning, copy-based recurrence, and neural generation for temporal knowledge graph forecasting. It learns temporal logical rules with time-consistent grounding to produce interpretable rule scores, integrates a time-aware copy mechanism for recurrent facts, and uses a rotation-based generator for novel links; a contrastive gate, trained to detect history-driven vs non-historical queries, assigns per-query mixture weights and can hard-mask implausible candidates. We add uncertainty-aware calibration and time-decay regularization to stabilize switching and ensure temporal consistency, and train the experts with auxiliary distillation so they benefit from each other’s signals. This yields strong performance on both repetitive and novel events while providing faithful, rule-based explanations when applicable.

result.text: The paper addresses how to exploit multiple possible linear representations in contextual bandits to minimize regret, noting that some representations can be "good" and yield constant problem-dependent regret while others do not. The key insight is that one can adaptively select or even implicitly construct a representation from a candidate set so that the learner's regret is never much worse than running LinUCB on the best representation and thus inherits constant regret whenever a good representation exists. The proposed method is a novel selection algorithm that maintains and evaluates M candidate representations, combining their performance with a logarithmic-in-M overhead to guarantee regret within a ln M factor of the best representation, and includes mechanisms to implicitly form a good representation when none of the initial candidates are good; theoretical guarantees and empirical experiments on standard contextual bandit benchmarks validate these claims.

result.text: The paper studies how the number of clients sampled per round (cohort size) affects model quality and training dynamics in federated learning, addressing scalability, analogies to centralized batch-size effects, and how to exploit large cohorts. The key insight is that increasing cohort size yields both familiar large-batch phenomena (diminishing returns, generalization gaps) and federated-specific issues (training instabilities, fairness degradation and client heterogeneity interactions) so larger cohorts are not uniformly beneficial. The authors empirically analyze many realistic federated settings, quantifying performance, convergence, and fairness as cohort size grows, and compare algorithmic choices and hyperparameter scaling strategies to identify which adjustments (e.g., learning-rate schedules, aggregation rules) mitigate problems and when larger cohorts help versus hurt.

Its key insight is to structure neural fields as polynomial neural fields (PNFs) that decompose a signal into a sum of manipulable, interpretable components (subbands) while retaining the representational strengths of neural fields. The authors develop a general theoretical framework for designing PNFs and instantiate it as Fourier PNFs that achieve state-of-the-art signal representation quality; they show how the polynomial composition enables direct subband operations for tasks like texture transfer and scale-space interpolation and provide empirical results and code validating both representation fidelity and manipulation capabilities.

result.text: The paper addresses how and in what order neural networks learn statistical structure from data, testing the distributional simplicity bias (DSB) that networks acquire low-order statistics before higher-order correlations. The key insight is that networks early in training implicitly match maximum-entropy distributions whose low-order moments equal the training set, and this preference can be observed in both continuous and discrete domains by linking token n-gram frequencies to moments of embedding vectors. Methodologically, the authors provide theoretical equivalence for discrete tokens, measure performance on maximum-entropy surrogates across training to show early-stage alignment and later divergence, and use optimal transport to edit low-order class statistics—demonstrating that early-training networks treat edited samples as belonging to the target class—supported by experiments on LLMs and code release.

args.text: We propose Robust Hyperparameter-SafeOpt, a safe exploration framework for Gaussian process (GP) optimization and learning-based control when kernel hyperparameters are unknown. The method maintains a data-driven confidence set over hyperparameters and computes uniform, frequentist error envelopes that hold for all hyperparameters in the set, choosing actions that maximize safe improvement under the worst-case model while allocating targeted probes that most shrink the hyperparameter set. This yields finite-time safety and near-optimal regret without assuming known hyperparameters, made tractable via surrogate bounds that combine effective-dimension control with sensitivity of the GP posterior to hyperparameters. Experiments on safe Bayesian optimization and safe control show faster safe-set expansion and higher reward than GP-UCB/SafeOpt baselines and fully Bayesian approaches while retaining provable validity.

result.text: The paper studies how recurrent neural circuits can reliably encode time-varying stimuli despite intrinsic neuronal noise, heterogeneous synaptic weights, chaotic dynamics, and synaptic delays, and asks which circuit features enable error scaling better than the classical 1/√N law. Its key insight is that tight balance between strong feedforward drive and equally strong recurrent feedback implements predictive coding that cancels errors and can produce superclassical 1/N scaling, and that this benefit can be maintained or degraded depending on the degree of balance, weight disorder, noise and delays. To make these dependencies tractable the authors introduce an analytically solvable model that separates the degree of balance from weight disorder and develop a mean-field theory that quantifies coding accuracy as a function of noise, chaos, delays and balance, thereby unifying and extending previous balanced network and predictive coding models.
