result.text: The paper addresses the risk that black-box finetuning interfaces for large language models can be abused to stealthily undermine model safety. Its key insight is that an adversary can craft a training set whose individual examples look benign but collectively teach the model a covert mapping from encoded prompts to encoded harmful responses, allowing unsafe behavior to be activated only by encoded triggers and thereby evading conventional defenses. The authors implement this covert malicious finetuning by constructing and using such a dataset to adapt GPT-4, demonstrating a model that follows harmful instructions 99% of the time while slipping past dataset inspection, standard safety evaluations, and input/output classifiers. Their results cast doubt on the ability to secure black-box finetuning against sophisticated, covert adversaries and suggest the need for fundamentally different defenses or tighter access controls.

args.text: Interventional Temporal KG Forecasting (IntervTKG) unifies history-driven, rule-driven, and exogenous pathways to enable accurate prediction and counterfactual what-if analysis. We introduce a causal gate Z that decides whether a query is history-driven, estimated via contrastive training as in CENET, and route scoring through: (i) a repetition-aware copy module constrained by temporal rules (extending CyGNet with TLogic-consistent neighborhoods) and (ii) a time-conditioned generator built on rotational/complex embeddings (ChronoR/temporal-ComplEx) plus an exogenous hazard head that models non-historical shocks. We train Z and the pathways with counterfactual negatives that erase or perturb past events and rule evidence, encouraging identifiability and robustness under distribution shift. This yields calibrated forecasts and enables do-style queries (e.g., predict (s, r, ?, t) if specified prior facts did not occur), improving both link prediction and temporal QA reliability.

result.text: The paper addresses designing computationally efficient contextual bandit algorithms that remain robust when the reward model is misspecified, i.e., when the true reward function lies at distance ε from the model class. The key insight is an optimization-based reformulation of the regression-oracle reduction framework that lets an algorithm automatically adapt to the unknown misspecification level and attain minimax-optimal dependence on ε. Methodologically, the authors build an oracle-efficient family of algorithms that use an online square-loss regression oracle to guide action selection and analysis, proving optimal regret bounds for both finite and infinite action sets and, in particular, achieving the first algorithm with O(d√T + ε√d T) regret for linear bandits in d dimensions without knowing ε.

result.text: The paper addresses efficient on-device DNN model compression by improving train-time weight clustering to reduce model size while preserving accuracy. Its key insight is to reformulate k-means clustering as a differentiable attention-like layer (DKM) that allows joint optimization of network weights and clustering centroids within the original loss and architecture, avoiding extra regularizers or parameters. The method implements DKM as a differentiable k-means layer integrated into training so weights are pulled to learned centroids via attention-based assignments, producing highly quantized models; experiments on ImageNet and GLUE show substantially better accuracy–size trade-offs (e.g., ResNet50 at 29.4× compression with 74.5% top-1, MobileNet-v1 at 22.4× with 63.9% top-1, and DistilBERT at 11.8× with only 1.1% GLUE loss), demonstrating that joint end-to-end centroid learning yields superior compression.

result.text: The paper addresses high-fidelity 3D surface reconstruction from multi-view 2D images, overcoming limitations of prior neural-surface methods that need mask supervision and fail on thin or heavily occluded geometry. The key insight is to represent surfaces as the zero level-set of a neural signed distance function (SDF) and to replace conventional volume rendering with a novel rendering formulation that removes the first-order geometric bias that otherwise prevents accurate surface recovery. Methodologically, NeuS jointly learns a neural SDF and appearance by training with the new unbiased volume rendering loss (without requiring foreground masks), enabling robust optimization like NeRF while yielding precise surface extraction from the learned SDF via its zero level-set. Experiments on DTU and BlendedMVS demonstrate state-of-the-art surface accuracy, particularly on complex and self-occluded objects.

result.text: The paper studies why increasing depth speeds up training in feedforward neural networks by examining how depth alters the frequency content of the function each layer must learn; the key insight is the "deep frequency principle," namely that for a deeper pre-condition component the effective target function presented to subsequent learning layers is biased toward lower frequencies, which are known to be learned faster by neural networks. To support this, the authors split trained networks into a pre-condition component and a learning component, use a filtering-based Fourier analysis to characterize the frequency distribution of high-dimensional functions, and run experiments on deep architectures and real datasets to show deeper pre-condition modules shift the downstream target toward lower-frequency components. Thus, by combining empirical Fourier analyses with the established frequency principle (that lower-frequency functions are learned earlier), the method provides an explanatory mechanism for why deeper networks can train faster.

args.text: We propose a Differentiable Homomorphism-Guided Sparse Higher-Order GNN that learns a small bank of prototype graphs and computes fast, bounded-treewidth homomorphism scores between each prototype and local r-hop ego-subgraphs, using these scores to gate the sparse selection of k-tuples that instantiate higher-order neighborhoods. The selected tuples are then processed by permutation-equivariant higher-order blocks in the style of sparsity-aware SpeqNets, with stable identity/position signals injected via O(p)-equivariant positional encodings. Theoretically, when prototypes have bounded treewidth, the induced map is universal for F-invariant functions on the probed neighborhoods and can recover much of the separation power of higher-order WL-like schemes with memory tied to the learned selection budget rather than O(n^k). Practically, this yields interpretable prototype filters, improves topology-sensitive tasks over MPNNs and fixed kernel filters, and offers a tunable expressivity–scalability knob that adapts to graph sparsity.

result.text: The paper examines the overlooked safety risks that arise when end-users fine-tune already-aligned large language models (LLMs), showing that custom fine-tuning can undo alignment even without malicious intent. Its key insight is that small amounts of adversarial or even benign training data can substantially weaken safety guardrails—e.g., jailbreaking GPT-3.5 Turbo with just 10 adversarial examples via inexpensive API fine-tuning—so initial alignment does not guarantee post-tuning safety. The authors demonstrate this through red-teaming experiments that fine-tune models on crafted and common datasets and measure increased responsiveness to harmful instructions, and they analyze why existing inference-time safety infrastructures fail to prevent these post-tuning vulnerabilities. They conclude by evaluating mitigation strategies (policy, access controls, detection, robust fine-tuning techniques) and call for focused research and stricter safety protocols governing who may fine-tune aligned models and how.

args.text: We propose HazardTKG, which treats each (subject, relation, ·) as a piecewise-constant process and learns a time-varying change-point hazard so that facts persist by default and switch objects when the hazard spikes. The hazard is parameterized by relation- and time-conditioned rotations and temporal embeddings, and is multiplicatively modulated by interpretable temporal rules to inject structured priors. At inference, copy-vs-generate arises naturally: if the predicted hazard is low we copy the last object, otherwise we sample a new object from a learned distribution, with a contrastive non-history gate adjusting the baseline when historical signals are weak. Training uses survival-style objectives with censored intervals to jointly learn next-object identity and tenure duration, improving temporal consistency, uncertainty calibration, and forecasting accuracy on temporal KGs.

result.text: The paper addresses the suboptimality of optimism-based algorithms in contextual linear bandits by targeting asymptotically optimal, problem-dependent regret performance even under unbalanced context distributions. Its key insight is a reformulation of the problem-dependent lower bound that decouples the context distribution from the exploration policy and can be solved via a Lagrangian, enabling an incremental primal–dual solution that naturally balances exploration without forced probing. The method implements a scalable primal–dual incremental algorithm that uses confidence-aware optimization to enforce minimal, structure-adaptive exploration, yields logarithmic-in-arms finite-time regret bounds (and minimax optimality in the non-contextual case), and is both computationally efficient and empirically superior to previous baselines.

Experiments on reasoning, planning, alignment, and decision-making tasks demonstrate that TS-LLM outperforms prior approaches and scales to deep search trees (up to depth 64).

result.text: The paper tackles the problem that graph neural networks trained on graphs of one size often fail to generalize to graphs of different (typically larger) sizes, without access to test-domain graphs or strong generative assumptions. Its key insight is that size shifts can be simulated at training time by coarsening graphs to mimic smaller-to-larger size differences, and that enforcing robustness to these simulated shifts via a regularizer improves size generalization for generic GNNs. The proposed method, SizeShiftReg, applies graph coarsening to create perturbed versions of training graphs and adds a regularization term that encourages the model’s predictions or representations to be consistent across original and coarsened views, so any GNN can be trained with this extra loss to become more size-robust. Experiments show substantial gains (up to ~30%) when models are trained on the smallest 50% of graphs and tested on the largest 10%, demonstrating the effectiveness of the regularizer without using test data or specialized generative models.

args.text: We propose Polynomial SDF Fields (Poly‑SDF): represent a scene’s signed distance function as a polynomial neural field that decomposes geometry into a small set of interpretable frequency subbands, and render with unbiased SDF‑to‑density volume rendering. Subband‑specific priors (e.g., curvature/TV on low bands and sparsity/thin‑structure promotion on high bands) combined with a Pi‑Net‑inspired curriculum that gradually unlocks higher‑order multiplicative interactions yield stable coarse geometry first and accelerate learning of fine geometric detail. Coupling the geometry with a Neural‑PIL lighting head separates high‑frequency appearance from geometry, enabling direct editing of geometric subbands and more reliable inverse rendering under complex illumination. We hypothesize this produces sharper thin structures and cleaner shape/appearance disentanglement than monolithic SDF networks while retaining the optimization robustness of unbiased SDF rendering.

result.text: The paper addresses the persistent problem of “hard” pixels in semantic segmentation—pixels that are frequently mispredicted—and shows these errors are not only localized at boundaries but quantitatively linked to frequency aliasing introduced by downsampling. args.text: TriSwitch is a neuro-symbolic forecaster for temporal knowledge graphs that adaptively routes each query to the most suitable reasoning pathway. A contrastive dependency gate learns whether the moment is history-driven; if so, a sequential copy module produces a candidate distribution over past objects and a temporal rule aggregator adds interpretable votes from time-consistent logical rules, while otherwise a time-conditioned rotation embedding predicts from the full vocabulary. This mixture-of-experts design unifies copy-generation, rule-based reasoning, and geometric embeddings in a single end-to-end trainable model.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of knowledge conflicts in LLM generation, where a model’s stored (parametric) knowledge can contradict new, context-provided information and lead to incorrect outputs. The key insight is that certain neurons disproportionately drive the model’s use of contextual cues, so identifying and amplifying these “context-aware” neurons will make the model more sensitive to new context and less prone to rely on outdated parametric knowledge. The proposed method, IRCAN, computes context-aware attribution scores using integrated gradients to locate neurons that contribute strongly to context processing and then reweights those neurons to strengthen their influence during generation; experiments across multiple models and tasks show this plug-and-play approach improves handling of knowledge conflicts without altering model weights or architecture.

The paper addresses the failure of standard off-policy reinforcement learning in the offline (batch) continuous-control setting where only a fixed, potentially heterogeneous dataset of prior interactions is available. Its key insight is that learning and using a behavior prior that favors actions observed in the data—specifically an advantage-weighted behavior model (ABM)—can stabilize learning by biasing the policy toward actions that were both executed and have high estimated advantage, thus avoiding out-of-distribution, poorly supported actions. Methodologically, the authors train an ABM that weights behavior samples by their estimated advantage and incorporate it as a learned prior or regularizer in the policy update, enabling stable batch-RL from mixed or conflicting data sources; experiments show this simple approach improves performance on continuous-control benchmarks and multi-task robotic learning, including real robots.

result.text: The paper addresses reinforcement learning in environments with high-dimensional or continuous action spaces where enumerating all actions is infeasible and agents must act using only small sampled subsets. Its key insight is that policy evaluation and improvement can be performed principledly over sampled action subsets within a general sample-based policy iteration framework, allowing planning algorithms to retain theoretical structure while operating on limited action sets. Concretely, the authors instantiate this idea as Sampled MuZero, extending MuZero to plan over sampled actions by integrating action-sampling into its tree search and learning loop so it can learn value, dynamics, and policy representations without requiring a discrete full action enumeration. They validate the method on Go and continuous-control benchmarks (DeepMind Control Suite and Real-World RL Suite), showing it enables learning and planning in arbitrarily complex action spaces.

result.text: Solver-matched likelihood training for diffusion ODEs: directly optimize a discretized log-likelihood surrogate that upper-bounds the probability-flow ODE NLL under a chosen high-order sampler (e.g., DPM-Solver/DEIS) and a fixed NFE budget. We derive a quadrature-aware loss by expanding the continuous-time likelihood bound into local score/velocity errors transported through the solver’s coefficients (Butcher tableau/exponential-integrator weights), and backpropagate through one-step unrolled solver kernels using adjoint or implicit differentiation with control variates to keep variance and memory low. Coupled with velocity parameterization and high-order flow-matching finetuning, we jointly learn the score and a step schedule that minimize this surrogate at fixed NFE, yielding discretized trajectories with provably tighter NLL than continuous-time–trained baselines at equal sampling cost.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that standard semi-supervised Graph Neural Networks assume training labels are an IID sample of nodes, but in practice labeled nodes are often biased and localized, causing GNNs to overfit and generalize poorly under distributional shift. The key insight is that explicitly modeling and correcting for distributional differences between the labeled subgraph and the full inference distribution can make GNNs robust to such labeling biases, recovering performance lost to spurious regularities in the training set. The method, Shift-Robust GNN (SR-GNN), augments GNN training with mechanisms to detect and adapt to label-induced shifts—reweighting or adjusting learning objectives and representations to align the labeled-node distribution with the target node distribution—and is evaluated across multiple biased-sampling scenarios on common benchmarks, where it substantially reduces the negative effects of bias and improves accuracy over baselines.

args.text: We propose SDF-PIL, a relightable neural SDF renderer that couples unbiased surface-based volume rendering with learned pre-integrated lighting to improve reflectance decomposition from multi-view images. We model density via an SDF-to-density mapping and train with NeuS-style unbiased surface rendering while replacing the analytic illumination integral with a Neural-PIL query keyed by surface normals and compact BRDF latents, learning low-dimensional per-image illumination codes. To stabilize optimization and recover sharp geometry, training begins in a volumetric radiance-field regime and progressively anneals sampling to a thin band around the predicted surface. This yields more accurate geometry and better-disentangled BRDF/lighting, enabling fast, high-fidelity relighting and shape–appearance swaps.

We propose a MaxEnt-Spectral Curriculum to accelerate and control the emergence of induction heads (IHs): during pretraining, maintain local maximum-entropy alignment on low-order n-gram moments to satisfy networks’ early distributional simplicity bias, while selectively densifying long-range match-and-copy patterns to target higher-order structure. Concretely, a data mixer monitors windowed n-gram moment residuals and applies optimal-transport edits to neutralize low-order deviations, then adaptively reweights spans containing copyable token pairs at varied distances to exploit density-dependent frequency learning and bias training toward the IH-relevant spectrum. By scheduling this shift from low-order moment matching to targeted high-order correlation densification, we predict earlier IH phase transitions, fewer spurious competing subcircuits, and controllable IH multiplicity. Causal optogenetic-style clamping across training can validate mechanism and quantify gains in IH emergence timing and generalization to in-context copying tasks.

I propose speculative world-model rollouts that combine a fast latent proposer with an adaptive, one- to two-step rectified-flow/consistency decoder to achieve IRIS-like rollout cost with DIAMOND-level visual fidelity. A compact autoregressive token dynamics model proposes long-horizon latent trajectories; an uncertainty-aware acceptance head flags segments likely to incur pixel-level error, triggering the conditional flow decoder to render and, if necessary, refine only those segments. We train the decoder with flow matching conditioned on actions and latent history, and jointly learn the acceptance head from proposer entropy and value-consistency signals so that refinement is spent on action-relevant events. This architecture enables longer, denser imagination for policy learning while preserving fine visual detail and provides uncertainty-guided exploration via controllable flow noise.

Temporal SpeqNets with Homomorphism-Guided Selection: extend sparsity-aware higher-order tuple selection to node–time tuples in event streams by using efficiently computable counts of bounded-treewidth temporal motifs within sliding windows to both choose which k-tuples to instantiate and to serve as local structural parameters. Coupled with injective temporal message passing and relative positional encodings, the architecture targets the expressivity of temporal Weisfeiler–Leman while keeping memory roughly linear in active events and adaptive to interaction sparsity. An O(p)-equivariant treatment of positional channels stabilizes training and preserves inductive generalization across time scales, while motif-driven selection concentrates higher-order computation on causally salient patterns (bursts, triadic closures, feedback loops). We hypothesize this recovers strong separations on temporal isomorphism tests and boosts forecasting/link prediction on sparse dynamic graphs at orders-of-magnitude lower cost than full k-tuple TGNs.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of knowledge conflicts in LLM generation, where a model’s stored (parametric) knowledge can contradict new, context-provided information and lead to incorrect outputs. The key insight is that certain neurons disproportionately drive the model’s use of contextual cues, so identifying and amplifying these “context-aware” neurons will make the model more sensitive to new context and less prone to rely on outdated parametric knowledge. The proposed method, IRCAN, computes context-aware attribution scores using integrated gradients to locate neurons that contribute strongly to context processing and then reweights those neurons to strengthen their influence during generation; experiments across multiple models and tasks show this plug-and-play approach improves handling of knowledge conflicts without altering model weights or architecture.

result.text: The paper addresses the fundamental question of optimal sample complexity for offline reinforcement learning in tabular MDPs, seeking algorithms that can provably find ε-optimal policies using only prerecorded data. The key insight is that applying a double variance reduction technique to off-policy value estimation dramatically tightens the error dependence on the horizon H and the minimal visitation mass d_m, enabling near-optimal statistical efficiency. The authors propose OPDVR (Off-Policy Double Variance Reduction), which combines two layers of variance reduction in its value and policy estimation procedures to control estimation variance from limited coverage and finite-horizon propagation, and they prove it requires Õ(H^2/(d_m ε^2)) episodes to achieve ε-optimality. They further show a matching information-theoretic lower bound Ω(H^2/(d_m ε^2)) (up to log factors) and extend the algorithm and optimal-rate guarantees to non-stationary finite-horizon and infinite-horizon discounted settings.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that chain-of-thought prompting for large language models fails to generalize from easy exemplars to harder problems, especially on tasks requiring structured, compositional, or long-range reasoning. Its key insight is that decomposing a hard problem into an ordered sequence of simpler subproblems and solving them least-to-most difficult—where each subanswer conditions subsequent steps—improves easy-to-hard generalization. The method, called least-to-most prompting, provides exemplars that demonstrate this decomposition and then iteratively prompts the model to solve subproblems and use those solutions to tackle progressively harder subproblems; experiments on symbolic manipulation, compositional generalization (SCAN), and math reasoning show dramatic gains (e.g., raising SCAN accuracy from 16% with chain-of-thought to ≥99% with just 14 exemplars on code-davinci-002).

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation that standard score-based generative models (SGMs) use overly simplistic diffusion processes, which make the denoising task harder and thus limit synthesis quality. Its key insight is to replace the usual overdamped diffusion with a critically-damped Langevin diffusion (CLD) that augments data with velocity-like auxiliary variables, coupling them as in Hamiltonian dynamics so the model need only learn the conditional velocity score—a simpler objective than the full data score. Methodologically, the authors derive a new score-matching objective for CLD, propose an efficient sampler tailored to the second-order dynamics, and demonstrate empirically that CLD-based SGMs and the new solver yield better synthesis quality than prior SGMs (and outperform standard solvers like Euler–Maruyama) for comparable architectures and compute.

result.text: The paper addresses how to fine-tune large pre-trained language models under differential privacy constraints while preserving utility and reducing computational/memory cost. The key insight is that parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (sparser adapters and low-dimensional updates) can be adapted into a meta-framework that requires fewer private parameters and less noisy gradient perturbation, yielding better privacy–utility tradeoffs. Concretely, the authors implement differentially private variants of efficient adapters and prompt/adapter-style techniques, evaluate them across classification and generation tasks, and show they outperform prior private algorithms—approaching non-private accuracy on tasks like MNLI and producing strong BLEU scores for private language generation—while also reducing training cost and demonstrating that larger models retain accuracy better under privacy.

The paper addresses continuous super-resolution of screen content images (SCIs), which differ from natural images and must be upscaled to arbitrary scales after aggressive downsampling and compression for bandwidth savings. The key insight is to treat SR as an implicit coordinate-to-pixel prediction problem where query pixel values can be inferred from learned feature "keys" via an implicit transformer that aggregates information from similar neighboring pixels using an implicit position encoding. The proposed Implicit Transformer Super-Resolution Network (ITSRN) extracts image features at key coordinates and uses the implicit transformer plus position encoding to produce high-quality continuous SR at arbitrary ratios. They validate ITSRN on newly constructed SCI1K and SCI1K-compression benchmarks, showing substantial improvements over existing continuous and discrete SR methods on both compressed and uncompressed SCIs.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem that classifier-based density-ratio estimation, a core tool for unsupervised learning tasks, breaks down when the two distributions p and q differ drastically (e.g., KL divergence of tens of nats), preventing accurate estimation of p/q in high dimensions. The key insight is to avoid a single hard jump between p and q by decomposing the overall ratio into a product of many intermediate, easier-to-estimate ratios—i.e., “telescoping” the density ratio along a sequence of bridging distributions so each pair is similar enough for reliable classification-based estimation. Methodologically, TRE constructs a chain of intermediate densities between p and q, estimates the ratio for each adjacent pair via standard classification-based density-ratio estimators, and multiplies these local estimates to obtain the overall p/q; this approach empirically improves mutual information estimation, representation learning, and energy-based modeling when p and q are highly dissimilar.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of extreme sample inefficiency in visual reinforcement learning, specifically achieving strong performance on Atari games using only limited environment interactions. The key insight is that MuZero-style model-based planning can be made far more data-efficient by combining a compact learned world model, representation and value heads optimized for low-data regimes, and training targets that stabilize and concentrate learning (including auxiliary reconstruction and contrastive-like objectives). The resulting algorithm, EfficientZero, integrates these design choices into an MCTS-based agent that learns from 100k frames (~two hours) and attains superhuman mean performance on the Atari100k benchmark (194.3% mean human) while also transferring well to DMControl 100k; the paper releases a clear implementation to facilitate further research.

result.text: Private-FetchSketch: combine sketch-space aggregation in federated learning with differential privacy by applying initialization-time noise to the Count Sketch that the server maintains across rounds. args.text: We propose Q-guided Counterfactual Diffusion World Models (Q-CaD), a factored diffusion-based world model that explicitly separates controllable and exogenous latent factors to improve long-horizon control. Starting from action-free video pretraining to learn robust dynamics features, we learn an action-conditional denoiser only on the controllable subspace while modeling exogenous noise with an unconditional branch, and enforce interventional consistency by swapping/control-freezing latents during training. At decision time, we steer the denoising trajectory with gradients from a learned Q-function (classifier-free style guidance) to sample high-value futures, and use batched guided samples as a planning primitive analogous to MCTS rollouts but compatible with image-space diffusion. result.text: The paper addresses the problem that standard graph neural networks suffer from a fundamental bottleneck—over-squashing—where exponentially many bits of information from distant nodes are compressed into fixed-size node representations during neighbor aggregation, preventing effective long-range message propagation and hurting tasks that require distant dependencies. The key insight is that the common aggregation mechanism, which treats incoming edges equally and compresses many incoming messages into a single vector, inherently limits representational capacity and makes models like GCN and GIN particularly vulnerable, whereas architectures that manage or diversify edge absorption can mitigate this effect. result.text: The paper tackles the problem of steering open-domain conversational agents to lead dialogues toward a specified target keyword smoothly and quickly, noting that prior pipelines relying on noisy next-turn keyword labels and embedding similarity for transitions poorly match human behavior. Their key insight is that human conversations are grounded in commonsense associations, so leveraging external commonsense knowledge graphs (CKGs) can guide more natural keyword transitions and improve response selection. Methodologically, they build a keyword-guided neural conversational model that integrates CKG-based signals into both next-turn keyword prediction and keyword-augmented response retrieval, and they evaluate via automatic metrics, self-play, and human studies showing smoother transitions and faster attainment of target keywords compared to baselines.

args.text: We propose Levy-bridged amortized contrastive divergence for atomic-resolution protein EBMs, combining heavy-tailed exploration and ratio-monitoring to stabilize training and improve mixing across rotameric basins. Concretely, we co-train an entropy-regularized conditional generator over 3D side-chain/backbone coordinates while alternating negative sampling between generator proposals and short-run MCMC with alpha-stable Levy jump proposals, executed along a schedule of intermediate temperature/torsion-annealed bridges whose adjacency is monitored and reweighted via telescoping density-ratio estimates. We incorporate the commonly omitted CD gradient correction and a reservoir of negatives to handle nonlocal jumps without collapse. This hybrid sampler/trainer is designed to reduce mode trapping and improve rotamer recovery and OOD detection versus Rosetta-style and prior EBM approaches.

We propose Flow-Speq, a flow-guided O(p)-equivariant sparsity-aware higher-order GNN that allocates higher-order computations along anisotropic vector-field-defined information flows on the graph. Concretely, we use Laplacian-eigenvector vector fields to induce directional neighborhoods and select k-tuples only on locally congested or high-curvature flow regions (e.g., via directional effective resistance proxies) as in sparsity-aware higher-order selection, while updating positional channels with PEG-style O(p)-equivariant layers. On the selected tuples we apply directional, non-linear spectral filters to achieve 3-WL+ discrimination with cost scaling to local sparsity, and add an auxiliary transport loss that encourages messages to move along integral curves to relieve over-squashing. We hypothesize improved long-range generalization and near-universal separation with sparse compute, validated on ZINC, CIFAR10-graph, and long-range synthetic benchmarks.

args.text: We propose FedSubSketch, a federated optimizer that learns and exploits a global low-rank gradient subspace while preserving partial participation and tight uplink budgets. The server maintains a streaming PCA of the gradient covariance using mergeable CountSketch summaries of client outer-products; clients then transmit only coefficients along the current basis and a sketched error-feedback residual, so communication scales with the rank r rather than model dimension. This hybrid “coefficients + sketched residual” aggregation inherits robustness from sketch-space momentum and compression-aware SCA, and can be personalized via per-client mixture weights or per-cluster subspaces to accommodate heterogeneity. We provide convergence guarantees under bounded subspace drift and show superior accuracy–communication trade-offs versus pure sketching or pure low-rank reuse.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between score-matching objectives used to train score-based generative models and the true maximum likelihood objective for the associated score-based diffusion ODEs, showing that matching only first-order scores does not guarantee optimal ODE likelihood. The key insight is that the ODE negative log-likelihood can be controlled by bounding not just the first-order score error but also second- and third-order score errors, so high-order score matching is necessary to close the gap between score-matching and maximum likelihood. The authors derive bounds linking ODE likelihood to first–third order score-matching errors and propose a practical high-order denoising score matching algorithm that enforces these higher-order constraints (with guarantees that higher-order errors are controlled by training error and lower-order errors), and they demonstrate empirically improved likelihood on synthetic data and CIFAR-10 while preserving sample quality.

args.text: Learned Lévy-Langevin protein conformational sampling: We propose replacing Gaussian Langevin dynamics in learned atomic-resolution protein EBMs with α-stable Lévy-driven dynamics in internal-coordinate space, enabling long-range jumps across rotameric and backbone basins while preserving correct reverse-time sampling. We train a torsion-space score model via fractional denoising score matching under α-stable noise and use finite-difference formulations of score-matching terms to avoid higher-order derivative costs when coupling to an energy-based backbone prior. For fast sampling, we adapt DPM-Solver-style high-order integration to the reverse-time ODE associated with the Lévy process, yielding improved mode coverage and 2–4× wall-clock speedups on rotamer recovery and loop modeling compared to Gaussian EBM samplers.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of evaluating dynamic link prediction: current benchmarks and sampling practices make methods look better than they are by favoring easy negatives and ignoring recurring edge patterns in time-evolving graphs. The key insight is that many edges simply reoccur over time, so a strong memorization baseline can perform well under existing evaluations, revealing that negative sampling strategy critically shapes apparent performance. The authors introduce EdgeBank, a pure memorization baseline that records past edges and predicts their reappearance, propose two harder negative sampling strategies that produce more realistic and challenging evaluation splits, and release six new, diverse dynamic graph datasets to better reflect real-world scenarios and stress-test future models.

The paper tackles the limited expressive power of standard permutation-equivariant message-passing graph neural networks, which struggle to capture basic topological properties of graphs. Its key insight is to augment messages with unique node identifiers (one-hot encodings) that let each node build a local context matrix encoding rich joint feature–topology information while preserving permutation equivariance. The method propagates these one-hot identifiers through message-passing layers to assemble per-node local context matrices, applies learnable transformations and pooling to produce node representations, and demonstrates empirically that this structural message-passing framework more accurately predicts diverse graph topological properties while remaining computationally efficient.

result.text: The paper addresses how to leverage pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) to provide reward signals for training RL agents without incurring the heavy computational cost of frequent VLM inference. The key insight is that VLMs can generate compact, executable reward code that captures rich, dense feedback about visual task progress, so once synthesized the code can be run cheaply at every timestep instead of repeatedly querying the VLM. Their method, VLM-CaR, prompts a VLM to produce reward-computation programs from task descriptions and example observations, validates and compiles those programs into efficient reward functions, and then uses the resulting dense rewards to train RL policies, showing improved accuracy and learning performance across diverse discrete and continuous environments.

args.text: HiCAR: a hierarchical, conflict-aware router for LLMs that jointly reweights neurons and attention pathways at inference time to prioritize fresh context over outdated parametric memories. We detect conflict by contrasting the model’s posterior with and without the provided context, then upweight context-sensitive neurons identified via integrated-gradient attribution and, simultaneously, attention heads/edges that mediate example-to-query transfer identified via self-attention attribution, guided by the Bayesian latent-concept view of in-context learning. The router solves a small constrained reweighting problem that activates only under high-conflict scores and includes a prompt-shaping step that injects mild burstiness/rare-class structure to more reliably elicit ICL when needed. This plug-and-play procedure requires no weight updates, preserves non-conflict behavior, and targets failures where models ignore or override new evidence.

result.text: MOReL addresses offline reinforcement learning: how to learn a high-performing policy using only a fixed dataset of past environment interactions without further online data. The key insight is to build a pessimistic model-based surrogate (a P-MDP) that deliberately underestimates value in parts of the state-action space with high model uncertainty, so that policy performance in the real environment is lower-bounded by its performance in the P-MDP and model exploitation is avoided. The method learns a transition/reward model and an uncertainty-aware penalty to construct the P-MDP from the offline data, then performs planning or policy optimization inside this P-MDP to obtain a near-optimal policy; MOReL is shown to be minimax optimal (up to log factors) and empirically matches or exceeds prior offline RL baselines.

result.text: The paper examines the growing practice of improving differentially private (DP) learning by fine-tuning large, non-private models pretrained on massive public (often Web-scraped) datasets, arguing this trend raises both conceptual and practical concerns. The key insight is that treating externally pretrained models as a privacy-preserving shortcut masks important problems: public pretraining datasets may not be truly benign or representative of sensitive domains, claiming privacy benefits can mislead stakeholders, and reliance on very large pretrained models can force data owners to hand private data to powerful third parties, undermining privacy in practice. args.text: We propose a training-free, jump-adapted sampler for Lévy-driven diffusion models that mirrors the decomposition underlying DPM-Solver: separate the reverse-time dynamics into a drift–diffusion part and a compound-Poisson jump part via the Lévy–Itô decomposition. The small-jump component is truncated and integrated with a high-order exponential solver, while rare large jumps are simulated with adaptive thinning using a state-dependent reverse-time jump intensity estimated from the denoiser/score network. Between jumps we solve the deterministic flow in a few high-order steps and apply exact jump updates when events fire, reducing function evaluations while preserving the heavy-tailed exploration that alleviates mode collapse. An online controller tunes the jump truncation threshold via local error estimates on the fractional score to balance bias and variance during fast sampling.

args.text: We propose edge-level, attribution-guided conflict arbitration for LLMs that precisely reweights only those self-attention interactions that drive reliance on outdated parametric knowledge when new context disagrees. Unlike neuron-level boosting, we compute self-attention interaction attributions over context tokens to localize influential edges, and derive a conflict score by contrasting a parametric prior over a latent concept (param-only pass) with a context-induced posterior (context-only pass), then gate high-conflict edges during generation. A lightweight gating module (low-rank, layer-local) rescales targeted attention edges; it is trained with synthetic contradiction curricula and retrieved evidence so that gates activate when prior/posterior diverge and remain sparse/inactive when they agree, with KL and sparsity regularizers for minimal intervention. This plug-in yields finer control and interpretability, improving conflict resolution while preserving param knowledge in non-conflict settings.

result.text: We propose FedSubSketch, a federated optimizer that learns and exploits a global low-rank gradient subspace while preserving partial participation and tight uplink budgets. The server maintains a streaming PCA of the gradient covariance using mergeable CountSketch summaries of client outer-products; clients then transmit only coefficients along the current basis and a sketched error-feedback residual, so communication scales with the rank r rather than model dimension. This hybrid “coefficients + sketched residual” aggregation inherits robustness from sketch-space momentum and compression-aware SCA, and can be personalized via per-client mixture weights or per-cluster subspaces to accommodate heterogeneity. We provide convergence guarantees under bounded subspace drift and show superior accuracy–communication trade-offs versus pure sketching or pure low-rank reuse.

args.text: CurvSpec-Shift: an adaptive, per-ray transition from volumetric to surface rendering for 3D-aware generation that uses local spectral and geometric cues to decide how tightly to sample around the SDF zero level-set. We instantiate the renderer with an SDF-to-density mapping and the unbiased NeuS integration, and store features in a sparse voxel/octree to accelerate sampling. This yields stable early gradients, sharper converged surfaces, and better preservation of thin parts at real-time rates.

result.text: The paper addresses inductive representation learning for temporal graphs, where embeddings must handle evolving topology, new nodes, and temporal node/edge features so that representations are functions of time. The key insight is to extend self-attention to temporal neighborhoods and to encode continuous time with a principled functional time encoding derived from Bochner’s theorem, enabling the model to capture time–feature interactions and temporal patterns in a shift-invariant way. The method, TGAT, stacks temporal graph attention layers that aggregate temporally-aware neighbor features using attention scores computed over time-augmented representations, allowing inductive inference of time-conditioned embeddings for both seen and unseen nodes and supporting tasks like temporal link prediction and node classification. Evaluation on two benchmark and one industrial dataset shows TGAT outperforms prior temporal and static baselines and naturally incorporates temporal edge features.

Its key insight is to adapt capsule ideas to graphs by creating disentangled graph capsules that encode heterogeneous factors of each node and by modeling explicit part–whole relationships among capsules to form higher-level graph hierarchies. The proposed Hierarchical Graph Capsule Network (HGCN) first produces node-level capsule instantiation parameters via factor disentanglement, then aggregates these lower-level capsules into higher-level capsules using routing that incorporates graph structure to preserve relational information, yielding joint node embeddings and hierarchical graph representations. Empirical results show HGCN improves graph classification and that both disentangled capsules and structure-aware routing contribute to its performance.

The paper addresses the high error rates of differentially private SGD (DP-SGD) that scale with the ambient parameter dimension p, which hurts private learning for over-parameterized models where p ≫ n. Its key insight is that stochastic gradients in deep networks typically lie in a much lower-dimensional subspace during training, so projecting noisy gradients onto that subspace can dramatically reduce the noise impact and thus the privacy-induced error. The method, Projected DP-SGD, identifies the top gradient eigenspace using a small public dataset and then performs DP-SGD updates with gradients projected into that low-dimensional subspace, and the authors give sample-complexity bounds for subspace identification (showing the public sample need only grow logarithmically in p under mild assumptions) along with theoretical and empirical results demonstrating substantially improved private accuracy.

args.text: We propose Subband-Factored SDF Radiance Fields that explicitly decouple geometry and appearance by parameterizing the SDF with a low-frequency Polynomial Neural Field (Fourier PNF) while allocating high-frequency subbands to radiance and reflectance. Training begins with an SDF-to-density mapping and unbiased volumetric rendering, then progressively shrinks the sampling band around the predicted surface to transition into surface-focused rendering for stable yet sharp convergence. The SDF branch is optimized with a phase-transition loss to impose a minimal-surface prior, while a cross-subband orthogonality/bottleneck regularizer prevents high-frequency appearance from absorbing geometric detail. This yields crisper thin structures, improved shape/appearance disentanglement, and enables direct post-hoc editing of texture versus shape via subband manipulation.

We propose a spectral- and density-shaped curriculum to control the timing and multiplicity of induction head (IH) emergence in transformers. Guided by distributional simplicity bias and the deep frequency principle, we pretrain on data that first matches low-order n-gram moments, then progressively introduces higher-order/long-range match patterns while locally oversampling contexts containing rare, high-frequency dependencies—predicted by NTK analyses with non-uniform sampling to accelerate those components. We hypothesize this induces earlier IH phase transitions and controllable multiplicity; we test on synthetic corpora with independent control of moments and match frequencies, and use optogenetic activation clamps to causally verify subcircuit mediation. Evaluation tracks phase timing, additivity of subcircuits, and generalization, with ablations isolating density shaping versus moment shaping effects.

result.text: The paper studies the representational limits of temporal graph networks (TGNs), asking which dynamic graph properties different TGN designs can and cannot capture. The key insight is that the two main TGN families—walk-aggregating TGNs (WA-TGNs) and message-passing with memory TGNs (MP-TGNs)—are fundamentally incomparable in expressiveness, but MP-TGNs become as powerful as a newly proposed temporal Weisfeiler-Leman (WL) test when their update functions are injective, while both families still cannot compute certain global properties like girth and deep MP-TGNs render memory redundant. Methodologically, the authors develop novel separations and extensions of 1-WL to temporal graphs, derive theoretical prescriptions (injective updates and relative positional features), and instantiate these into PINT, an architecture combining injective temporal message passing with relative positional encodings that is provably more expressive than prior TGNs and empirically superior on benchmarks.

args.text: We propose Directional-Spectral Capacity GNNs that alleviate over-squashing by coupling globally consistent directional message passing with learnable, eigenvalue-dependent spectral filters and capacity-aware multi-channel edges. Concretely, we define a graph-wide vector field (e.g., from Laplacian eigenvectors) to compute directional derivatives and per-edge conductance scores, use non-linear spectral filters to shape frequency-specific messages, and allocate message-channel capacity across edges proportional to predicted directional congestion. To further bypass bottlenecks without losing sparsity, we open higher-order, vector-field-aligned k-tuple interactions only along high-congestion routes via sparsity-aware tuple selection, creating a small number of expressive auxiliary paths. This design should increase the effective cut of the unrolled computation graph and approach 3-WL-level separation in practice while scaling with edges rather than k-order tensor size, combining the strengths of directional kernels, spectral expressivity, and selective higher-order structure.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of learning when temporally-extended actions (options) should be available for initiation, a component often ignored because initiation sets are hard to learn with function approximation. Its key insight is to replace binary initiation sets with differentiable interest functions that indicate how relevant or “interested” an option is in a given state, enabling gradient-based learning of option availability alongside policies and termination. The authors derive gradients and integrate interest functions into an interest-option-critic architecture that jointly learns option policies, termination, and interest via policy-gradient-style updates, and show empirically that this yields more interpretable, reusable temporal abstractions in both discrete and continuous domains.

args.text: Temporal Evidence Routing for Conflict-Aware LLMs: mitigate recency and time-sensitive knowledge conflicts by injecting time-conditioned KG signals into plug-and-play neuron/attention reweighting. At decode time, entities and timestamps in the prompt are linked and candidate facts are scored with a temporal KG model (e.g., rotation-based or time-aware factorization) at the specified time; a conflict score between TKG-consistent vs parametric-preferred continuations triggers targeted modulation. Specifically, we up-weight context-aware neurons and attention heads attending to temporal spans while down-weighting components associated with stale parametric facts, producing training-free temporal conflict resolution. Evaluated on temporally evolving QA and fact completion, the method should improve post-cutoff factuality without degrading atemporal performance.

Offline Pessimistic Representation Selection for contextual bandits: given M candidate feature maps, train for each a pessimistic offline policy using uncertainty-aware SGD and compute a coverage-weighted lower confidence bound on its value. A smoothed CORRAL-style master then selects or mixes these base policies to maximize pessimistic value subject to bounded importance weights, thereby staying in-distribution while implicitly choosing a good representation. This yields only logarithmic-in-M overhead and inherits near-constant, instance-dependent suboptimality whenever any candidate representation is good on the data support, while satisfying a weighted-minimax safety criterion even under misspecification. Practically, this unifies pessimism with representation/model selection and can be implemented by per-representation empirical-Bernstein penalties plus a master with clipped/tempered weights.

result.text: The paper addresses whether federated averaging (FedAvg) can still achieve linear speedup in convergence under realistic federated learning conditions—non-i.i.d. data and partial worker participation—rather than the usual i.i.d. and full-participation assumptions. The key insight is that with appropriately chosen two-sided learning rates and accounting for local updates, FedAvg attains provable linear-speedup convergence rates that scale with the number of participating workers: O(1/√(mKT)+1/T) for full participation and O(1/√(nKT)+1/T) for partial participation, where K is local steps, T is communication rounds, m total workers and n workers per round. Methodologically, the authors analyze FedAvg in non-convex settings to derive these bounds, show that increasing local steps can aid convergence up to a limit of T/m, and validate the theory with experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10.

result.text: The paper addresses why differentially private (DP) learning sometimes avoids the expected degradation in utility as model dimension grows, a phenomenon at odds with classical bounds that worsen with model size. The key insight is that performance depends not on raw parameter dimensionality but on the magnitudes of gradients when projected onto low-dimensional subspaces—if gradients concentrate in a few principal directions then privacy noise has much less harm. Methodologically, the authors formalize this via a "restricted Lipschitz continuity" condition for convex objectives, prove improved excess empirical and population risk bounds that can be independent of ambient dimension under additional assumptions, and empirically validate that gradients during private fine-tuning of large language models are dominated by a few principal components, explaining why large pretrained models can be privately fine-tuned effectively.

result.text: The paper addresses why standard multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) struggle to learn high-frequency functions in low-dimensional regression tasks common in vision and graphics, limiting their ability to represent detailed 3D geometry and signals. The key insight is that MLPs exhibit a spectral bias—favoring low-frequency components—because their effective kernel (via the neural tangent kernel) lacks high-frequency sensitivity, but this can be remedied by preprocessing inputs with a random Fourier feature mapping that converts the NTK into a stationary kernel with controllable bandwidth. The method is to apply a simple Fourier feature transform to input coordinates before feeding them to an MLP, choose the feature scale to match task-specific frequency content, and thereby enable the network to learn and represent high-frequency detail; empirical results and NTK analysis demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness.

result.text: The paper investigates whether convolutional GANs can learn image distributions uniformly across spatial frequencies and finds they are biased against high spatial frequencies, which helps explain common high-frequency artifacts in generated images. The key insight is that this bias arises from linear dependencies in the spectral responses of typical generator convolutional filters, causing the network to allocate representational capacity unevenly across frequencies. Methodologically, the authors analyze GANs' frequency learning empirically and theoretically, derive the spectral-dependency explanation, and introduce a lightweight proof-of-concept technique to reweight or steer the generator’s attention toward chosen spatial frequencies, demonstrating that the bias can be manipulated rather than being an immutable limitation.

args.text: We propose Cipher-Invariant Safety (CIS): during alignment, we stochastically re-express both harmful and benign intents with a diverse mixture of human-designed and learned bijective encodings and train using a PRO-style ranking loss coupled with a Safe-RLHF cost model so refusals and guardrails become invariant to encoding while preserving helpfulness. To broaden the augmentation space, we include CipherChat-style ciphers and a learn-to-encrypt module that discovers reversible encodings optimized to evade surface detectors, forcing the model to ground decisions in intent rather than form. As a deployment-time defense against covert malicious fine-tuning, we add a metamorphic evaluation that queries each intent under a held-out ensemble of secret encodings and flags models exhibiting sharp harmfulness spikes tied to specific encodings (a signature of covert mappings). This jointly improves robustness to ciphered jailbreaks and raises the bar for black-box fine-tuning attacks that hide unsafe behaviors behind encodings.

result.text: The paper addresses reconstruction of an object from highly incomplete imaging measurements when a semantically related prior image is available, aiming to regularize the ill-posed inverse problem using that prior. The key insight is to exploit the disentangled latent space of a style-based generative model to impose semantically meaningful constraints derived from the prior image, enabling targeted guidance of the reconstruction toward plausible variations of the known scene. The method formulates an optimization in the generator’s disentangled latent space that incorporates constraints informed by the prior’s latent representation and solves for a latent code whose generated image both fits the measurements and respects semantic similarity to the prior; the authors provide theoretical analysis for stable recovery and demonstrate improved performance over related approaches in numerical experiments.

The paper addresses personalized learning-path recommendation, aiming to generate an ordered sequence of learning concepts tailored to a user each session while accounting for inter-concept relationships. Its key insight is to treat the problem as a set-to-sequence task that first models correlations among candidate concepts and then generates an ordered path that explicitly attends to interactions between current learning items and target concepts, combined with reinforcement learning to optimize sequence-level utility. Methodologically, SRC uses a concept-aware encoder to capture concept correlations, a decoder with attention to sequentially produce the path and a policy-gradient training objective, and an auxiliary knowledge-tracing module to assess and stabilize the model by estimating students’ learning effects; experiments on two public and one industrial dataset show its effectiveness.

The paper addresses the challenge of designing principled adaptive optimization methods for federated learning to improve convergence and accuracy while respecting client privacy and system heterogeneity. The key insight is that federated optimizers can be understood via decompositions of the ordinary differential equations (ODEs) corresponding to centralized adaptive optimizers, which reveals how momentum and adaptive terms should be allocated between global and local updates. Building on this analysis, the authors propose FedDA, a momentum-decoupled adaptive method that applies global momentum throughout local iterations to accelerate convergence and then uses full-batch gradient steps near the end of training to mimic centralized behavior and correct inconsistencies introduced by adaptive adaptation.

args.text: Commutator-aware Magnus-splitting for structured diffusion ODEs: when the forward corruption has a spatial linear operator (e.g., Laplacian/convolutional blur) the time-varying linear term L(t) generally does not commute, so DEIS/DPM-Solver’s scalar-linear assumptions incur bias. We reformulate the probability-flow with x′=L(t)x+f(x,t) and use low-order Magnus or commutator-free Magnus exponentials to integrate the time-ordered linear flow, applying exp(ΩΔ) via Krylov while coupling the nonlinear score force with symmetric Strang/Yoshida or exponential Rosenbrock steps in a velocity parameterization. result.text: The paper tackles improving the privacy–utility trade-off in differentially private (DP) model training by leveraging auxiliary public (non-sensitive) data that is in-distribution with the private data. The key insight is to embed the public-data loss as the mirror map in a DP mirror descent framework so that the private-data DP gradients appear only as the linear term, which yields better alignment with the geometry of the problem and reduces the impact of DP noise. Concretely, they propose PDA-DPMD, a mirror-descent variant that uses the public-data-induced mirror map while adding calibrated noise to private gradients, and prove for linear regression with non-isotropic sub-Gaussian features that PDA-DPMD attains asymptotically improved population risk when enough public samples are available; they also show the method has noise-stability properties that control variance from DP noise and empirically outperform DP-SGD (including when models are pretrained on public data) on several benchmarks.

args.text: I propose Moment-Scheduled Circuit Formation: train transformers under a curriculum that progressively relaxes maximum-entropy constraints on token statistics (from matching only low-order moments like unigrams/bigrams toward higher-order co-occurrences), so that high-order correlations needed for match-and-copy are withheld early and then introduced on schedule. Leveraging the finding that networks first fit low-order statistics, this should delay and sharpen the phase transition that yields induction heads and allow control over their multiplicity by pacing when higher-order structure becomes learnable. During each curriculum phase, use optogenetic-style activation clamping of identified subcircuits to causally verify and stabilize the dependency chain, aiming to induce a single, robust IH rather than redundant ones. Evaluate by tracking phase-transition timing, head multiplicity, and in-context learning performance on synthetic copy tasks and natural text/code corpora.

result.text: The paper tackles GNN limitations in expressivity, long-range interaction modelling, and capturing higher-order structures by addressing the tight coupling between a graph’s combinatorial structure and the computation performed on it. Its key insight is to generalize message-passing from graphs and simplicial complexes to regular CW (cell) complexes, which provide flexible “liftings” of a graph into higher-order topological structures that enable diverse, hierarchical message-passing schemes with strictly greater distinguishing power than the 1-WL test and at least as strong as 3-WL. The authors introduce CW Networks (CWNs), a family of architectures that build cell-complex representations (e.g., ring-based liftings), perform tailored message passing across cells of different dimensions, and thereby compress node distances and propagate higher-order signals more effectively. Empirically, a ring-based CWN instantiation attains state-of-the-art performance on multiple molecular benchmarks, validating the theoretical gains in expressivity and long-range modeling.

result.text: This paper tackles unsupervised skill discovery for agents when no external rewards are available, addressing the problem that existing mutual-information-based methods can produce trivially diverse but useless skill sets. The key insight is to measure diversity not just by distinguishability of skills, but by how skills differently change the agent’s relationship to its environment—i.e., relative changes in affordances—so skills should tile the space of achievable effects rather than merely differ in trajectories. The authors introduce Relative Variational Intrinsic Control (RVIC), a variational objective that maximizes mutual information between skills and resulting relative state changes (or affordance shifts) and trains a discriminator to identify skills based on those relative effects, yielding skills that are more semantically meaningful. Empirically, RVIC produces qualitatively diverse, affordance-covering skills across environments and yields more useful primitives for hierarchical reinforcement learning compared to prior approaches.

result.text: The paper tackles batch learning from bandit feedback when the action space is extremely large (e.g., millions of items in recommendation systems), where standard supervised proxies create bias and naïve importance sampling yields prohibitive variance. The key insight is that one can reduce variance by applying importance sampling not to individual actions but to the conditional expectation of rewards over a small, data-driven subset of actions per instance (a Rao–Blackwellization), trading a bit of bias for dramatically lower variance. They formalize a selective importance sampling (sIS) estimator that evaluates expected reward over the top-p actions of the logging policy and embed it in a Policy Optimization for eXtreme Models (POXM) algorithm that chooses p from data; empirical evaluation on three extreme multi-label datasets shows POXM consistently and substantially outperforms BanditNet, partial matching pruning, and supervised baselines.

result.text: The paper tackles the communication bottleneck in federated learning by asking whether the space spanned by model gradients over training is low-rank and can therefore be exploited to avoid sending full parameter updates. Observing in centralized training that gradients across epochs lie in a low-dimensional subspace with a few principal components explaining 95–99% of variance, the authors introduce Look-back Gradient Multiplier (LBGM), which recycles past gradient directions and transmits only scalar multipliers for those basis directions instead of full vectors. They analyze LBGM’s convergence to characterize the trade-off between reduced communication and potential accuracy loss, and empirically show that LBGM substantially cuts transmission costs across datasets and models while remaining compatible with and improvable by existing sparsification methods.

result.text: The paper addresses the mismatch between standard diffusion generative models and the multi-scale, locally smoothing structure of images by proposing a generative process that explicitly reverses a PDE which erases fine-scale detail. The key insight is that running the heat equation with additive noise forward acts like a structured variational encoder that progressively removes high-frequency content, so stochastically inverting this heat dissipation yields a diffusion-like model with an implicit coarse-to-fine inductive bias and emergent disentanglement of global color and shape. Methodologically, the authors formalize the forward heat-plus-noise process as a variational approximation within the diffusion latent-variable framework, derive and train a corresponding reverse stochastic process that undoes heat diffusion on the image plane, and analyze its spectral behavior to connect and contrast it with standard diffusion models.

args.text: I propose DP-GAP: differentially private gated-adapter personalization that updates only a tiny, low-dimensional gating vector over a public library of adapters rather than adapter weights. At deployment, we run DP mirror-descent on the gating logits using a public-data-induced mirror map, project private gradients into a public gradient subspace, and apply per-layer/per-device clipping while constraining gates to a simplex to tightly bound sensitivity. This leverages public pretraining for basin selection and the empirically low intrinsic gradient dimension in LLMs to outperform DP-PEFT and full-weight Projected DP-SGD baselines in privacy–utility, with fast, on-device user-level DP personalization. We evaluate across classification and generation, varying adapter count and subspace rank, and report improved accuracy at fixed epsilon with lower memory/compute than DP-LoRA.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of reconstructing accurate continuous surfaces from 3D point clouds by learning signed distance functions (SDFs). Its key insight is to supervise the network not by direct SDF regression alone but by a differentiable “pulling” operation that moves arbitrary query points toward their closest surface neighbors using the network-predicted signed distance and its gradient, thereby tightly coupling value and gradient learning. The method trains a neural network that, for each query 3D location, predicts an SDF value and gradient and then applies a stride equal to that predicted distance (forward or backward along the gradient depending on the sign) to pull the query onto the surface; the pulling loss between pulled points and real surface samples is backpropagated to update both SDF values and gradients, yielding improved surface reconstruction and single-image reconstruction performance.

args.text: Propose a causal curriculum that steers the emergence and multiplicity of transformer induction heads by gradually introducing higher-order token correlations while selectively clamping or perturbing candidate attention subcircuits during training. Building on the distributional simplicity bias that early-stage networks implicitly match maximum-entropy surrogates preserving low-order moments, use optimal-transport-based edits to corpus n-gram and co-occurrence statistics to create a ladder of training distributions that isolate when higher-order structure appears. The hypothesis is that abrupt phase transitions in loss and the sudden proliferation of induction heads partly reflect statistical shocks rather than solely circuit interdependencies; by decoupling the timing of higher-order statistics from the gradient signals reaching specific subcircuits, we can causally test this and either smooth or deliberately sharpen phase transitions. Methodologically, interleave moment-edited curricula with optogenetics-inspired activation clamping, and track subcircuit development, loss dynamics, and head multiplicity to map which statistical increments trigger which subcircuits and to achieve targeted control over their formation.

We propose Temporal Pairwise Anonymous Walk Networks (TPAWN): a temporal GNN that computes permutation-equivariant pairwise embeddings via injective temporal message passing with relative positional encodings, while aggregating information over causal anonymous walks to capture universal dynamic motifs without node identities. This design aligns with temporal WL-style expressivity prescriptions and avoids the large-graph degeneracy of node-level predictors by operating directly in the pairwise space. To counter reoccurrence memorization, we incorporate a decayed edge-reappearance prior as a feature but train and evaluate with recurrence-aware hard negatives and challenging splits, ensuring measured gains reflect true inductive generalization across time and graph size. We hypothesize TPAWN achieves state-of-the-art temporal link prediction OOD, with provable node-relabeling invariance and strengthened guarantees for pairwise predictors.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of designing neural network architectures for data defined on simplicial complexes, specifically targeting trajectory prediction while ensuring the model respects the topological and combinatorial structure of the complex. Its key insight is that architectures should satisfy three principled properties—permutation equivariance, orientation equivariance, and simplicial awareness—so outputs are independent of arbitrary node indexing and simplex orientation and depend on the full simplicial complex rather than a subset of dimensions. Building on algebraic topology, the authors propose a simple convolutional architecture acting on chain complexes that, when paired with an odd nonlinear activation, provably meets those three properties. Empirically, this principled simplicial neural network improves extrapolation and generalization to unseen trajectories on both synthetic and real datasets.

args.text: We propose Cipher-Invariant Constrained Alignment: train reward (helpfulness) and cost (harmlessness) models on groups of semantically equivalent but surface-diverse prompts/responses created by a stochastic cipher/paraphrase engine, and add a cross-cipher consistency regularizer so safety judgments are invariant to encipherment. During policy optimization, use Safe-RLHF’s Lagrangian formulation while forming listwise preference sets that include multiple ciphered variants of each exchange, encouraging the policy to optimize helpfulness subject to a cipher-robust safety constraint. An adversarial cipher generator (trained to maximize cost-model disagreement) is used online to discover new transformations, hardening the system against emergent ciphers and covert channels. We evaluate on CipherChat-style jailbreaks and after black-box fine-tuning, targeting reductions in ciphered violation rates without sacrificing helpfulness on natural language tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of solving linear inverse image-restoration tasks (e.g., super-resolution, deblurring, inpainting, colorization) by sampling from the posterior of natural images given measurements without requiring task-specific supervised training. The key insight is that a pre-trained denoising diffusion generative model can be leveraged as a universal prior and combined with a principled probabilistic update—motivated by variational inference—to produce efficient posterior samples for any linear measurement operator and noise level. The method, called Denoising Diffusion Restoration Models (DDRM), modifies the diffusion sampling process to incorporate measurement consistency by projecting noisy latent estimates onto measurement-constrained subspaces at each diffusion timestep, yielding an unsupervised algorithm that is broadly applicable, yields high-quality perceptual reconstructions, runs substantially faster than prior unsupervised approaches, and generalizes beyond the diffusion model’s training distribution.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of multi-semester planning in recommender systems, where a user supplies a few future items of interest and the system must predict a sequence of intervening items (e.g., filling the rest of a student’s degree plan). The key insight is that pre-specified future reference items can be leveraged at inference time to improve consecutive-item prediction, and that adaptations of masked training and contextual embeddings from self-attention models can be used to condition recommendations on both past history and future targets. result.text: The paper addresses the limited expressivity of standard graph neural networks due to their symmetric, local aggregation schemes by introducing globally consistent directional and asymmetric message passing. The key insight is to define a vector field over the graph and use directional derivatives and projections of node-specific messages into that field to create directional convolutional kernels, which both generalize CNNs on grids and enable global information flow. Methodologically, they construct directional graph networks (DGNs) by choosing the graph Laplacian eigenvectors as the vector field, applying directional smoothing and derivatives via projections, and enabling graph analogs of CNN augmentations (reflection, rotation, distortion); empirically this yields substantial error reductions on CIFAR10-graph and ZINC benchmarks and allows embedding intrinsic physical/biological axes into graph models.

The paper addresses the degradation of adaptive optimization methods under differential privacy, where noise added for privacy undermines adaptive preconditioners and harms training performance. The key insight is that non-sensitive side information can be used to construct a fixed or cheaply-updated preconditioner that approximates the geometry adaptive methods would learn, thereby reducing the amount of privacy noise that must be injected into the gradients. The proposed method, AdaDPS, integrates side-information-based preconditioning into private optimization so that less noise is needed for the same privacy budget; the authors prove reduced noise requirements and empirically validate the framework on centralized and federated benchmarks, showing substantial absolute accuracy gains and improved privacy–utility trade-offs.

args.text: We propose Phase-Annealed SDF Rendering (PASR), a neural volume-rendering objective that marries phase-transition losses with SDF-to-density mappings. PASR parameterizes density as the Laplace CDF of a temperature-scaled SDF and co-anneals the temperature with the rendering support from volumetric to near-surface regimes, preserving broad gradients early while converging to unbiased, sharp surfaces later. We derive a transmittance/opacity approximation error bound that shrinks monotonically with temperature and tie the annealing schedule to the learned interface width estimated from the phase loss, stabilizing optimization and improving thin-structure fidelity. This unifies phase-transition regularization with SDF-based rendering, NeuS-style unbiased gradients, and volumetric-to-surface curricula into a single principled training scheme.

result.text: The paper addresses why standard multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) struggle to learn high-frequency functions in low-dimensional regression tasks common in vision and graphics, limiting their ability to represent detailed 3D geometry and signals. The key insight is that MLPs exhibit a spectral bias—favoring low-frequency components—because their effective kernel (via the neural tangent kernel) lacks high-frequency sensitivity, but this can be remedied by preprocessing inputs with a random Fourier feature mapping that converts the NTK into a stationary kernel with controllable bandwidth. The method is to apply a simple Fourier feature transform to input coordinates before feeding them to an MLP, choose the feature scale to match task-specific frequency content, and thereby enable the network to learn and represent high-frequency detail; empirical results and NTK analysis demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness.
