args.text: We propose EdgeGate-PAIRWalk, a dynamic link prediction framework and evaluation protocol that explicitly disentangles edge reoccurrence from first-time edge formation. Motivated by EdgeBank’s findings, a learnable gate routes each candidate edge either to a memorization head (optimized for reappearance scoring) or to a novelty head that computes pairwise-equivariant embeddings from CAW-style anonymized temporal walks augmented with relative positional time encodings and injective update functions suggested by temporal WL theory. The pairwise novelty head is designed to retain predictive power out-of-distribution on much larger graphs, while the gate is calibrated by edge recency statistics and trained with harder negative sampling to avoid inflated scores from easy negatives. We further stratify evaluation by novelty vs reoccurrence to audit over-reliance on memorization and to isolate genuine temporal-motif generalization.

result.text: The paper addresses the limited expressive power of graph-based neural models for capturing higher-order, multi-way interactions in relational systems by moving beyond pairwise edges to simplicial complexes. The key insight is that performing message passing on simplices (faces of different dimensions) and analysing expressivity with a Simplicial Weisfeiler–Lehman (SWL) colouring yields a model class—Message Passing Simplicial Networks (MPSNs)—that can distinguish structures beyond the standard WL test and is at least as powerful as 3-WL. Methodologically, the authors define SWL to characterise discriminative power, design MPSNs that propagate messages across faces with orientation-equivariant layers, compare representational capacity to ReLU GNNs via linear region counts, and empirically validate superiority on hard-to-distinguish strongly regular graphs and oriented simplicial classification tasks.

args.text: Leverage vision-language models to compile small executable predicates that detect state-dependent affordances and subgoal completions from language task specs and a few labeled observations, then reuse these programs to parameterize options: predicates initialize interest (initiation) functions, termination/effect checkers, and dense progress rewards that run cheaply every step without further VLM calls. Build an interest-option-critic agent whose interest, policies, and terminations are learned jointly from experience but are warm-started by the compiled affordance code, and apply deep intra-option off-policy updates so each transition trains all options whose predicates fire or are consistent with the observed action. This produces an interpretable, reusable option library aligned to environment affordances and improves sample efficiency on open-ended tasks with highly state-dependent action availability.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of reconstructing medical images from partial or indirect measurements (inverse problems) in CT and MRI, where supervised learning methods trained on paired data with a fixed measurement model often fail to generalize to unseen measurement processes. The key insight is to decouple learning from the measurement process by training a score-based generative model as a flexible prior over medical images, then using this learned prior at test time to sample reconstructions that satisfy any given measurement model. Methodologically, the authors first train a score-based model on unpaired medical images to learn the image distribution, and at inference they perform conditional sampling guided by both the learned score (prior) and the likelihood from the observed measurements to produce images consistent with the data; this unsupervised approach achieves comparable or better reconstruction quality and far better generalization to unknown measurement processes than supervised methods.

args.text: We propose PESS-RS, an offline contextual bandit algorithm that performs representation selection by training a smoothed master over candidate feature mappings with a pessimistic objective and low-variance offline evaluation. Each base policy is trained with a pessimistic regularizer and a smoothing transform that caps density ratios, and the master routes contexts to bases to maximize a certified lower confidence bound on policy value computed with selective importance sampling (Rao–Blackwellizing over top-p logged actions) to control variance in extreme action spaces. Theoretically, PESS-RS enjoys near-oracle performance: it competes with the best candidate representation up to a logarithmic overhead and a coverage/misspecification penalty, recovering constant problem-dependent regret offline whenever a “good” representation exists and the logging policy provides adequate local support. Practically, it unifies multi-representation selection, batch pessimism, and stable evaluation, and extends naturally to two-stage recommenders by allocating item pools to the best base per context under the same pessimistic certification.

result.text: The paper tackles the slow sampling speed of diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs), which typically require hundreds or thousands of neural-network evaluations to generate samples. The key insight is an exact formulation of the diffusion ODE solution that analytically isolates the linear part and, after a change of variables, rewrites the remaining contribution as an exponentially weighted integral of the neural network, enabling high-order numerical integration rather than leaving everything to black-box ODE solvers. Based on this, the authors derive DPM-Solver, a dedicated high-order ODE solver with convergence-order guarantees that works for both discrete- and continuous-time DPMs without additional training and drastically reduces required function evaluations. Empirically, DPM-Solver produces high-quality samples in about 10–20 evaluations (e.g., 4.70 FID at 10 steps and 2.87 FID at 20 on CIFAR-10) and yields roughly 4–16× speedups over prior training-free samplers.

result.text: I propose Public-anchored Subspace Adapters (PaSA-DP): use a small public dataset to learn, per layer, an orthonormal low-rank adapter basis that spans the top gradient subspace, then privately fine-tune only the coefficients over these anchors with per-layer clipped, coefficient-space DP-SGD. We allocate noise across basis directions proportional to public-estimated sensitivity via restricted-Lipschitz constants, and adapt rank on-the-fly with a privacy-preserving (noisy) eigengap test; basin selection is handled by freezing backbone weights from public pretraining and only moving within the adapter subspace. This unifies parameter-efficient DP fine-tuning and projected DP-SGD with efficient per-layer/per-device clipping, yielding dimension-robust privacy–utility and near non-private accuracy at small epsilon while keeping memory cost LoRA-like and scaling cleanly to distributed settings.

args.text: We propose Spectral-Subband SDF Rendering: represent the scene SDF as a Fourier polynomial neural field that decomposes geometry into interpretable frequency subbands, and map SDF to density via a Laplace CDF whose scale is conditioned per subband. This enables closed-form, subband-decomposed transmittance error bounds that drive adaptive, footprint-aware ray sampling and a curriculum that optimizes low-frequency subbands with unbiased volumetric losses before progressively tightening high-frequency subbands toward surface-focused rendering, combining stability with crisp surface recovery. The approach reduces samples, improves thin-structure fidelity and anti-aliasing, and allows direct geometric editing by manipulating subbands.

We propose a hazard-aware, conformal evaluation and modeling protocol for temporal link prediction that removes easy negatives and yields calibrated uncertainty under distribution shift. Non-edges are sampled conditioned on edge recency, node degrees, and community to match per-pair hazard rates, and predictors use permutation-equivariant pairwise heads built on anonymized temporal walks to preserve inductivity and OOD robustness. We then conformalize scores over blocked time splits to obtain finite-sample coverage-guaranteed prediction sets and report coverage-calibrated recall and expected set size alongside standard AUC. The protocol plugs into expressive temporal GNNs with injective, relative-position message passing and stress-tests models for both performance and calibration across datasets.

result.text: The paper studies whether common graph neural networks can detect and count small attributed substructures, a capability crucial for tasks in chemistry, biology and social networks. The key insight is that existing message-passing GNNs and modestly powerful higher-order architectures have intrinsic limitations: MPNNs, 2-WL and 2-IGNs cannot perform induced-subgraph counting for patterns of size three or more, although they can count simple star-shaped subgraphs, while higher-order k-WL and k-IGNs can count more complex patterns but k-WL with only finitely many iterations remains limited. Methodologically, the authors prove these expressiveness results by reductions to Weisfeiler-Lehman-style distinguishing power (including showing equivalence of 2-WL and 2-IGN for graph distinction), validate the theory with experiments on MPNNs and 2-IGNs, and propose a local relational pooling variant that empirically improves substructure counting and real-world task performance.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of sampling from the posterior distribution of linear inverse problems with additive Gaussian noise, enabling recovery methods that capture uncertainty rather than producing a single point estimate. args.text: We propose PessiMoE, a weighted-minimax offline item-pool allocation scheme for two-stage recommenders that learns which nominator should own which items to minimize worst-case regret across user–item instances. The core idea is to cast gating as minimizing a difficulty-aware weighted-minimax objective, yielding pessimistic allocations that are robust to the harmful nominator–ranker interactions observed in two-stage systems. To optimize this objective from bandit logs at extreme scale, we estimate counterfactual per-nominator contributions with a Rao–Blackwellized selective importance-sampling estimator over top-p logged actions, trading small bias for large variance reduction and stable training. Under standard coverage assumptions, we prove the learned allocation attains the weighted-minimax rate and improves end-to-end precision/recall over Mixture-of-Experts baselines in large-scale experiments.

Adaptive Cohort–Sketch SNR Scheduling: jointly schedule per-round cohort size and sketch/compression parameters to maintain a target signal-to-noise ratio in the server’s linear sketch under central DP via one-time initialization noise and clipping, improving utility at a fixed total client budget. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of poor and noisy geometry reconstruction in neural volume rendering, where prior methods model geometry indirectly via a generic density field and extract surfaces from arbitrary density level sets. The key insight is to reverse this relationship by modeling volume density as an explicit function of a signed distance function (SDF), specifically using the Laplace cumulative distribution function applied to the SDF, which provides a strong geometric inductive bias, enables a bound on opacity approximation error for accurate ray sampling, and facilitates disentanglement of shape and appearance. The method implements this SDF-to-density mapping within a neural volume rendering pipeline, uses the error bound to drive efficient and precise ray sampling for tight coupling of geometry and radiance, and trains the model in an unsupervised multiview setting to produce higher-fidelity geometry and allow swapping of shape and appearance across scenes.

result.text: The paper tackles lifelong reinforcement learning in non-stationary, non-episodic environments where standard RL fails due to the inability to plan long-horizon behavior and adapt without resets. args.text: We propose PEP-RS: a pessimistic ensemble over candidate representations for offline contextual bandits that safely selects or composes features using only logged data. For each representation, we train a policy with a pessimism-regularized SGD objective and evaluate it using a selective importance sampling OPE that Rao–Blackwellizes over top-p logged actions to cut variance, while an advantage-weighted behavior prior further biases policies toward well-supported actions to avoid OOD error. A weighted-minimax selection rule then chooses the representation (or a learned convex combination) that maximizes a pessimistic lower confidence bound on value, yielding guarantees within a log M overhead of the best “good-on-support” representation and adapting to misspecification on uncovered regions. Theory ties the bound to coverage and effective dimension, and the estimator is plug-and-play for extreme action spaces.

result.text: The paper addresses how to design differentially private adaptive gradient methods for convex optimization that retain the advantages of adaptivity (like AdaGrad) despite the destructive effect of isotropic privacy noise in high dimensions. The key insight is that non-isotropic gradient clipping and noise addition—aligned with the geometry of the gradients—preserves useful directional information so that adaptive schemes can still exploit non-isotropic gradient structure under privacy constraints. Concretely, the authors develop and analyze private variants of adaptive SGD and AdaGrad that perform clipping and add noise in a geometry-aware (non-isotropic) manner, proving regret upper bounds that are worst-case optimal and showing theoretically and empirically that private AdaGrad outperforms private adaptive SGD, which itself outperforms standard private SGD in settings with non-isotropic gradients.

args.text: We propose Hierarchical Polynomial SDF Fields (H-PolySDF), which represent a scene’s signed distance function as a polynomial neural field decomposition into interpretable subbands, enabling direct multiscale geometry editing while accelerating high-frequency convergence. Concretely, we predict the SDF with multiplicative polynomial interactions over Fourier-featured coordinates, apply per-band eikonal/normal-consistency constraints, and render via an SDF-to-density mapping for unbiased, sharp reconstructions. Training follows a coarse-to-fine curriculum that first emphasizes low-order bands with full volumetric sampling, then progressively upweights higher-order bands while shrinking sampling to a narrow surface neighborhood, stabilizing optimization and yielding compact, crisp surfaces. At inference, reweighting or transferring subbands affords controllable edits such as removing fine bumps, transplanting engravings, or adjusting coarse shape without retraining.

I propose frequency-equalizing preconditioners: a learnable front-end (or intermediate) module trained to flatten the downstream model’s effective NTK spectrum under the data distribution, so convergence rates are balanced across spatial frequencies rather than biased to low-frequency modes. Concretely, we jointly estimate coarse NTK spectral energy and local sample density p(x), and optimize the preconditioner to equalize per-mode gradient energy while enforcing anti-alias constraints via a learned filter bank matched to location-dependent Nyquist limits; for conv nets this includes orthogonalized, bandpass-steerable filters and optional learned Fourier-feature injections. Applied to GAN generators, the preconditioner counteracts spectral under-allocation and reduces high-frequency artifacts; in semantic segmentation, it reduces “hard” pixels by suppressing aliased components and upweighting learnability of high-frequency boundaries without overfitting.

result.text: The paper addresses the slow convergence of standard gradient-based optimization, which updates parameters locally and can get stuck making only small progress along loss level sets. Its key insight is that exploiting symmetries of the loss landscape to "teleport" parameters along loss-invariant group actions can reposition them to regions where subsequent local updates converge faster, effectively achieving a large nonlocal move without changing the current loss. Methodologically, the authors derive explicit loss-invariant group actions for representative test functions and multilayer neural nets, prove a necessary condition under which such symmetry teleportation improves the convergence rate and relate the procedure to second-order methods, then implement algorithms that combine teleportation with gradient descent and AdaGrad and empirically demonstrate faster convergence on synthetic problems, multilayer regression and MNIST.

The paper tackles improving graph neural networks by providing a principled multi-scale representation and pooling scheme that better preserves signal and geometry on graphs. Its key insight is that framelet (wavelet-like) decompositions separate graph signals into low- and high-frequency coefficients across scales, enabling convolutions and pooling that conserve information while isolating noise and fine-detail structure. The method defines framelet-based graph convolution and an induced pooling that aggregates low-/high-pass spectra, and introduces shrinkage as an activation that thresholds high-frequency coefficients per scale to denoise and compress signals; experiments show state-of-the-art results on node and graph prediction tasks and substantial gains in denoising and compression compared with ReLU.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of offline reinforcement learning where standard off-policy methods overestimate action values due to distributional shift between a static dataset and the learned policy, causing poor performance especially on complex, multi-modal data. The key insight is to learn a conservative Q-function that intentionally underestimates values for out-of-distribution actions so that the Q-estimate lower-bounds the true policy value, preventing spurious optimistic updates. Methodologically, Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) adds a simple Q-value regularizer to the Bellman error objective that penalizes Q-values of actions sampled from a broad set (e.g., policy and dataset actions) while preserving accuracy on dataset actions; this regularizer can be implemented on top of existing deep Q-learning or actor-critic algorithms and is shown theoretically to produce a value lower bound and empirically to yield substantially better returns across discrete and continuous benchmarks.

args.text: I propose Semantic-Anchored Diffusion Posterior Sampling: solve linear inverse problems by sampling from a diffusion-based posterior while softly constraining samples to remain close to a provided, semantically related reference image in a disentangled representation space. Concretely, augment DDRM-style measurement projections with a semantic guidance gradient at each timestep that minimizes distance between an encoder’s representation of the current sample and the reference (e.g., StyleGAN W+/self-supervised features), with a schedule that emphasizes identity-preserving factors late in sampling and relaxes along measurement-constrained directions. This combines the robustness and uncertainty quantification of diffusion/score-based posteriors with the targeted regularization of related-image priors, aiming to preserve subject/scene identity under severe undersampling or distribution shift. Evaluate on MRI and natural image restoration, comparing to DDRM/SNIPS and StyleGAN-latent priors, and analyze tradeoffs via controllable semantic weights and uncertainty decomposition.

We propose Ranker-Aware Pessimistic Nominators (RAPN), which jointly trains item-pool allocation and scoring in a two-stage recommender by optimizing a pessimistic surrogate of downstream ranker utility estimated purely from logged data. RAPN minimizes a weighted-minimax regret objective where weights reflect instance difficulty and ranker disagreement, and uses selective importance sampling over top-p logged actions to obtain low-variance, scalable offline policy gradients for the nominator. To prevent out-of-distribution exposure and nominator–ranker collapse, we apply pessimistic regularization to both modules, adapting offline contextual bandit pessimism to the two-stage setting and coupling it with a conservative model-based surrogate where uncertainty is high. The result is an end-to-end batch-optimal training criterion that directly targets counterfactual utility of the composed system and resolves nominator–ranker mismatch under distribution shift.

Its key insight is to structure neural fields as polynomial neural fields (PNFs) that decompose a signal into a sum of manipulable, interpretable components (subbands) while retaining the representational strengths of neural fields. The authors develop a general theoretical framework for designing PNFs and instantiate it as Fourier PNFs that achieve state-of-the-art signal representation quality; they show how the polynomial composition enables direct subband operations for tasks like texture transfer and scale-space interpolation and provide empirical results and code validating both representation fidelity and manipulation capabilities.

args.text: I propose a Density-Adaptive Nyquist Curriculum (DANC) for semantic segmentation that estimates a per-pixel equivalent sampling rate from the training set and augmentations, converts it to a local Nyquist frequency, and gates feature bandwidth accordingly throughout training. Early epochs apply spatially varying de-aliasing and downsampling to suppress content above each pixel’s Nyquist, then gradually relax the gates in proportion to local sample density p(x), enabling high-frequency learning only where data support it. To counter spectral bias, we inject Fourier features whose bandwidth is modulated by the same density map so scarce regions receive lower-bandwidth encodings early while dense regions admit higher frequencies; this schedule aligns with kernel spectral learning curves to accelerate convergence without aliasing. We hypothesize DANC reduces boundary and displacement errors while speeding fine-detail learning in densely sampled areas, with ablations comparing fixed versus adaptive filters and curricula.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of controlling partially observed, stochastic dynamic processes on temporal graphs when only a limited number of interventions are possible, a setting relevant to tasks like epidemic testing, influence maximization, and misinformation inspection. Its key insight is that combining reinforcement learning with graph neural networks yields a scalable, data-driven policy that can reason about graph-structured state and uncertainty while avoiding exhaustive enumeration of exponential states and combinatorial actions. Methodologically, the authors cast intervention selection as a sequential decision problem over a temporal graph process, use GNNs to embed local and global graph-time information under partial observability, and train RL policies to output intervention priorities (or distributions) that guide tractable, near-optimal choices; they validate the approach on epidemic testing and influence maximization tasks.

args.text: I propose Hodge-SAN: a cell-complex Transformer that performs attention over k-cells using positional encodings derived from the eigenbases of the k-dimensional Hodge Laplacians, combined with multi-scale framelet gating to modulate frequency bands before attention. Starting from a CW/simplicial lifting of the input graph, we attach spectral encodings to nodes, edges, and higher cells, apply fully-connected attention within each k, and constrain cross-k attention by boundary/coboundary incidence masks with learnable directional biases. This design targets SWL/3-WL+ expressivity while mitigating over-squashing by shortening effective paths in the lifted complex and enabling global, anisotropic information flow across dimensions. To scale, we replace full spectra with polynomial or Nyström approximations per Hodge Laplacian and share multi-scale filters across cells of the same dimension.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of adapting reinforcement learning agents from safe, non-critical training domains to real-world safety-critical target environments where failures are costly. The key insight is that exposure to diverse source environments lets an agent learn a probabilistic model of dynamics and where catastrophes occur, which can be used to estimate risk and drive risk-averse planning during adaptation. Their method, CARL, trains a model-based RL system that captures uncertainty over transitions and catastrophic states across varied sources, and then uses this uncertainty-aware model to plan conservatively in new target environments—avoiding actions that might lead to catastrophic states—resulting in safer, more sample-efficient adaptation. Empirically, CARL produced cautious exploration and achieved higher returns with fewer failures than strong adaptation baselines on driving, cartpole, half-cheetah, and robotic manipulation tasks.

args.text: We propose Semantically-Guided Diffusion Posterior Sampling (SGDPS) for linear inverse problems when a semantically related exemplar image is available. Building on diffusion-based restoration, we augment each timestep with a proximal “semantic projection” that nudges the sample toward a neighborhood defined by the exemplar in a robust embedding space (e.g., CLIP), akin to prior-image constraints used with StyleGAN latents but without requiring a GAN prior. Coupling measurement-consistency projections with exemplar-conditioned guidance and posterior noise improves fidelity and perceptual plausibility under extreme undersampling and distribution shift; we further bound the bias–variance tradeoff when the embedding is Lipschitz and the exemplar lies within a radius of the ground truth in embedding space. Experiments on MRI/CT and natural-image deblurring show consistent gains over exemplar-less diffusion priors, with ablations confirming the benefits of the proximal schedule and adaptive guidance strength.

Goal-conditioned pessimistic offline sequence recommendation for learning paths: we model student knowledge as a latent MDP learned from logs and construct a pessimistic surrogate MDP that penalizes transitions with high uncertainty, ensuring safe value estimates when planning purely offline. We condition the planner on user-specified target concepts to shape rewards and attention, integrating future goals into planning, and optimize policies with a pessimism-regularized SGD objective adapted from offline contextual bandits to control overestimation on unseen concept combinations. For evaluation and training feedback we use a Rao–Blackwellized selective importance sampler over top-p path-prefixes to achieve low-variance OPE in the combinatorial action space. This yields conservative-but-competent path generation that better reaches targets than set-to-sequence RL and goal-agnostic BERT-style planners while providing performance lower bounds under standard uncertainty assumptions.

result.text: The paper studies how the number of clients sampled per round (cohort size) affects model quality and training dynamics in federated learning, addressing scalability, analogies to centralized batch-size effects, and how to exploit large cohorts. The key insight is that increasing cohort size yields both familiar large-batch phenomena (diminishing returns, generalization gaps) and federated-specific issues (training instabilities, fairness degradation and client heterogeneity interactions) so larger cohorts are not uniformly beneficial. The authors empirically analyze many realistic federated settings, quantifying performance, convergence, and fairness as cohort size grows, and compare algorithmic choices and hyperparameter scaling strategies to identify which adjustments (e.g., learning-rate schedules, aggregation rules) mitigate problems and when larger cohorts help versus hurt.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that differentially private (DP) training of deep models suffers severe utility degradation when models have many parameters because standard DP noise scales poorly with gradient dimensionality. The key insight is that individual gradients can be decomposed into a low-dimensional "anchor" subspace embedding plus a small-norm residual, allowing privacy noise to be allocated and scaled differently for the informative low-dimensional component and the insignificant residual. The proposed method, Gradient Embedding Perturbation (GEP), projects per-example gradients onto a non-sensitive anchor subspace to obtain compact embeddings and residuals, then injects calibrated DP noise separately into the embedding and residual according to the privacy budget before aggregating and updating model parameters; this decomposition reduces perturbation variance, breaks the dimensionality barrier, and yields substantially better accuracy (e.g., 74.9% on CIFAR-10, 95.1% on SVHN at ε=8) with modest computational cost.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of decomposing images of an object into shape, spatially-varying BRDF, and per-image illumination—an important but underconstrained task that existing neural renderers (e.g., NeRF/NeRD) handle poorly, especially for detailed illumination recovery. Its key insight is to replace the expensive analytic illumination integral in rendering with a learned neural query—Neural-PIL—that effectively pre-integrates lighting effects, and to regularize decomposition with learned low-dimensional smooth manifold priors for BRDF and illumination. The method trains a reflectance decomposition network that predicts geometry, BRDF parameters, and per-image lighting while using Neural-PIL to produce rendered radiance efficiently; separate auto-encoders enforce compact, smooth latent spaces for BRDF and illumination to stabilize and improve recovery. This combination yields more accurate BRDF and lighting estimates and enables higher-fidelity novel view synthesis and relighting than prior approaches.

result.text: The paper studies why increasing depth speeds up training in feedforward neural networks by examining how depth alters the frequency content of the function each layer must learn; the key insight is the "deep frequency principle," namely that for a deeper pre-condition component the effective target function presented to subsequent learning layers is biased toward lower frequencies, which are known to be learned faster by neural networks. To support this, the authors split trained networks into a pre-condition component and a learning component, use a filtering-based Fourier analysis to characterize the frequency distribution of high-dimensional functions, and run experiments on deep architectures and real datasets to show deeper pre-condition modules shift the downstream target toward lower-frequency components. Thus, by combining empirical Fourier analyses with the established frequency principle (that lower-frequency functions are learned earlier), the method provides an explanatory mechanism for why deeper networks can train faster.

result.text: The paper tackles the computational and memory burden of unsupervised high-resolution image registration, where U-Net–style networks predict dense full-resolution displacement fields. The key insight is that typical anatomical deformations are band-limited and can be represented compactly in a low-dimensional Fourier domain, so predicting band-limited coefficients and decoding them deterministically yields nearly the same registration quality with far fewer learned parameters and operations. The method, called Fourier-Net, replaces the U-Net decoder with a parameter-free model-driven decoder: a CNN encoder predicts a low-resolution, band-limited Fourier representation of the displacement field, which is zero-padded and transformed via an inverse discrete Fourier transform to produce the dense spatial displacement; this design yields much lower computational cost and faster inference while maintaining or improving accuracy on 3D brain registration benchmarks.

args.text: We propose a Hodge-guided Multi-Order Directional Transformer that unifies directional message passing with higher-order simplicial reasoning by building globally consistent fields from harmonic components of the 0-, 1-, and 2-order Hodge Laplacians. These harmonic fields define asymmetric, orientation-aware directional kernels for nodes, edges, and faces, while their spectra yield learnable multi-order positional encodings that drive a joint attention mechanism over nodes–edges–faces. By aligning information flow with cycle- and cavity-tracking harmonic directions, the model breaks symmetries important for long-range dependencies and alleviates over-squashing, targeting 3-WL/SWL-level expressivity with efficient masked receptive fields and low-rank spectral parameterizations. This yields a drop-in architecture for molecules and proteins that natively encodes rings, conjugation paths, and surface motifs, while remaining scalable compared to full higher-order lifts.

Executable Affordance Options via VLM Synthesis: Prompt a vision-language model to synthesize compact, executable predicates over observations that detect state-dependent affordances and define option initiation/termination conditions, then compile these predicates to run cheaply at every step. Use the predicates both as dense reward signals and as hard action/skill constraints: learn interest-option-critic policies over these code-defined options, and drive unsupervised skill discovery by maximizing relative changes in the resulting affordance vector rather than raw state differences. Plan in the learned skill space while enforcing safety by estimating catastrophe risk and applying conservative value learning during offline/online updates. We hypothesize this reduces VLM query cost, improves sample efficiency, and yields safer exploration in open-ended domains such as Minecraft-based benchmarks.

I propose reference-conditioned diffusion posterior sampling for inverse problems where a semantically related prior image is available but not perfectly aligned. At each diffusion step, we combine measurement-consistency projection with a conditional score formed by adding the pretrained diffusion prior’s score to the gradient of a learned reference-alignment energy, computed via a lightweight encoder with cross-attention to the reference and an uncertainty-gated contrastive objective to prevent over-copying under distribution shift. A simple low-dimensional warp (e.g., affine/elastic) is jointly sampled or marginalized to account for plausible geometric differences, and the guidance strength is scheduled by a conflict detector comparing measurement residuals and reference-induced features. This plug-and-play scheme preserves DDRM’s generality while leveraging exemplar semantics, yielding identity- and structure-preserving reconstructions with calibrated uncertainty under extreme undersampling and OOD operators.

result.text: Conformal Pessimism for Offline Contextual Bandits: Integrate split-conformal calibrated lower bounds on neural reward predictions into the pessimistic SGD objective for offline contextual bandits. We compute per-context, per-action lower bounds using residuals reweighted by estimated density ratios between the offline logging distribution and the target context distribution, yielding stronger conservatism in low-support regions in line with weighted-minimax guidance. To mitigate model misspecification, we aggregate multiple candidate representations and oracle-efficient regressors and select the most conservative conformal score per context, while borrowing ABM’s insight to softly bias toward data-supported actions without requiring a fixed behavior prior. This aims to retain the empirical strength of pessimistic NN bandits while providing distribution-free finite-sample safety under shift and heterogeneity.

result.text: The paper addresses why and how training a compact student model to mimic a larger teacher’s class probabilities (knowledge distillation) can outperform direct training on labels and how to make distillation more reliable. The key insight is to view distillation as a semiparametric inference problem where the student is the finite-dimensional target, the true Bayes class probabilities are an infinite-dimensional nuisance, and the teacher provides a plug-in nuisance estimate, which lets one analyze the impact of teacher error on student risk using modern semiparametric tools. Methodologically, the authors derive prediction-error guarantees for standard distillation under this framework and propose two practical improvements—cross-fitting to reduce overfitting bias from the teacher, and loss correction to adjust for teacher underfitting—then empirically validate that these enhancements consistently improve student performance on tabular and image benchmarks.

args.text: I propose DP-ModePath: constrain private fine-tuning to a low-loss weight-space curve computed from public data via mode connectivity between the base and a public-finetuned model. We parameterize each layer by a tiny set of coefficients (curve position and a few tangent directions drawn from public top-gradient eigenspaces) and run DP-SGD only on these coefficients with per-layer/per-device clipping and anisotropic Gaussian noise shaped by the public curvature, optionally projecting residual gradients into the public subspace. This preserves basin selection while slashing effective dimensionality, yielding stronger privacy–utility and stability than isotropic DP-PEFT or full-model projected DP-SGD at the same budget with minimal memory/compute. We analyze sensitivity along the path and allocate privacy across directions via zCDP composition to further improve signal-to-noise.

We propose Polynomial-SDF Radiance Fields that combine polynomial neural fields with SDF-to-density neural volume rendering to yield editable, fast-converging high-frequency geometry and lighting. The signed distance is represented as a Fourier Polynomial Neural Field whose multiplicative interactions (in the spirit of Π-Nets) shift the NTK spectrum to favor high-frequency components, while mapping SDF to density via a Laplace-CDF ensures accurate ray sampling and disentangled shape/appearance. We integrate a Neural-PIL-style lighting module per subband to pre-integrate illumination and enable frequency-selective relighting and more stable reflectance/illumination decomposition. Training uses a curriculum that progressively increases polynomial degree and transitions from volumetric to surface-focused sampling, accelerating convergence on fine details and producing cleaner, more compact surfaces.

Density-Equalizing Positional Encodings (DEPE): To counter the locality-dependent spectral slowdown induced by non-uniform sampling, learn a bijective input warp T that approximately uniformizes the empirical data density and then apply a standard global Fourier-feature MLP in the warped coordinates. By pushing p(x) to near-uniform, the NTK eigen-decay and convergence times for a local mode become approximately location-invariant, while Fourier features provide controllable high-frequency sensitivity; practically, T can be parameterized as a (near) volume-preserving normalizing flow trained to maximize entropy of T#p and penalize metric distortion. Theory predicts more uniform error across space and faster acquisition of fine detail in sparse regions, and experiments on coordinate-based reconstruction and inverse problems with spatially varying sample densities should validate the gains over fixed-scale or globally tuned encodings. A simple alternating schedule that updates T to equalize batch density and then optimizes the predictor in the warped domain provides a practical training recipe.

result.text: The paper studies why different normalization layers work or fail in deep networks by extending theoretical analyses of BatchNorm to a range of recent alternatives, aiming to predict their effects on training and signal propagation. The key insight is that a small set of mechanistic properties—control of activation growth, preservation of sample-specific activation differences, and the induced gradient norms—explain both benefits and pathologies across normalization methods: activation-based normalizers can prevent exponential activation growth in ResNets, GroupNorm preserves informative per-sample distinctions while larger group sizes collapse these distinctions (linking to LayerNorm’s slow convergence), and tiny group sizes produce large early-layer gradient norms that destabilize training (as in InstanceNorm). Methodologically, the authors analyze randomly initialized deep networks with different normalization schemes to quantify forward and backward dynamics (activation scale, inter-sample activation similarity, and gradient norms), derive how these metrics depend on normalization design parameters (e.g., group size, parametric vs. activation-based normalization), and validate that these unified mechanisms explain observed speed–stability trade-offs and guide principled normalization design.

args.text: Directional spectral rewiring on cell complexes for de-squashing long-range signals: we learn a small set of eigenvalue-dependent, band-limited graph filters and use their per-node responses to define a global vector field whose integral curves induce a sparse set of orientation-consistent teleportation edges that bypass bottlenecks. We augment the graph with these frequency- and direction-aware virtual edges, lift it into a lightweight ring-based CW complex, and perform simplicial message passing so information can traverse both 1- and 2-cells, compressing distances while preserving orientation equivariance. A curvature/energy regularizer (effective-resistance/Ollivier–Ricci proxies) encourages rewiring that reduces over-squashing, while a spectral sparsity prior limits added edges per band for scalability. The module plugs into MPNNs or spectral Transformers and targets improved long-range reasoning, with theoretical support via decreased effective resistance bounds and empirical gains on benchmarks requiring distant dependencies.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of generating high-quality synthetic images for object detection where geometric constraints (e.g., bounding boxes, camera views) must be respected, a requirement not well-served by existing diffusion-based or copy-paste approaches. Its key insight is that geometric conditions can be expressed as structured text prompts, allowing off-the-shelf pre-trained text-to-image diffusion models to be repurposed for layout-to-image generation without bespoke layout encoders. The method, GeoDiffusion, translates bounding boxes and additional geometric cues into prompt tokens and conditioning schemes that guide a T2I diffusion model to produce images that adhere to specified object placements and camera perspectives; this yields better detection-ready images than prior L2I methods while being about four times faster to train and demonstrably improving detector performance.

args.text: I propose Retrieval-Guided Posterior Diffusion for inverse problems, which augments DDRM-style sampling with exemplar-conditioned semantic guidance from a small set of retrieved, semantically related prior images. At each diffusion step we combine the standard measurement-consistency projection with a feature-space energy (from a frozen encoder) whose gradient pulls the current sample toward a convex combination of the exemplars’ embeddings, enabling personalization without retraining the prior. We estimate exemplar–target mismatch online and adapt the guidance weight accordingly, downweighting or disabling it when retrieval is unreliable to preserve robustness. This yields measurement-consistent, uncertainty-aware reconstructions that better preserve subject-specific structure and remain stable under distribution shift compared to unconditional or single-MAP generative priors.

result.text: This paper studies batch policy optimization in finite-armed stochastic bandits, asking what performance guarantees are possible when policies must be built from fixed offline data before any further interaction. The key insight is that a unified class of confidence-adjusted index algorithms—interpolating optimistic, pessimistic, and neutral adjustments—are all minimax optimal in the batch setting, but classical instance-dependent optimality is unattainable: any algorithm that is optimal on one instance can suffer arbitrarily larger regret on another. To better discriminate algorithms the authors introduce a weighted-minimax criterion tied to the difficulty of predicting the optimal value and show this criterion justifies pessimistic design principles for batch policy optimization.

result.text: The paper addresses the mismatch between population-level calibration and the need for reliable, individual-sample calibrated predictions—important for fairness and robustness—by asking whether one can guarantee calibration not just on average but for each sample in regression settings. The key insight is that perfect individual calibration is unattainable with deterministic predictors but becomes achievable if predictions are randomized: by outputting randomized credible intervals one can eliminate systematic bias for any sample at the cost of increased variance, effectively trading bias for variance to remove subgroup-specific miscalibration. The authors operationalize this insight by proposing a training objective that enforces individual calibration under randomized forecasting and train randomized regression functions to minimize that objective; empirically these models improve calibration on arbitrarily chosen subgroups and yield higher utility in decision tasks where adversaries can exploit miscalibrated predictions.

The paper addresses the complexity and fragmented design choices in diffusion-based generative models that obscure which components truly drive sample quality and efficiency. Its key insight is that sampling, training, and score-network preconditioning choices can be cleanly separated into a unified design space, and that several targeted modifications across these axes—rather than wholesale architectural changes—unlock large gains in speed and fidelity. Methodologically, the authors formalize this design space, identify and apply specific improvements to sampling algorithms, training objectives, and network preconditioning, and demonstrate their modular benefits by retrofitting prior pretrained score networks and retraining models to achieve state-of-the-art FIDs (e.g., CIFAR-10 unconditional and class-conditional) with far fewer network evaluations.

result.text: The paper studies why differentially private (DP) learning under realistic privacy budgets lags on vision tasks, showing that end-to-end private deep networks often underperform simple linear models trained on handcrafted features. The key insight is that the bottleneck is feature quality: with limited private data, noisy DP training destroys representations, so either substantially more private data or transfer of features learned on related public data is needed to match non-private performance. Methodologically, the authors compare DP training of deep models versus private linear classifiers on fixed handcrafted or publicly pretrained features across standard datasets, and introduce these strong baselines to demonstrate that improving DP learning requires better features (via public transfer) or orders-of-magnitude more private examples.

result.text: The paper tackles slow and view-entangled 3D-aware image synthesis caused by per-sample MLP-based radiance fields, which force costly ray sampling or low-res rendering with upsampling and can change object geometry/appearance with viewpoint. Its key insight is that sparse voxel grids combined with 3D convolutions, progressive growing, free-space pruning and regularization can replace monolithic MLPs to achieve fast, single-pass, and more 3D-consistent generation, while disentangling foreground (3D voxel grid) from background (2D) yields a compact scalable representation. The method builds a generator that produces a sparse volumetric feature grid for the foreground and a separate 2D background, renders images via a single forward pass through 3D convolutions and differentiable volume rendering, and applies pruning and progressive resolution increases during training to maintain efficiency and fidelity. As a result, VoxGRAF enables efficient, high-quality, and viewpoint-consistent novel-view synthesis without per-ray MLP queries.

result.text: The paper studies how neural networks’ frequency bias—the tendency to fit low-frequency components before high-frequency ones—interacts with non-uniform training data density, showing that realistic, non-uniform sampling alters which frequencies are learned first. The key insight is that local sample density rescales NTK spectral decay so that convergence time for a pure harmonic of frequency κ at point x scales as O(κ^d / p(x)), meaning high-density regions accelerate learning of high-frequency components while low-density regions slow them. Methodologically, the authors analyze the Neural Tangent Kernel: they derive analytic NTK eigenfunctions for two-layer networks on the circle (S^1), prove convergence bounds for deep fully connected networks via the NTK spectral decomposition, and validate predictions with empirical experiments comparing shallow and deep network behavior.

args.text: We propose Temporal Pairwise Equivariant Networks (TPEN) for dynamic link prediction under strict inductive and out-of-distribution evaluation. TPEN computes a joint representation for each candidate node pair via pair-centric, temporally ordered anonymous walks with relative time encodings and injective message updates, yielding pairwise embeddings whose limiting behavior remains non-degenerate as graph size grows. To counter memorization-driven inflation, we train with a hardness-aware negative sampler conditioned on historical recurrence statistics and evaluate on the harder EdgeBank splits. This marries the OOD benefits of pairwise structural embeddings with temporal expressivity from TGAT/PINT-style encodings and CAW/FiGTNE walk-based anonymization.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of enabling deep graph convolutional networks (GCNs) by tackling the common over-smoothing problem that causes node representations to become indistinguishable as layers increase. The key insight is that preserving initial node features via residual connections and using identity mapping can prevent feature collapse and stabilize propagation, allowing meaningful depth. They introduce GCNII, a simple extension of vanilla GCN that incorporates initial residual connections and identity mapping into each layer, with theoretical analysis and empirical results showing these techniques mitigate over-smoothing and let much deeper GCNs outperform prior methods on semi- and full-supervised graph tasks.

args.text: Executable Affordance-Constrained Reward Code (ACRC): extend VLM-synthesized reward programs to also encode state-dependent affordances and option pre/postconditions, so the code specifies not only what constitutes progress but also which temporally-extended skills are admissible where. Concretely, prompt the VLM to propose reward predicates alongside differentiable interest functions and precondition/effect schemata for options; learn and refine these with intra-option off-policy updates while validating conservatively with offline-style penalties to avoid optimistic use of out-of-distribution preconditions. Plan over this code-defined skill graph with a learned skill-dynamics model, selecting sequences of options that satisfy affordance constraints and maximize dense rewards, yielding safer, more sample-efficient long-horizon control. We expect this to reduce reward hacking and improve transfer in non-stationary settings compared to reward-only code generation.

Semantically Anchored Diffusion Restoration (SADR) conditions posterior-sampling–based inverse imaging on an auxiliary, semantically related prior image to preserve subject- or scene-specific attributes under extreme undersampling. Building on diffusion restoration methods, we augment each denoising step with an additional gradient term from a semantic anchor energy −||E(x)−E(a)||^2/(2σ^2), where E is a frozen representation (e.g., CLIP/medical encoder) or a linearized StyleGAN latent around the anchor a; in parallel, we enforce measurement consistency via DDRM-style projections. This realizes sampling from p(x|y,a) ∝ p(y|x) p(x) p_sem(x|a), stabilizing identity and structure while retaining uncertainty quantification, and admits fast implementation with backprop through E and closed-form data projections. We will evaluate on longitudinal MRI and multiview reconstruction with subject templates, expecting improved fidelity and fewer hallucinations versus DDRM alone and GAN-manifold prior methods.

result.text: The paper addresses designing computationally efficient contextual bandit algorithms that remain robust when the reward model is misspecified, i.e., when the true reward function lies at distance ε from the model class. The key insight is an optimization-based reformulation of the regression-oracle reduction framework that lets an algorithm automatically adapt to the unknown misspecification level and attain minimax-optimal dependence on ε. Methodologically, the authors build an oracle-efficient family of algorithms that use an online square-loss regression oracle to guide action selection and analysis, proving optimal regret bounds for both finite and infinite action sets and, in particular, achieving the first algorithm with O(d√T + ε√d T) regret for linear bandits in d dimensions without knowing ε.

result.text: The paper addresses reducing uplink communication in federated learning under realistic challenges—partial client participation and heterogeneous data—while handling the distortion introduced by communication compression. Its key insight is that the classical stochastic controlled averaging (SCA) can be reformulated into an equivalent but simpler and more communication-efficient implementation that halves uplink cost and serves as a foundation for compression-aware algorithms. Building on that reformulation, the authors develop two algorithms—SCALLION for unbiased compressors and SCAFCOM for biased compressors—that integrate compressed updates without extra assumptions on compression error or limits on heterogeneity, and they prove improved communication and computation complexity relative to prior work. Empirically, both methods match full-precision FL performance with much less uplink transmission and beat recent compressed-FL baselines under the same communication budget.

result.text: The paper tackles the slow sampling bottleneck of diffusion models (DMs), which typically need hundreds to thousands of discretization steps to produce high-quality samples. The key insight is that discretization error—particularly how the learned diffusion process is numerically integrated—dominates sample quality, and that the learned stochastic dynamics exhibit a semilinear structure that can be exploited. Building on this, the authors introduce the Diffusion Exponential Integrator Sampler (DEIS), which applies exponential integrator techniques from ODE solvers to the DM sampling ODE/PDE, reducing discretization error by treating linear and nonlinear components separately and thereby enabling accurate sampling with very few score evaluations. DEIS is model-agnostic, works with pre-trained DMs, and empirically achieves state-of-the-art low-NFE performance (e.g., high-quality CIFAR-10 samples in ~10–15 steps).

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of poor privacy–utility tradeoffs when training deep networks with differential privacy, noting that standard practice simply reuses non-private architectures (often with ReLU) and then applies DP-SGD, which amplifies bias and variance via gradient clipping and can suffer from exploding gradients. The key insight is that unbounded activations like ReLU exacerbate clipping-induced noise and instability, whereas bounded, smooth activations can reduce gradient explosion and thereby improve private training without weakening the privacy definition. Concretely, the authors introduce and analyze a family of bounded "tempered sigmoid" activations, show analytically and empirically that they curb exploding gradients and lead to lower bias/variance under DP-SGD, and demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR10 by simply replacing activations while keeping standard DP mechanisms and analysis intact.

result.text: The paper addresses why polynomial neural networks (PNNs), particularly the Π-Net parametrization, excel at tasks requiring high-frequency detail despite the well-known neural network spectral bias that favors low frequencies. The key insight is that multiplicative polynomial interactions alter the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) eigen-spectrum, producing larger eigenvalues for higher-frequency components and thus accelerating their learning compared with standard networks. Methodologically, the authors derive a spectral analysis of the NTK for PNNs, characterize how the Π‑Net parametrization shifts spectral bias toward higher frequencies, and validate the theory with extensive experiments on synthetic and vision tasks showing faster convergence of high-frequency modes.

result.text: The paper tackles accelerated multi-coil MR image reconstruction from undersampled k-space by improving how complex-valued image features are modeled and fused across coils and frequencies. The key insight is that treating real and imaginary channels separately while decomposing features into multiple spatial-frequency bands (octaves) and enabling both within-band updates and cross-band exchanges yields richer representations and larger effective receptive fields with reduced redundancy. Methodologically, the authors reformulate complex convolutions as a Dual-Octave Convolution that splits inputs and kernels into real/imaginary components and four spatial-frequency groups, performs intra-group feature updating and inter-group information exchange to aggregate contextual information, and integrates this block into a reconstruction network trained and evaluated on multi-coil knee data under varied undersampling patterns and acceleration factors, showing superior reconstruction quality.

args.text: We propose DuCaL, a dual-channel temporal link predictor that explicitly separates reoccurring-edge modeling from first-time edge discovery. A dyad-specific survival/Hawkes head captures repeat edges, while a CAW-driven anonymized temporal motif head predicts novel edges; both produce pairwise, relative-time–aware representations and are fused by a learned gate for OOD-robustness on large graphs. To encode hierarchy and calibrate uncertainty for rare events, both heads share a hyperbolic variational latent state updated via injective temporal message passing with relative positional features. Evaluation under EdgeBank’s harder negatives with disaggregated repeat-vs-new metrics tests whether models truly generalize beyond memorization.

result.text: The paper addresses limitations of standard message-passing GNNs—specifically their tendency to lose structural information about nodes’ neighborhoods and their poor capture of long-range, non-local dependencies in disassortative graphs. The key insight is that aggregating neighborhood information is improved by embedding nodes into a continuous geometric space that preserves structural roles and distances, enabling permutation-invariant aggregation that respects both local structure and global geometry. The method constructs a geometric aggregation scheme composed of node embeddings, a structural-neighborhood definition based on positions in the embedding space, and a bi-level aggregation that aggregates separately across structural sectors before combining them; this scheme is instantiated as Geom-GCN, a graph convolutional network that uses the learned geometry to perform transductive learning and empirically yields state-of-the-art results on various benchmark datasets.

args.text: We propose Programmatic Affordance Models for Hierarchical RL: extend code-as-reward by prompting VLMs to synthesize an executable library of affordance predicates, option schemas (initiation/termination), and compact effect models over abstract state from environment docs, example rollouts, and language goals, so once compiled they provide dense rewards, state-dependent action masks, and skill-level transition simulators without further VLM calls. Using these predicates as intrinsic signals, we discover skills that tile changes in affordances, then learn interest-weighted options with intra-option off-policy updates and perform risk-aware planning in the learned skill model, unifying affordance-aware exploration, sample-efficient option learning, and safe long-horizon control. We hypothesize large gains in data-efficiency, transfer, and safety compared to reward-only program synthesis and skill-planning baselines across open-ended and safety-critical tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of turning noise into realistic data by building a unified, principled framework for score-based generative modeling that both generalizes and improves diffusion methods. The key insight is that a forward stochastic differential equation (SDE) can smoothly perturb data into a known prior while the reverse-time SDE depends only on the time-dependent score (gradient of log-density) of the perturbed distribution, so learning those scores lets one run the reverse dynamics to generate samples. Methodologically, the authors train neural networks to estimate time-dependent scores, then use numerical SDE solvers (augmented by a predictor–corrector scheme) to sample from the reverse SDE, derive an equivalent neural ODE for exact likelihoods and faster sampling, and apply the approach to tasks like class-conditional generation and inpainting, achieving state-of-the-art image-generation results.

args.text: Pool-Pessimistic Offline Training for Two-Stage Recommenders: Jointly learn nominators and their item-pool allocations offline by combining selective importance sampling over pool-conditional action sets with pessimistic value adjustments calibrated to data support. We estimate end-to-end utility with a pooled sIS estimator to drastically cut variance in extreme action spaces, and inject pessimism via conformal or weighted-minimax lower bounds on pool-level rewards so nominators avoid overconfident allocations in low-support regions while the ranker remains aligned with their exposures. A bilevel objective alternates between (i) training nominators with a POXM-style, pool-conditional sIS objective plus pessimistic regularization and (ii) optimizing a Mixture-of-Experts gate to reassign items across pools under coverage constraints that improve support and reduce counterfactual mismatch for the ranker. This yields stable, offline-trainable pipelines that mitigate nominator–ranker interaction pathologies, lower estimator variance, and provide distribution-free safety margins under pool shifts.

result.text: The paper addresses the high communication cost of federated/local SGD, where occasional model averaging still requires large payloads per round for modern models. Its key insight is that combining local updates with an error-compensated double-compression scheme (and an analogous momentum variant) preserves convergence properties while dramatically reducing per-round communication. Methodologically, the authors design and analyze compressed local SGD algorithms that apply two-stage compression with error feedback to worker-to-server and server-to-worker communications, prove nonconvex convergence rates that match full-precision local SGD’s linear speedup in the number of workers while improving communication complexity, and corroborate these gains empirically.

result.text: I propose DP-ModePath: constrain private fine-tuning to a low-loss weight-space curve computed from public data via mode connectivity between the base and a public-finetuned model. We parameterize each layer by a tiny set of coefficients (curve position and a few tangent directions drawn from public top-gradient eigenspaces) and run DP-SGD only on these coefficients with per-layer/per-device clipping and anisotropic Gaussian noise shaped by the public curvature, optionally projecting residual gradients into the public subspace. This preserves basin selection while slashing effective dimensionality, yielding stronger privacy–utility and stability than isotropic DP-PEFT or full-model projected DP-SGD at the same budget with minimal memory/compute. We analyze sensitivity along the path and allocate privacy across directions via zCDP composition to further improve signal-to-noise.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of how to train implicit neural representations (INRs) for surface reconstruction without having to choose between occupancy or signed distance formulations and without incurring unknown biases from existing losses. The key insight is to draw an analogy to phase transitions in fluids and design a loss whose learned density converges to an occupancy function while its log-transform converges to a distance function, thereby unifying both representations in the limit. Methodologically, the authors propose and analyze this phase-transition-inspired loss, prove that its minimizer satisfies reconstruction constraints and minimizes surface perimeter (imposing a useful minimal-surface inductive bias), and demonstrate that training INRs with this loss yields state-of-the-art reconstructions on standard benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses the limited expressivity of standard graph neural networks due to their symmetric, local aggregation schemes by introducing globally consistent directional and asymmetric message passing. The key insight is to define a vector field over the graph and use directional derivatives and projections of node-specific messages into that field to create directional convolutional kernels, which both generalize CNNs on grids and enable global information flow. Methodologically, they construct directional graph networks (DGNs) by choosing the graph Laplacian eigenvectors as the vector field, applying directional smoothing and derivatives via projections, and enabling graph analogs of CNN augmentations (reflection, rotation, distortion); empirically this yields substantial error reductions on CIFAR10-graph and ZINC benchmarks and allows embedding intrinsic physical/biological axes into graph models.

args.text: Affordance-Programmed Options (APO) combine language-to-code rewards with learned temporal abstractions to yield reusable, safer skills from weak supervision. From a natural-language task and a few annotated observations, a VLM is prompted to synthesize compact code that defines affordance predicates and parameterized options (differentiable interest/termination and pseudo-rewards), which we compile into gating modules and train with intra-option off-policy updates. We then plan over these options with a learned skill-dynamics model, apply conservative Q regularization when training from offline logs, and propagate model uncertainty to gate risky initiations. By eliminating repeated VLM calls while enforcing affordance-aware initiation, APO should accelerate learning and transfer on MineDojo-like language tasks and robotic manipulation with substantially safer exploration versus baselines.

We propose Semantically-Guided Diffusion Restoration (SGDR) for linear inverse problems when a semantically related prior image is available: posterior sampling with a diffusion prior is anchored to a correspondence-warped version of the prior throughout the reverse dynamics. Dense correspondences from a self-supervised encoder define a time-dependent guidance term and cross-attention control inside the score network, combined with DDRM-style measurement projections at each step to maintain data consistency. This yields samples that both honor measurements and remain on a plausible semantic manifold induced by the prior, improving fidelity and stability under extreme undersampling and distribution shift compared to unguided diffusion or GAN-latent optimization. The method unifies semantic-prior guidance with score-based posterior inference and inherits the robustness benefits demonstrated by posterior sampling in clinical MRI.

Pessimistic Joint Nominator–Ranker Learning: we propose an offline training objective that jointly optimizes a Mixture-of-Experts nominator pool and a ranker under a weighted-minimax, pessimistic criterion to eliminate harmful nominator–ranker interactions. The objective estimates top-K value with a selective importance sampling estimator that Rao–Blackwellizes over each nominator’s top-p candidates, and applies per-context lower-confidence corrections using variance-aware sIS and density-ratio reweighting to penalize low-support nominator–item regions. This yields distribution-shift-aware, finite-sample conservative value estimates for both the gating (item-pool allocation) and ranking parameters, recovering the empirical strength of pessimistic neural offline bandits while ensuring safety in large action spaces. We hypothesize bounds under the weighted-minimax metric and robustness to mild misspecification by plugging in oracle-efficient regressors within the estimator, and validate on two-stage recommendation benchmarks with ablations over p and allocation entropy constraints.

result.text: The paper addresses slow convergence in federated learning arising from non-i.i.d. client data, which the authors attribute in part to catastrophic forgetting during local client updates that degrades performance on data learned by other clients. Their key insight is to alleviate this forgetting by regularizing local training with a loss evaluated on pseudo data that encode the global model's knowledge of previous clients, thereby preserving cross-client information while clients train locally. They propose FedReg, which generates pseudo samples from the global model and adds a regularization term using these pseudo data during each client's local optimization, accelerating convergence and improving robustness and privacy against gradient inversion attacks. Experiments show FedReg notably speeds up training—especially for deep networks and highly non-i.i.d. data—while enhancing classification privacy and attack resilience.

The key insight is that parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (sparser adapters and low-dimensional updates) can be adapted into a meta-framework that requires fewer private parameters and less noisy gradient perturbation, yielding better privacy–utility tradeoffs. result.text: The paper addresses high-fidelity 3D surface reconstruction from multi-view 2D images, overcoming limitations of prior neural-surface methods that need mask supervision and fail on thin or heavily occluded geometry. The key insight is to represent surfaces as the zero level-set of a neural signed distance function (SDF) and to replace conventional volume rendering with a novel rendering formulation that removes the first-order geometric bias that otherwise prevents accurate surface recovery. Methodologically, NeuS jointly learns a neural SDF and appearance by training with the new unbiased volume rendering loss (without requiring foreground masks), enabling robust optimization like NeRF while yielding precise surface extraction from the learned SDF via its zero level-set. Experiments on DTU and BlendedMVS demonstrate state-of-the-art surface accuracy, particularly on complex and self-occluded objects.

result.text: The paper tackles the puzzle of why simple optimization methods reliably find good solutions in highly non-convex neural network training by asking whether independently trained models actually lie in the same basin up to permutation symmetries of hidden units. The key insight is that many apparent distinct minima are equivalent under unit permutations, so by reordering hidden units one can align two models into a shared, approximately convex basin enabling direct weight-space merging. They introduce three algorithms that permute units of one model to match a reference model and empirically show this “re-basin” yields functionally equivalent weights with near-linear mode connectivity across architectures and datasets (including zero-barrier connectivity for ResNets on CIFAR-10), while also exploring how width and training time affect connectivity and presenting a counterexample that highlights limits of the single-basin hypothesis.

The paper tackles the problem of evaluating dynamic link prediction: current benchmarks and sampling practices make methods look better than they are by favoring easy negatives and ignoring recurring edge patterns in time-evolving graphs. The key insight is that many edges simply reoccur over time, so a strong memorization baseline can perform well under existing evaluations, revealing that negative sampling strategy critically shapes apparent performance. The authors introduce EdgeBank, a pure memorization baseline that records past edges and predicts their reappearance, propose two harder negative sampling strategies that produce more realistic and challenging evaluation splits, and release six new, diverse dynamic graph datasets to better reflect real-world scenarios and stress-test future models.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that standard graph neural networks suffer from a fundamental bottleneck—over-squashing—where exponentially many bits of information from distant nodes are compressed into fixed-size node representations during neighbor aggregation, preventing effective long-range message propagation and hurting tasks that require distant dependencies. The key insight is that the common aggregation mechanism, which treats incoming edges equally and compresses many incoming messages into a single vector, inherently limits representational capacity and makes models like GCN and GIN particularly vulnerable, whereas architectures that manage or diversify edge absorption can mitigate this effect. The authors analyze how this bottleneck prevents even fitting training data, empirically demonstrate over-squashing in extensively tuned GNNs, and propose breaking the bottleneck—by altering message-passing or graph connectivity—to improve performance, achieving state-of-the-art results without extra weights or hyperparameter tuning.

args.text: We propose Affordance-Compiled Options: using a vision–language model to synthesize executable code that defines option initiation predicates, termination conditions, and pseudo-reward/cost signals from task-language and a few annotated observations, effectively turning the VLM into an option-and-affordance compiler. The compiled predicates parameterize interest functions and affordance constraints for a reusable option library, while option policies are trained safely from offline data via conservative Q-learning and refined online with deep intra-option off-policy updates; a learned option-dynamics model enables planning in skill space. During adaptation, the same code-generation pathway produces conservative cost predicates for risk-aware planning, yielding safer, more sample-efficient transfer in non-stationary or constrained environments. We hypothesize this will greatly cut inference cost versus per-step VLM queries, improve compositional generalization, and provide interpretable safety hooks via human-auditable affordance/reward code.

result.text: We propose PESS-RS, an offline contextual bandit algorithm that performs representation selection by training a smoothed master over candidate feature mappings with a pessimistic objective and low-variance offline evaluation. Each base policy is trained with a pessimistic regularizer and a smoothing transform that caps density ratios, and the master routes contexts to bases to maximize a certified lower confidence bound on policy value computed with selective importance sampling (Rao–Blackwellizing over top-p logged actions) to control variance in extreme action spaces. Theoretically, PESS-RS enjoys near-oracle performance: it competes with the best candidate representation up to a logarithmic overhead and a coverage/misspecification penalty, recovering constant problem-dependent regret offline whenever a “good” representation exists and the logging policy provides adequate local support. Practically, it unifies multi-representation selection, batch pessimism, and stable evaluation, and extends naturally to two-stage recommenders by allocating item pools to the best base per context under the same pessimistic certification.

result.text: The paper tackles improving sample quality and likelihood of diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) when generating with a limited subset of timesteps by addressing how to choose the model covariance given that the model mean is imperfect. The key insight is that the optimal diagonal or full covariance for a DPM can be expressed in closed form but must be corrected when the mean estimate is biased; both the optimal and corrected covariances decompose into conditional expectations over functions of the latent noise, which can be learned. They therefore propose to estimate these conditional expectations via neural networks (implementing the diagonal case for efficiency) with parameter sharing and a two-stage training procedure, yielding improved likelihoods and notably better sample quality in few-step generation across discrete and continuous timesteps.

result.text: The paper studies why publicly pretraining models yields disproportionately large gains when those models are later trained under differential privacy, positing that private optimization struggles primarily with choosing a good "basin" in the non‑convex loss landscape while fine-tuning within a chosen basin is relatively easier. The key insight is that training decomposes into two phases—basin selection (global, fragile to privacy noise) and local optimization (robust but sensitive to data shift or scarcity)—and that public pretraining supplies a basin-selection initialization that private learning alone cannot reliably discover. To substantiate this, the authors give theoretical constructions proving a separation between private training with and without public pretraining and run controlled experiments on CIFAR‑10 and LibriSpeech showing that public pretraining markedly improves private training by enabling basin selection before privacy‑constrained updates.
