result.text: The paper addresses estimating optical flow from spike camera outputs—continuous binary spike streams with ultra-high temporal resolution—where prior work considered only two-frame motion and relied on synthetic graphics data with poor real-world generalization. The key insight is that temporal-spatial structure in spike data can be captured by using the differential of spike firing times to form a temporal-spatial representation and by exploiting continuous motion cues through joint correlation decoding rather than pairwise comparisons. The proposed Spike2Flow architecture aggregates spatial information and decodes motion correlations across continuous spike streams to predict dense flow, and the authors also introduce a real-world spike camera dataset to improve training and evaluation, demonstrating state-of-the-art results on synthetic and real spike data.

args.text: We propose Temporal Pairwise Survival GNNs that cast dynamic link prediction as time-to-event modeling over dyads, decomposing the hazard into a recurrence term (memorization of previously seen edges) and a novelty term (motif-driven new edge formation). The architecture uses pairwise, injective temporal message passing with relative positional and continuous-time encodings for expressiveness and OOD stability, and parameterizes uncertainty via hyperbolic variational dyad latents; training maximizes a survival likelihood augmented with time-calibration losses. We define an evaluation protocol that constructs per-timestep risk sets and motif-balanced negatives to neutralize easy negatives from pure memorization, reporting concordance and time-calibrated Brier scores alongside standard AUCs. This unifies EdgeBank’s evaluation insights with CAW-style temporal motifs and TGAT/PINT foundations, separating memorization from genuine dynamic generalization while remaining robust on larger unseen graphs.

result.text: The paper investigates two fundamental limitations of graph neural networks (GNNs): their representational limits when restricted to purely local information and their generalization behavior in data-dependent settings. The key insight is that any GNN that computes node representations solely from local neighborhoods—including standard message-passing models and stronger spatial variants that use local ordering or orientations—cannot distinguish or compute certain global graph properties, a fact formalized via a new graph-theoretic framework. Complementing this negative result, the authors derive the first data-dependent generalization bounds for message-passing GNNs that explicitly incorporate their local permutation invariance, yielding much tighter guarantees than prior VC-dimension analyses and comparable tightness to Rademacher bounds for recurrent networks. Together, these contributions delineate both what local GNNs cannot learn and how reliably they generalize when trained on graph data.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of solving linear inverse image-restoration tasks (e.g., super-resolution, deblurring, inpainting, colorization) by sampling from the posterior of natural images given measurements without requiring task-specific supervised training. The key insight is that a pre-trained denoising diffusion generative model can be leveraged as a universal prior and combined with a principled probabilistic update—motivated by variational inference—to produce efficient posterior samples for any linear measurement operator and noise level. The method, called Denoising Diffusion Restoration Models (DDRM), modifies the diffusion sampling process to incorporate measurement consistency by projecting noisy latent estimates onto measurement-constrained subspaces at each diffusion timestep, yielding an unsupervised algorithm that is broadly applicable, yields high-quality perceptual reconstructions, runs substantially faster than prior unsupervised approaches, and generalizes beyond the diffusion model’s training distribution.

args.text: I propose a recurrence-decoupled pairwise temporal WL model for dynamic link prediction that explicitly separates edge reoccurrence from novel link formation. A nonparametric memorization head handles reoccurrence, while a pairwise encoder built on anonymized temporal walks with injective temporal message passing and relative positional features (temporal WL) produces OOD-stable pairwise embeddings for novel links. A survival-style gating function (using recency and frequency hazard features) routes examples between heads, and training uses hard temporal negatives and size-OOD splits so the memorizer cannot mask novelty, improving generalization to much larger unseen graphs. The encoder can be instantiated via CAW sampling for identity-free temporal context and PINT-style injective updates, and evaluated on EdgeBank datasets augmented with size-OOD protocols.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of "over-squashing" in graph neural networks, where information from distant nodes gets compressed and distorted during message passing, limiting GNN performance on tasks needing long-range interactions; this is commonly attributed to graph bottlenecks but lacked a precise formulation. The key insight is that over-squashing corresponds to negatively curved edges in the graph: such edges act as combinatorial bottlenecks that concentrate and distort many incoming messages, and can be detected via a novel edge-based discrete curvature measure. The authors define this new curvature, prove a formal relationship between negative curvature and the deterioration of information flow in message passing, and propose a curvature-driven graph rewiring algorithm that adds or reweights edges to reduce negative curvature; experiments show that this rewiring alleviates over-squashing and improves GNN performance on long-range tasks.

args.text: We propose Option-as-Code: using vision–language models to synthesize compact, executable programs that define option structure—initiation predicates, termination conditions, and pseudo-rewards—from language task specs and a few annotated observations. The compiled predicates instantiate affordance-aware availability and directly parameterize interest functions, while intra-option off-policy updates exploit each transition to train any option whose code-consistent action was taken. By constraining action availability via an affordance MDP and providing dense, cheap signals from the program, the option-critic backbone learns faster and yields more reusable, interpretable skills. We evaluate on MineDojo-style language tasks, comparing against purely learned options and VLM reward-only baselines.

result.text: We propose FedSubSketch, a federated optimizer that learns and exploits a global low-rank gradient subspace while preserving partial participation and tight uplink budgets. The server maintains a streaming PCA of the gradient covariance using mergeable CountSketch summaries of client outer-products; clients then transmit only coefficients along the current basis and a sketched error-feedback residual, so communication scales with the rank r rather than model dimension. This hybrid “coefficients + sketched residual” aggregation inherits robustness from sketch-space momentum and compression-aware SCA, and can be personalized via per-client mixture weights or per-cluster subspaces to accommodate heterogeneity. We provide convergence guarantees under bounded subspace drift and show superior accuracy–communication trade-offs versus pure sketching or pure low-rank reuse.

result.text: The paper addresses the often-overlooked privacy cost of hyperparameter tuning in differentially private learning, showing that choosing hyperparameters based on multiple training runs can leak sensitive information even if individual trainings are analyzed. Its key insight is that Renyi Differential Privacy (RDP) provides a natural and tighter framework to quantify the cumulative privacy loss from repeated private training runs and hyperparameter selection, improving prior analyses. Methodologically, the authors formalize hyperparameter search as a composition of RDP mechanisms, extend and sharpen composition bounds (building on Liu and Talwar), and prove that if each candidate run is itself differentially private then the additional leakage from tuning is limited under reasonable assumptions. The result yields practical guarantees for hyperparameter search procedures, demonstrating that tuning need not greatly worsen overall privacy when RDP-based accounting is used.

We propose PessiMoE, a weighted-minimax offline item-pool allocation scheme for two-stage recommenders that learns which nominator should own which items to minimize worst-case regret across user–item instances. The core idea is to cast gating as minimizing a difficulty-aware weighted-minimax objective, yielding pessimistic allocations that are robust to the harmful nominator–ranker interactions observed in two-stage systems. To optimize this objective from bandit logs at extreme scale, we estimate counterfactual per-nominator contributions with a Rao–Blackwellized selective importance-sampling estimator over top-p logged actions, trading small bias for large variance reduction and stable training. Under standard coverage assumptions, we prove the learned allocation attains the weighted-minimax rate and improves end-to-end precision/recall over Mixture-of-Experts baselines in large-scale experiments.

result.text: FetchSGD addresses the dual challenges in federated learning of heavy communication costs and degraded convergence when client participation is sparse. The key insight is to use a linear, mergeable Count Sketch to compress client model updates so that momentum and error accumulation can be maintained centrally inside the sketch rather than on each client, which preserves state across intermittent clients and enables high compression without losing critical optimization history. Concretely, each client sketches its local gradient/update with a Count Sketch, the server merges these sketches to form an aggregate sketch, performs momentum and error correction in sketch space, and reconstructs sparse updates for model updates; the authors prove convergence guarantees for this procedure and validate it empirically on ResNets and a transformer showing strong communication savings and robust convergence.

result.text: The paper addresses inductive representation learning for temporal graphs, where embeddings must handle evolving topology, new nodes, and temporal node/edge features so that representations are functions of time. The key insight is to extend self-attention to temporal neighborhoods and to encode continuous time with a principled functional time encoding derived from Bochner’s theorem, enabling the model to capture time–feature interactions and temporal patterns in a shift-invariant way. The method, TGAT, stacks temporal graph attention layers that aggregate temporally-aware neighbor features using attention scores computed over time-augmented representations, allowing inductive inference of time-conditioned embeddings for both seen and unseen nodes and supporting tasks like temporal link prediction and node classification. Evaluation on two benchmark and one industrial dataset shows TGAT outperforms prior temporal and static baselines and naturally incorporates temporal edge features.

args.text: Curvature-Conditioned Spectral Graph Mixers (CSGM) combine full-spectrum Laplacian positional encodings with curvature-aware pairwise gating and sub-quadratic structured mixers to deliver long-range reasoning at scale. We add SAN-style encodings to node features, compute discrete edge curvatures to form additive biases or gates that upweight messages across negatively curved (bottleneck) edges, and replace quadratic attention with Monarch-matrix mixers acting in node space and a compact set of spectral channels for efficient complexity. To stabilize propagation and denoise, we apply graph-framelet shrinkage per frequency band, learning scale-dependent thresholds that preserve informative high-frequency substructures without over-smoothing. We hypothesize CSGM matches or exceeds SAN on isomorphism and long-range benchmarks while scaling to much larger graphs, with ablations isolating the gains from curvature conditioning and Monarchization.

We propose Affordance-Constrained Intra-Option Learning for Offline RL: learn a state-conditional affordance model from the dataset and use it to both regularize option initiation via differentiable interest functions and to gate off-policy intra-option updates. Concretely, we add a KL prior that aligns each option’s interest with affordance probabilities and, during off-policy credit assignment, weight updates for any option whose policy could have produced the observed primitive action by an affordance-consistent posterior, while applying a CQL-style conservative penalty at the option-value level to suppress out-of-distribution option executions. This yields safer, more data-efficient option discovery from static logs by preventing spurious updates for unavailable actions and curbing overestimation for unseen option–state pairs. We hypothesize improved transfer and faster fine-tuning in online continuation, and evaluate on D4RL locomotion and long-horizon manipulation datasets with ablations on the affordance prior and conservative regularizer.

args.text: Time-warped, solver-matched flow distillation: instead of adopting the native diffusion clock, we jointly learn a monotone time reparameterization and a small step grid with a low-NFE velocity field to directly minimize a discretized ODE negative log-likelihood surrogate whose tightness is controlled by high-order score errors. A high-NFE teacher supplies plug-in estimates of second- and third-order terms via variance-reduced Jacobian–vector probes, while we unroll one-step DPM-Solver/DEIS kernels so the student learns per-step residual corrections under the warped clock. The learned warp equalizes local curvature of the probability-flow dynamics, reducing quadrature error and closing the training–evaluation gap for deterministic flows at 8–12 steps. In practice, the schedule adapts to concentrate steps where the velocity varies rapidly, improving likelihood without degrading sample quality.

result.text: The paper addresses the mismatch between reported architectural differences for long-sequence modeling and the real impact of training practices, showing that comparing models from random initialization overestimates gaps between Transformers and state space models (SSMs). The key insight is that data-driven priors obtained via standard denoising pretraining on downstream-like data largely close performance gaps and can render specialized SSM parameterizations redundant. Methodologically, the authors pretrained various architectures (vanilla Transformers and SSMs) with denoising objectives on task-relevant data and then evaluated them on benchmarks like Long Range Arena and PathX-256, finding that pretrained Transformers match or exceed SSM performance and that fair supervised comparisons therefore require incorporating such pretraining.

args.text: Spectral-Feedback GANs: integrate complex Dual-Octave Convolution blocks into the generator to partition features into multiple spatial-frequency bands, and route capacity/updates across bands using a Fourier-domain attribution of the discriminator’s gradients. This directly addresses the generator’s linear spectral dependencies and high-frequency under-allocation by adaptively reweighting band-wise learning rates and adding a spectral consistency loss that matches the real–fake power spectrum per band. We further inject learned Fourier features at the generator input and through skip connections to stabilize high-frequency phase while preserving training stability. The result should reduce high-frequency artifacts and provide controllable texture sharpness with minimal overhead.

We propose PATH-M: Pairwise Anonymous Temporal Hyperbolic Motifs for OOD-robust dynamic link prediction. For each candidate pair and query time, PATH-M samples causal anonymous walks that bridge the pair within a temporal window, replaces node identities with anonymized hitting-count statistics, and biases walk generation by temporal consistency; the resulting pairwise motif multiset is encoded with time-aware contexts and mapped to a hyperbolic variational head to capture hierarchy and calibrated uncertainty. This design leverages theory that pairwise permutation-equivariant embeddings avoid the degeneracy of node-level predictors under graph-size extrapolation, and it directly targets evaluation pitfalls by training and testing with recurrence-aware, hard negatives. We expect PATH-M to deliver strong inductive generalization and uncertainty calibration on dynamic graphs where simple edge-memorization baselines otherwise dominate.

result.text: We propose PEP-RS: a pessimistic ensemble over candidate representations for offline contextual bandits that safely selects or composes features using only logged data. For each representation, we train a policy with a pessimism-regularized SGD objective and evaluate it using a selective importance sampling OPE that Rao–Blackwellizes over top-p logged actions to cut variance, while an advantage-weighted behavior prior further biases policies toward well-supported actions to avoid OOD error. A weighted-minimax selection rule then chooses the representation (or a learned convex combination) that maximizes a pessimistic lower confidence bound on value, yielding guarantees within a log M overhead of the best “good-on-support” representation and adapting to misspecification on uncovered regions. Theory ties the bound to coverage and effective dimension, and the estimator is plug-and-play for extreme action spaces.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of achieving full fine-tuning (FFT) accuracy for large language models under tight computational and memory constraints by improving parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). In this space, represent each task as a compact patch (e.g., sparse low-rank deltas) and compose multiple tasks at inference by convexly combining their patches, leveraging mode connectivity to maintain low or zero barriers while preserving base accuracy. Compared to raw weight interpolation, the alignment-plus-renormalization step reduces variance collapse and improves cross-task compatibility, enabling scalable multi-task composition with explicit bounds on deviation from the base via constrained coefficients.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of learning when temporally-extended actions (options) should be available for initiation, a component often ignored because initiation sets are hard to learn with function approximation. Its key insight is to replace binary initiation sets with differentiable interest functions that indicate how relevant or “interested” an option is in a given state, enabling gradient-based learning of option availability alongside policies and termination. The authors derive gradients and integrate interest functions into an interest-option-critic architecture that jointly learns option policies, termination, and interest via policy-gradient-style updates, and show empirically that this yields more interpretable, reusable temporal abstractions in both discrete and continuous domains.

args.text: We propose joint diffusion posterior sampling with operator uncertainty for inverse problems: model the forward operator as Ã = A + Δ with Δ confined to a structured, low-dimensional family (e.g., low-rank/banded convolutional perturbations or coil-sensitivity drifts), and sample the joint posterior p(x, Δ | y). Building on diffusion-based restoration with measurement projections, we alternate (i) score-based x-updates equipped with Newton-like, operator-aware data-consistency steps and (ii) stochastic proximal updates of Δ driven by residuals and a structural prior, optionally seeded by lightweight calibration data. This yields calibrated uncertainty over both image and operator and markedly improves robustness to real-world distribution and sensing changes, outperforming single-operator methods under blur-kernel mis-specification or MRI sensitivity drift. We outline identifiability conditions that couple prior strength and Δ’s capacity, and show accurate reconstructions alongside faithful operator estimates on blind deblurring and out-of-distribution MRI.

result.text: Pool-Pessimistic Offline Training for Two-Stage Recommenders: Jointly learn nominators and their item-pool allocations offline by combining selective importance sampling over pool-conditional action sets with pessimistic value adjustments calibrated to data support. We estimate end-to-end utility with a pooled sIS estimator to drastically cut variance in extreme action spaces, and inject pessimism via conformal or weighted-minimax lower bounds on pool-level rewards so nominators avoid overconfident allocations in low-support regions while the ranker remains aligned with their exposures. A bilevel objective alternates between (i) training nominators with a POXM-style, pool-conditional sIS objective plus pessimistic regularization and (ii) optimizing a Mixture-of-Experts gate to reassign items across pools under coverage constraints that improve support and reduce counterfactual mismatch for the ranker. This yields stable, offline-trainable pipelines that mitigate nominator–ranker interaction pathologies, lower estimator variance, and provide distribution-free safety margins under pool shifts.

result.text: Time-warped, solver-matched flow distillation: instead of adopting the native diffusion clock, we jointly learn a monotone time reparameterization and a small step grid with a low-NFE velocity field to directly minimize a discretized ODE negative log-likelihood surrogate whose tightness is controlled by high-order score errors. A high-NFE teacher supplies plug-in estimates of second- and third-order terms via variance-reduced Jacobian–vector probes, while we unroll one-step DPM-Solver/DEIS kernels so the student learns per-step residual corrections under the warped clock. The learned warp equalizes local curvature of the probability-flow dynamics, reducing quadrature error and closing the training–evaluation gap for deterministic flows at 8–12 steps. In practice, the schedule adapts to concentrate steps where the velocity varies rapidly, improving likelihood without degrading sample quality.

args.text: We propose a rendering-aware SDF pulling loss that integrates the SDF "pull-to-surface" supervision with SDF-based neural volume rendering. Combined with SDF-to-density mapping and unbiased SDF rendering, and guided by the associated opacity error bounds for adaptive sampling, this yields faster geometry convergence, sharper surfaces, and reduced sample budgets. result.text: The paper studies how generalization error in kernel regression and wide neural networks (via the Neural Tangent Kernel) evolves with training set size, addressing why and when different parts of a target function are learned. args.text: We propose curvature-guided CW-complex lifting to alleviate over-squashing: use discrete edge curvature to identify bottlenecks and add targeted 2- and 3-cells that bundle multiple paths across those edges, then run cross-dimensional message passing on the lifted complex. This preserves original connectivity while widening information channels and effectively shortening geodesic distances without indiscriminate rewiring. The cell construction is learned end-to-end with a curvature-regularized objective, and the resulting CWN propagates long-range signals in fewer layers. By unifying curvature-driven topology design with higher-order message passing, it should outperform both curvature-only rewiring and CWNs with fixed liftings on long-range dependency tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of estimating expectations under the stationary distribution of a Markov chain when only a fixed offline dataset of transitions is available, a common constraint in reinforcement learning and Monte Carlo applications where additional environment interaction is impossible. The key insight is that one can consistently correct the mismatch between the empirical data distribution and the true stationary distribution by estimating a stationary density ratio derived from the chain’s stationary properties, and that this estimation can be cast as a stable variational divergence minimization problem. The proposed method, GenDICE, learns this density ratio via a simple optimization that enforces the stationary constraints through a convex-concave reformulation and then uses the learned ratio to reweight observed samples for consistent stationary expectation estimates. The authors prove consistency and provide error bounds for the estimator, and empirically validate strong performance on offline PageRank and off-policy policy evaluation benchmarks.

args.text: We propose text-conditioned posterior sampling for ill-posed medical imaging inverse problems, leveraging free-text clinical context (orders, indications, or preliminary reports) to disambiguate measurements while preserving strict data consistency. Concretely, we augment diffusion-based restoration sampling with a differentiable multimodal text–image alignment score from a large VLM adapted to medical data, adding a text-consistency energy to the posterior alongside the likelihood, and interleave it with per-timestep projection to the measurement-consistent subspace. To maintain efficiency and calibration, we use Newton-preconditioned stochastic updates for the posterior score while treating the VLM alignment as a soft prior, yielding samples that are both measurement-consistent and semantically aligned with clinician intent (e.g., “rule out hemorrhage,” “post-op hardware present”). We expect improved robustness and reduced hallucination under distribution shift, demonstrated on undersampled MRI and limited-angle CT with real clinical text, while preserving uncertainty quantification via posterior sampling.

result.text: The paper addresses active learning in realistic open-set scenarios where the unlabeled pool contains both known and unknown classes, which breaks assumptions of most AL methods and reduces sampling effectiveness. The key insight is that separating and exploiting both known-class and unknown-class uncertainties via entropy yields more informative and useful sample selection than treating all unknowns as noise or ignoring them. The method, Entropic Open-set AL (EOAL), computes two entropy scores per unlabeled sample—one measuring uncertainty relative to known-class distributions and another relative to modeled unknown-class distributions—and combines these to better distinguish and prioritize samples for annotation; experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet show EOAL outperforms prior state-of-the-art approaches.

args.text: DP-Kalman-Subspace FL: model per-round global gradients as evolving in a slowly drifting low-rank subspace with autoregressive coefficient dynamics; the server maintains DP-initialized linear sketches to run streaming subspace identification and a Kalman filter that predicts next-step coefficients, so clients transmit only clipped innovation coefficients plus a sketched residual. Leveraging CountSketch linearity and compression-aware SCA, momentum and error feedback operate in sketch space and compose with secure aggregation, while one-time initialization noise provides central DP without per-round degradation. We analyze communication and convergence via bounds on innovation energy and subspace drift, showing bits scale with unpredictability rather than model dimension and remain robust under partial participation. Empirically, predictive coding improves accuracy–communication–privacy trade-offs over static low-rank reuse or pure sketching on heterogeneous FL workloads.

result.text: The paper addresses why certain convolutional architectures like S4 excel at long-range sequence modeling despite convolution’s typical locality and S4’s complexity making it hard to use. The key insight is that two simple, interpretable properties of S4’s effective global convolutional kernel—(1) an efficient parameterization whose parameter count grows sub-linearly with sequence length, and (2) a decaying kernel structure that assigns larger weights to nearby positions than distant ones—are sufficient to capture long-range dependencies. Based on this, the authors propose Structured Global Convolution (SGConv), a lightweight global convolutional kernel design that enforces those two principles and can be implemented efficiently; empirically SGConv matches or outperforms S4 on long-range benchmarks (Long Range Arena, Speech Commands) and improves efficiency and performance when inserted into standard language and vision models.

args.text: We propose SDF-guided ray pulling for neural SDF renderers: during training, ray samples are differentiably shifted along the predicted SDF gradient by a stride proportional to the local signed distance, analogous to point "pulling" in supervised SDF learning, to land near the zero level set before evaluating color and transmittance. This couples image residuals directly to both SDF values and gradients at surface-adjacent points, tightening geometry–appearance supervision and reducing sample inefficiency. We use NeuS’s unbiased SDF rendering as the base objective while leveraging the Laplace-CDF SDF-to-density mapping’s opacity error bound to set adaptive pull step sizes and trust regions, skipping or damping pulls where the bound signals ambiguity. The result is faster convergence, fewer floaters, and sharper thin structures, with improved stability from bound-aware, gradient-consistent pulling.

We propose Permutation-Aligned Patch Composition for open-vocabulary models: before interpolating or adding task patches, we re-basin each task-finetuned checkpoint to the base model by solving for neuron permutations and then renormalize preactivations to prevent variance collapse. After alignment, we optimize a sparse, nonnegative combination of the patched weight deltas with per-layer gating conditioned on the text prompt, yielding a single composed patch that adds multiple capabilities while preserving base zero-shot accuracy. This unifies patching with mode re-basin connectivity, enabling low-barrier multi-task composition and reducing interference across tasks trained at different scales. On CLIP-style models, we expect dozens of aligned patches can be composed with near-zero ImageNet loss while jointly improving several target tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses how to adapt Transformer architectures to graphs by providing meaningful node positions so attention can operate effectively without relying on graph sparsity. Its key insight is that a learned positional encoding derived from the full Laplacian spectrum lets a fully-connected Transformer distinguish graph structure and substructures (via spectral “resonance”) while avoiding GNN over-squashing. The proposed Spectral Attention Network (SAN) computes a learnable encoding from the complete Laplacian eigenbasis, adds these encodings to node features, and feeds the result to a standard fully-connected Transformer, yielding a model that is theoretically more expressive on graph isomorphism and empirically competitive or superior to state-of-the-art GNNs and attention-based baselines on standard benchmarks.

result.text: This paper tackles unsupervised skill discovery for agents when no external rewards are available, addressing the problem that existing mutual-information-based methods can produce trivially diverse but useless skill sets. The key insight is to measure diversity not just by distinguishability of skills, but by how skills differently change the agent’s relationship to its environment—i.e., relative changes in affordances—so skills should tile the space of achievable effects rather than merely differ in trajectories. The authors introduce Relative Variational Intrinsic Control (RVIC), a variational objective that maximizes mutual information between skills and resulting relative state changes (or affordance shifts) and trains a discriminator to identify skills based on those relative effects, yielding skills that are more semantically meaningful. Empirically, RVIC produces qualitatively diverse, affordance-covering skills across environments and yields more useful primitives for hierarchical reinforcement learning compared to prior approaches.

args.text: We propose Joint Diffusion–Operator Posterior Sampling (JDOPS) for blind or mismatched linear inverse problems, which samples the image and forward-operator parameters jointly to capture uncertainty from both sources. JDOPS conditions the score-based image prior on a compact operator embedding computed on-the-fly via randomized probes of the measurement map, and alternates projection-guided image diffusion steps with Langevin updates on operator parameters under physics-informed priors or weak calibration constraints. An amortized operator-proposal network, meta-trained across diverse operator families, accelerates mixing and enables rapid adaptation to out-of-distribution sensing. Marginalizing over operator samples yields uncertainty-calibrated reconstructions that remain data-consistent and robust when the true sensing model deviates from training assumptions.

result.text: The paper addresses active learning in realistic open-set scenarios where the unlabeled pool contains both known and unknown classes, which breaks assumptions of most AL methods and reduces sampling effectiveness. The key insight is that separating and exploiting both known-class and unknown-class uncertainties via entropy yields more informative and useful sample selection than treating all unknowns as noise or ignoring them. The method, Entropic Open-set AL (EOAL), computes two entropy scores per unlabeled sample—one measuring uncertainty relative to known-class distributions and another relative to modeled unknown-class distributions—and combines these to better distinguish and prioritize samples for annotation; experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet show EOAL outperforms prior state-of-the-art approaches.

Leveraging CountSketch linearity and compression-aware SCA, momentum and error feedback operate in sketch space and compose with secure aggregation, while one-time initialization noise provides central DP without per-round degradation. We analyze communication and convergence via bounds on innovation energy and subspace drift, showing bits scale with unpredictability rather than model dimension and remain robust under partial participation. Empirically, predictive coding improves accuracy–communication–privacy trade-offs over static low-rank reuse or pure sketching on heterogeneous FL workloads.

result.text: The paper addresses how to extend diffusion-based generative modeling beyond standard isotropic Gaussian noise by formalizing heat-dissipation (blurring) processes and understanding their relation to denoising diffusion. The key insight is that blurring diffusion—previously framed as inverse heat dissipation—can be reinterpreted as Gaussian diffusion with non‑isotropic, spatially structured noise, revealing the inductive bias imposed by blurring and linking the two viewpoints. Methodologically, the authors derive this equivalence, analyze its implications, and introduce a generalized family of Blurring Diffusion Models that interpolates between standard isotropic denoising diffusion and inverse heat dissipation, enabling practitioners to choose or learn noise structures that combine benefits of both regimes.

args.text: We propose a multiview SDF radiance field that augments SDF-based volume rendering with a phase-transition regularizer to impose a principled minimal-surface prior during photometric training. Concretely, we map SDF to density via a Laplace CDF with a rendering formulation that provides opacity error bounds and unbiased surface gradients, and we jointly optimize a phase-transition objective on the induced occupancy that encourages sharp, thin interfaces consistent across views. A differentiable perimeter penalty is realized by accumulating the double-well potential and gradient-norm terms along rays, while the opacity error bound drives adaptive sampling focused near high-gradient interfaces to couple geometry and radiance where it matters most. This yields crisper geometry, fewer floaters, and improved recovery of thin/occluded structures without masks in sparse-view settings compared to prior SDF-NeRF variants.

result.text: The paper tackles the vulnerability of deep reinforcement learning agents to small l_p-bounded adversarial input perturbations that can drastically reduce performance in real-world deployments. The key insight is that robustness can be improved by directly minimizing a tractable upper bound on the worst-case loss under adversarial perturbations, derived from efficient robustness verification techniques, rather than relying solely on empirically crafted adversarial examples. The authors introduce RADIAL-RL, a training procedure that incorporates this upper-bound minimization into RL optimization and demonstrate it yields substantially more robust Atari-2600 agents than prior robust-training baselines when tested against strong PGD attacks. They also propose Greedy Worst-Case Reward (GWC), an efficient, attack-agnostic evaluation that estimates the worst-case cumulative reward by accounting for action importance and temporal dependencies, providing a better proxy for true adversarial impact than per-step action-flip metrics.

The paper studies the representational limits of temporal graph networks (TGNs), asking which dynamic graph properties different TGN designs can and cannot capture. The key insight is that the two main TGN families—walk-aggregating TGNs (WA-TGNs) and message-passing with memory TGNs (MP-TGNs)—are fundamentally incomparable in expressiveness, but MP-TGNs become as powerful as a newly proposed temporal Weisfeiler-Leman (WL) test when their update functions are injective, while both families still cannot compute certain global properties like girth and deep MP-TGNs render memory redundant. Methodologically, the authors develop novel separations and extensions of 1-WL to temporal graphs, derive theoretical prescriptions (injective updates and relative positional features), and instantiate these into PINT, an architecture combining injective temporal message passing with relative positional encodings that is provably more expressive than prior TGNs and empirically superior on benchmarks.

args.text: We propose a Hodge-Spectral Transformer for simplicial complexes that treats k-simplices (nodes, edges, faces, …) as tokens and equips each token with learnable positional encodings derived from the full spectra of the Hodge Laplacians L_k, preserving orientation via signed incidence structure and odd nonlinearities. Attention operates both within each dimension and across dimensions by projecting queries/keys into eigenvector-induced directional fields and routing messages along boundary/coboundary maps, yielding orientation-equivariant kernels that generalize directional graph convolutions to higher-order cells. This design subsumes SWL-style message passing in an attention framework to reach at least 3-WL-level expressivity, while mitigating over-squashing through curvature-aware head allocation and optional curvature-driven rewiring that increases bandwidth on negatively curved edges/simplices. We expect strong gains on long-range, higher-order tasks (e.g., dynamics on complexes, motif- and flow-sensitive benchmarks) where global spectral cues and simplicial structure jointly matter.

result.text: The paper addresses the mismatch between standard reinforcement learning—which assumes all actions are always available—and real agents’ contextual action constraints by formalizing "affordances" within Markov Decision Processes. The key insight is that state-dependent affordances both reduce planning complexity by limiting available actions and improve model learning by constraining transition dynamics, yielding simpler, more generalizable transition models especially under function approximation. Methodologically, the authors develop theoretical results characterizing how affordances affect planning and learning, provide illustrative examples, and propose a practical algorithm to learn affordances from data to produce compact transition models that speed planning and enhance sample-efficient learning.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of using deep generative priors for compressed sensing MRI, specifically addressing the CSGM framework’s prior failure on clinical, out-of-distribution data. Its key insight is that posterior sampling (rather than single MAP estimates) from a learned generator using Langevin dynamics yields high-quality, robust reconstructions even when the true images or measurement process deviate from the training distribution. Methodologically, the authors train a generative model on brain scans from the fastMRI dataset and perform posterior sampling via Langevin dynamics to produce reconstructions, supporting their empirical results with theoretical analysis showing stability to distributional and sensing changes.

result.text: The paper addresses open-set active learning where unlabeled pools contain unknown-class (open-set) noise, creating a trade-off between selecting pure (clean) examples and informative (uncertain) ones. The key insight is that this purity–informativeness dilemma can be adaptively resolved by learning a selection policy that balances both factors using the multi-round nature of active learning instead of relying on a held-out validation set. The authors introduce Meta-Query-Net (MQ-Net), a meta-learned scorer trained on query sets across rounds and regularized with a novel skyline loss that encodes dominance relations among unlabeled examples to better capture relative purity and informativeness. Experiments across open-set active learning scenarios show MQ-Net substantially outperforms prior methods, delivering large gains in final accuracy.

result.text: The paper tackles the communication bottleneck in federated learning by asking whether the space spanned by model gradients over training is low-rank and can therefore be exploited to avoid sending full parameter updates. Observing in centralized training that gradients across epochs lie in a low-dimensional subspace with a few principal components explaining 95–99% of variance, the authors introduce Look-back Gradient Multiplier (LBGM), which recycles past gradient directions and transmits only scalar multipliers for those basis directions instead of full vectors. They analyze LBGM’s convergence to characterize the trade-off between reduced communication and potential accuracy loss, and empirically show that LBGM substantially cuts transmission costs across datasets and models while remaining compatible with and improvable by existing sparsification methods.

result.text: The paper addresses the mismatch between standard diffusion generative models and the multi-scale, locally smoothing structure of images by proposing a generative process that explicitly reverses a PDE which erases fine-scale detail. The key insight is that running the heat equation with additive noise forward acts like a structured variational encoder that progressively removes high-frequency content, so stochastically inverting this heat dissipation yields a diffusion-like model with an implicit coarse-to-fine inductive bias and emergent disentanglement of global color and shape. Methodologically, the authors formalize the forward heat-plus-noise process as a variational approximation within the diffusion latent-variable framework, derive and train a corresponding reverse stochastic process that undoes heat diffusion on the image plane, and analyze its spectral behavior to connect and contrast it with standard diffusion models.

result.text: The paper addresses why the Structured State Space (S4) model—an SSM-based architecture that empirically handles very long sequences—works despite using a seemingly ad-hoc “HiPPO” initialization whose theoretical role was unclear. The key insight is a generalized HiPPO framework that interprets S4 as projecting input histories onto an orthogonal basis of exponentially-warped polynomials (specifically Legendre polynomials) and shows that different orthogonal bases (e.g., Fourier) yield different long-range behaviors, thereby explaining S4’s ability to represent long dependencies and guiding principled choices like timescale initialization. Methodologically, the authors derive this generalized class of HiPPO matrices, connect them to time-invariant SSM parameterizations, propose alternative S4 variants based on other bases, and use these theoretical prescriptions to initialize and train improved SSMs, empirically boosting long-range performance on benchmarks like Long Range Arena.

result.text: The paper addresses the unclear mechanism by which deformable convolution aligns frames for video super-resolution and why it outperforms classic flow-based alignment. The key insight is that deformable convolution decomposes into spatial warping plus convolution, revealing that both deformable and flow-based alignments share a common formulation but differ critically in the diversity of learned offsets; greater offset diversity in deformable alignment yields better-aligned features and higher SR quality. Methodologically, the authors analyze this decomposition, empirically show that increased offset diversity improves alignment, introduce an offset-fidelity loss that guides offset learning using optical flow to prevent offset overflow and instability, and also propose ways to inject offset diversity into flow-based alignment to boost its performance.

result.text: The paper tackles the vulnerability of deep reinforcement learning agents to small l_p-bounded adversarial input perturbations that can drastically reduce performance in real-world deployments. The key insight is that robustness can be improved by directly minimizing a tractable upper bound on the worst-case loss under adversarial perturbations, derived from efficient robustness verification techniques, rather than relying solely on empirically crafted adversarial examples. The authors introduce RADIAL-RL, a training procedure that incorporates this upper-bound minimization into RL optimization and demonstrate it yields substantially more robust Atari-2600 agents than prior robust-training baselines when tested against strong PGD attacks. They also propose Greedy Worst-Case Reward (GWC), an efficient, attack-agnostic evaluation that estimates the worst-case cumulative reward by accounting for action importance and temporal dependencies, providing a better proxy for true adversarial impact than per-step action-flip metrics.

result.text: The paper addresses limitations of existing graph neural networks—such as sensitivity to depth, oversmoothing, and bottlenecks—by reinterpreting graph learning as a continuous diffusion process governed by a partial differential equation (PDE). args.text: We propose curvature-aligned directional GNNs that derive a globally consistent vector field from discrete edge curvature by solving a curvature-weighted potential flow that points away from negatively curved bottlenecks. Messages are then projected and split along this field with directional kernels, allocating channels to multiple low-curvature directions and attenuating propagation through highly negative-curvature edges; a lightweight curvature-neutral rewiring step adds only a few edges where necessary. This couples curvature-driven control of congestion with directional message passing to reduce over-squashing (measured via cumulative negative curvature) while retaining standard message-passing scalability.

result.text: The paper tackles lifelong reinforcement learning in non-stationary, non-episodic environments where standard RL fails due to the inability to plan long-horizon behavior and adapt without resets. Its key insight is that planning in an abstract skill space—using unsupervised, intrinsically rewarded skill discovery plus a learned skill-level dynamics model—enables robust, long-horizon decision-making and adaptation while reducing dependence on episodic interactions. The method, Lifelong Skill Planning (LiSP), learns temporally-extended skills from online or offline data via intrinsic objectives, trains a predictive model over skill transitions, and performs planning in this skill space to select sequences of skills that steer the agent around non-stationarity and catastrophic failures. Empirically, LiSP shows improved long-horizon control and resilience on non-episodic gridworld and MuJoCo variants by enabling skill discovery from offline data and using model-based skill planning to avoid failures.

args.text: Active Diffusion Posterior Acquisition (ADPA): For MRI/CT under a fixed time budget, perform closed-loop measurement selection by repeatedly (i) running a few iterations of a diffusion/denoiser-based posterior sampler to obtain spatially resolved uncertainty, (ii) approximating the expected information gain of each feasible measurement (e.g., k-space line or projection) via a local Gaussian posterior induced by the denoiser Jacobian with Newton-like preconditioning, and (iii) acquiring the argmax under trajectory constraints. By leveraging score-based priors that decouple reconstruction from the measurement model, the method generalizes across unknown operators and noise levels while the posterior-aware design targets high-ambiguity regions. A pragmatic implementation reuses the sampler’s gradients to estimate Fisher information with Hutchinson tricks, enabling real-time selection. Compared to fixed sampling patterns, ADPA reduces posterior entropy and improves PSNR/SSIM at equal scan time, while producing calibrated uncertainty for downstream decisions.

result.text: The paper addresses active learning in realistic, challenging settings—such as class imbalance with rare classes, out-of-distribution (OOD) examples in the unlabeled pool, and redundancy—where standard acquisition strategies fail. The key insight is that submodular information measures (SIM) can capture notions of representativeness, relevance, and diversity in a unified, principled way, allowing acquisition functions to be tailored to different practical issues (e.g., focusing on rare classes or avoiding OOD data) while remaining scalable. The authors propose SIMILAR, an active learning framework that applies various SIM-based acquisition functions to select batches of examples, leveraging submodularity for efficient greedy optimization and extensions that incorporate label priors or query-specific constraints to handle imbalance and OOD. Empirically, SIMILAR consistently outperforms existing methods on image classification benchmarks (CIFAR-10, MNIST, ImageNet), yielding substantial gains especially for rare-class and OOD scenarios, and is released as part of the DISTIL toolkit.

result.text: Adaptive Cohort–Sketch SNR Scheduling: jointly schedule per-round cohort size and sketch/compression parameters to maintain a target signal-to-noise ratio in the server’s linear sketch under central DP via one-time initialization noise and clipping, improving utility at a fixed total client budget. Leveraging CountSketch linearity, we derive closed-form SNR and error-feedback contraction that scale with the number of participating clients and sketch width, and design a controller that adjusts cohort size n_t, sketch width, and top-k reconstruction to keep SNR above a threshold estimated online from sketch-space variance and loss improvement. Integrated with compression-aware SCA, the procedure preserves unbiasedness under partial participation and yields convergence bounds that outperform fixed-cohort or fixed-compression baselines; a fairness module prioritizes underrepresented clients subject to system constraints. Experiments probe participation volatility and privacy budgets, showing stable accuracy–communication–privacy trade-offs and secure-aggregation compatibility.

args.text: We propose Polynomial-NeuS, an interpretable radiance–SDF field that factorizes shape and reflectance into polynomial/Fourier subbands, enabling explicit control and faster learning of high-frequency detail. The SDF and BRDF latents are represented with Fourier PNFs whose multiplicative interactions shift spectral bias toward higher frequencies, while we retain unbiased SDF volume rendering via NeuS or the Laplace-CDF SDF-to-density mapping with its error-bounded sampling. Band-specific regularization ties low-frequency geometry to opacity/normal smoothness, sparsifies high-frequency bands, and leverages compact BRDF/illumination manifolds to stabilize decomposition. This yields cleaner surfaces, quicker convergence, and scale-aware editing/relighting (e.g., swapping only micro-geometry bands), providing a testbed for frequency-wise disentanglement in neural rendering.

result.text: The paper tackles the vulnerability of deep reinforcement learning agents to adversarial or noisy perturbations in state observations, which can cause suboptimal actions and failed tasks, and notes that straightforward transfers of classification defenses (e.g., adversarial training) often fail for RL. Its key insight is to formalize the problem via a state-adversarial Markov decision process (SA-MDP) and derive a principled policy-regularization approach that directly targets robustness in the RL setting rather than borrowing classification techniques. The method applies this regularizer across a broad family of DRL algorithms (PPO, DDPG, DQN) for both discrete and continuous actions, evaluates against strong white-box attacks (including new attacks introduced by the authors), and demonstrates substantial robustness gains and sometimes improved clean performance; code is released for reproducibility.

args.text: HyTWL-TGN is a temporally-expressive, uncertainty-aware temporal GNN for dynamic link prediction under hard negatives. It combines injective temporal message passing with relative positional features (per temporal-WL prescriptions) and continuous-time attention via functional time encodings to capture fine-grained dynamics, while modeling node states as hyperbolic normal distributions in a variational decoder to capture hierarchy and provide calibrated uncertainty. Training uses a recurrence-aware hard-negative curriculum extending recent evaluation protocols by mixing reoccurring-edge decoys and temporally-close non-edges, and optimizes an uncertainty-weighted contrastive likelihood to discourage overconfident memorization. We hypothesize improved generalization to novel edges and superior calibration under temporal distribution shift compared to prior TGNs.

We propose CurvSparseSAN: a graph Transformer that uses curvature-guided sparse attention to break over-squashing bottlenecks while keeping sub-quadratic cost. During training, we score edges by a learned predictor supervised by a discrete curvature signal and add/reweight a small budget of virtual shortcuts across highly negative-curvature bottlenecks; nodes carry full-spectrum Laplacian positional encodings and attention logits include curvature-based biases. To avoid amplifying noise through shortcuts, we insert multi-scale framelet gates that shrink high-frequency coefficients before attention. This end-to-end scheme aims to match fully connected spectral Transformers on long-range reasoning while being more efficient and robust to graph bottlenecks.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of sampling from the posterior distribution of linear inverse problems with additive Gaussian noise, enabling recovery methods that capture uncertainty rather than producing a single point estimate. The key insight is that combining Langevin-style stochastic sampling with Newton-like preconditioning and a pre-trained MMSE Gaussian denoiser yields a tractable posterior score that both honors the measurement operator and admits efficient iterations. Methodologically, the authors derive an explicit posterior score using an SVD of the degradation operator, then implement a stochastic iterative sampler (SNIPS) that leverages the denoiser as a score-approximation and Newton-type updates to produce multiple high-quality, measurement-consistent samples for tasks like deblurring, super-resolution, and compressive sensing.

result.text: The paper addresses how to build effective outlier/OOD detectors using only unlabeled in-distribution data, noting that existing unlabeled-data methods often perform no better than random while top-performing detectors rely on costly supervised labels. The key insight is that strong self-supervised representations, when paired with a simple Mahalanobis-distance detector in feature space, are sufficient to separate in-distribution samples from outliers and can match or exceed some supervised methods. result.text: The paper tackles the slow sampling speed of diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs), which typically require hundreds or thousands of neural-network evaluations to generate samples. The key insight is an exact formulation of the diffusion ODE solution that analytically isolates the linear part and, after a change of variables, rewrites the remaining contribution as an exponentially weighted integral of the neural network, enabling high-order numerical integration rather than leaving everything to black-box ODE solvers. Based on this, the authors derive DPM-Solver, a dedicated high-order ODE solver with convergence-order guarantees that works for both discrete- and continuous-time DPMs without additional training and drastically reduces required function evaluations. result.text: The paper addresses the gap between the community standard of "adaptive attacks" for evaluating adversarial defenses and the reality that many such evaluations are incomplete, leaving purported defenses vulnerable. Its key insight is that failures to fully adapt attacks often stem from methodological oversights—such as not modeling the defense's transformations, gradient masking, randomized or non-differentiable components, or incorrect threat models—rather than from genuine robustness, so systematically constructing stronger adaptive strategies can break many published defenses. The authors analyze thirteen recent defenses and distill practical techniques (e.g., white-box modeling of all defense components, gradient estimation or proxy gradients for non-differentiable parts, expectation over transformation for randomness, careful loss/attack selection, and verification-style checks) to craft complete adaptive attacks, demonstrating how to modify attacks to account for each defense’s specifics. Their method is less a single algorithm than a prescriptive evaluation methodology for designing and documenting adaptive attacks so defenses are tested against the strongest feasible adversary.

args.text: CurvSAN-Framelets: a curvature- and multiscale-guided spectral graph Transformer that mitigates over-squashing without explicit rewiring. We extend fully-connected spectral attention by (i) adding attention bias terms proportional to a discrete edge curvature score to discourage routing through negatively curved bottlenecks and (ii) generating per-scale keys/queries from graph framelet coefficients with learnable shrinkage, so low-frequency structure and denoised high-frequency details inform separate heads. This curvature-aware, multiscale attention expands the effective receptive field while preserving signal geometry, combining the benefits of curvature mitigation and framelet denoising in a single model. We hypothesize and test that it outperforms SAN and curvature-rewiring baselines on long-range benchmarks by reducing congestion and noise amplification.

We propose a self-calibrating diffusion posterior sampler for blind inverse problems where the measurement operator and noise statistics are unknown or drift over time. The method alternates score-based reverse diffusion steps with Newton-preconditioned data-consistency updates while jointly estimating a low-dimensional operator/noise parameterization via an EM-like loop that maximizes a pseudo-likelihood using samples from the current posterior; when the forward map is locally linearizable we recover DDRM-style projections, and in general we fall back to SNIPS-like preconditioning. To rapidly adapt to new devices or protocols, we include a lightweight few-shot adapter that initializes the operator parameters from ~100 paired measurements and is then refined online during sampling, yielding calibrated uncertainty over both the image and the forward model. This approach unifies and extends diffusion posterior sampling beyond fixed known linear operators, showing robustness to operator mismatch akin to posterior-sampling MRI reconstructions while remaining unsupervised across tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of training large-scale models efficiently and robustly when labeled data is costly and real-world datasets are noisy or imbalanced. Its key insight is that selecting a training subset that maximizes validation log-likelihood can simultaneously improve generalization, speed, and robustness, and that this discrete selection problem exhibits (weak) submodularity for many common losses. The method formulates subset selection as a mixed discrete-continuous bi-level optimization and instantiates it with an iterative algorithm (GLISTER-ONLINE) that alternates data selection and parameter updates, accompanied by theoretical analysis for simple classifiers and convergence/validation-loss reduction guarantees for a broad class of losses. They also introduce GLISTER-ACTIVE for batch active learning and empirically demonstrate improved efficiency and accuracy across training-time reduction, robustness to label noise/imbalance, and active learning benchmarks.

result.text: NightRain tackles the challenge of nighttime video deraining where real paired data are unavailable and synthetic-trained models fail due to complex light effects, low-light noise, and resulting artifacts like over-saturation and color shifts. The key insight is to create pseudo paired data and corrective signals from unlabeled real videos: regions with high confidence of being rain-free are matched to their input counterparts to form region-based real pairs for progressive learning, while clear-night videos provide corrective supervision by exposing the characteristic differences between inputs and model outputs (e.g., color and saturation errors). Methodologically, NightRain employs an adaptive-rain-removal module that extracts confident rain-free regions and uses a teacher-student framework to iteratively train the student on increasingly difficult regions, alongside an adaptive-correction module that learns error maps from clear-night videos to correct color and saturation shifts, yielding substantial empirical gains in PSNR and visual quality.

args.text: We propose PolySDF, a polynomially decomposed signed distance field in which geometry is expressed as a sum of learned subband fields mixed by a low-degree multiplicative polynomial (PNN/PNF-style) that yields interpretable, manipulable geometric components. We render via SDF-to-density formulations (NeuS/VolSDF) while maintaining SDF validity with Eikonal regularization and periodic reinitialization, and add a phase-transition-inspired regularizer to bias toward minimal, well-conditioned surfaces. The polynomial mixer shifts spectral bias to accelerate learning of high-frequency geometric detail, while sparsity and orthogonality across subbands promote disentanglement and stability. This enables explicit per-subband geometry editing and cross-scene part transfer and is expected to deliver faster convergence and crisper thin structures than monolithic SDF baselines.

result.text: The paper investigates why deep RL policies remain brittle by examining whether decision boundary geometry and loss landscape sensitivities align across different states and MDPs; specifically it asks if adversarial or high-sensitivity directions are shared across environments. The key insight is that neural policies trained on distinct but related games exhibit correlated high-sensitivity directions, implying that non-robust, easily exploitable features are learned and reused across training MDPs. To support this, the authors introduce a framework to measure decision boundary and loss-landscape similarities, run experiments across multiple Atari environments from the Arcade Learning Environment, and show statistically significant correlations in perturbation directions that most affect policy outputs. This suggests that shared adversarial features are an inherent property of the training environments and points toward the need for methods that identify and mitigate such common non-robust features to build more robust RL agents.

result.text: The paper tackles whether neural networks can learn the formal semantics of linear-time temporal logic (LTL) by solving the trace generation problem: given a satisfiable LTL formula, produce a trace that satisfies it. The key insight is to treat formula-to-trace generation as a sequence translation task and leverage a Transformer model’s capacity to capture complex structured mappings, expecting it to generalize from syntactic patterns to semantic satisfaction. Methodologically, the authors train a standard Transformer on pairs of LTL formulas and satisfying traces, explore representations and hyperparameters, and evaluate on held-out formulas; after a few hours of GPU training the model outputs the exact syntactic trace 89% of the time and—crucially—produces traces that satisfy the target formula in over 99% of cases, demonstrating semantic generalization beyond noisy training labels.

The paper tackles improving graph neural networks by providing a principled multi-scale representation and pooling scheme that better preserves signal and geometry on graphs. Its key insight is that framelet (wavelet-like) decompositions separate graph signals into low- and high-frequency coefficients across scales, enabling convolutions and pooling that conserve information while isolating noise and fine-detail structure. The method defines framelet-based graph convolution and an induced pooling that aggregates low-/high-pass spectra, and introduces shrinkage as an activation that thresholds high-frequency coefficients per scale to denoise and compress signals; experiments show state-of-the-art results on node and graph prediction tasks and substantial gains in denoising and compression compared with ReLU.

result.text: The paper tackles lifelong reinforcement learning in non-stationary, non-episodic environments where standard RL fails due to the inability to plan long-horizon behavior and adapt without resets. Its key insight is that planning in an abstract skill space—using unsupervised, intrinsically rewarded skill discovery plus a learned skill-level dynamics model—enables robust, long-horizon decision-making and adaptation while reducing dependence on episodic interactions. The method, Lifelong Skill Planning (LiSP), learns temporally-extended skills from online or offline data via intrinsic objectives, trains a predictive model over skill transitions, and performs planning in this skill space to select sequences of skills that steer the agent around non-stationarity and catastrophic failures. Empirically, LiSP shows improved long-horizon control and resilience on non-episodic gridworld and MuJoCo variants by enabling skill discovery from offline data and using model-based skill planning to avoid failures.
